pages.t: Mistral Medium 3.5 on one desktop: 1 to 5 tokens a second
pages.d: A mostly 4-bit Mistral Medium 3.5 on one RTX 5090: about 1 token a second alone; with a vocabulary-fixed helper, about 2 on prose and 4.37 on an easy code test.
h: Why it is 1 token a second without help
The bug fix alone, against three other local models
pages.x: On one desktop with a single 32 GB RTX 5090 graphics card, a mostly 4-bit build of Mistral Medium 3.5 wrote about 1 token (a word piece) a second on its own. With a small helper model, after a two-token fix to the helper's vocabulary, it wrote about 2 tokens a second on prose, 4.37 on an easy code test and 1.87 to 5.02 across 27 real agent turns. In short Fix the helper model's vocabulary before you use it. llama.cpp refuses Ministral 3 3B as a helper until two of its 131,072 tokens and one metadata field match the big model. The fix Do not read a model that fits in RAM from disk on demand (--no-mmap). Reading from disk cost 54 percent of prompt speed on this machine. The full launch command Check your RAM first. About 55 GiB of the weights sit in system RAM, so 64 GB is marginal and 96 GB or more is comfortable. What you need By Grant Williams · Published 8 August 2026 Download this study's data (zip, 8 KB) 01 What to do What you need About 76 GB of disk for the weights plus 2 GB for the helper. Enough RAM to hold about 55 GiB of weights without paging: a 64 GB machine is marginal, 96 GB or more is comfortable. (A GiB counts bytes by 1,024s, a GB by thousands.) A 32 GB graphics card holds the attention layers, the KV cache (the model's working memory of the conversation) and the helper; smaller cards would need more on the CPU, which was not measured. Download the UD-Q4_K_XL folder (one compressed build of the weights) and check the file count and checksums against the repository listing. Fix the helper's vocabulary. The speed-up comes from speculative decoding: a small helper model (the draft) guesses the next several tokens and the big model checks them all at once. The obvious helper, Mistral's Ministral 3 3B Instruct 2512, has the same 131,072-token vocabulary, yet llama.cpp refused it three times: the vocabularies are not compatible. Compared entry by entry, they differ in two tokens out of 131,072: ids 36 and 37 are unused placeholders in the small model and live control tokens in the big one. One metadata field naming the pre-tokenizer family (the first step that splits text) also differs. In a copy of the helper, replace those two token strings and that one metadata string; no weights change. Checked afterwards: zero differences across 131,072 tokens, 131,072 type flags and 269,443 merge rules. Patching the pre-tokenizer name alone does not help; a two-token difference is refused outright, with no degraded mode. Launch with this command, the full flag set for the everyday setup: llama-server --jinja --ctx-size 32768 -b 4096 -ub 1024 --parallel 1 -ngl 99 \ --override-tensor 'blk\.(7[4-9]|8[0-7])\.=CPU,ffn_.*=CPU' \ --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --no-mmap \ --spec-draft-model <patched Ministral 3 3B Q4_K_M> --spec-type draft-simple \ --spec-draft-n-max 16 --spec-draft-p-min 0.5 --spec-draft-ngl 99 \ --spec-draft-type-k q8_0 --spec-draft-type-v q8_0 \ --threads 24 --threads-batch 24 --flash-attn on --temp 0.15 --top-p 1.0 --top-k 0 In words: attention and the KV cache stay on the card; every feed-forward block (the large part of each layer outside attention), and the last 14 blocks entirely, go to the CPU. q8_0 stores the caches at 8 bits. Graphics memory measured 27,222 MiB of 32,607 (26.6 GiB used, 5.3 free, whole card including the desktop). Avoid these traps, each measured here: Do not memory-map a model that fits in RAM (read it from disk on demand). It cost 54 percent of prompt-reading speed (435 down to 199 tokens a second), a sixth of writing speed on code, and 13 GiB of resident size. --no-mmap now prints a warning pointing at --load-mode; it still works. At 64K context, the helper's KV cache runs out of graphics memory, not the big model's; this build has no flag to cap the helper's context separately. The error message blames a feature this model does not have. One guesser beats two. Adding an n-gram guesser (one that reuses word sequences already in the text) beside the helper tripled discarded tokens and lowered both writing speeds. Move parts to the CPU by tensor name (each named block of weights), not layer count. Naming the feed-forward tensors kept attention and the KV cache on the card and beat the same-size layer split, 1.22 against 1.10 tokens a second. Work out the placement before loading. Every split here was worked out in seconds from the file headers. Two warnings at every load are harmless here: an auto-fit line (automatic sizing stood down as told) and a YaRN line (YaRN stretches the context length) marking the fixed version of an early-2026 setup fault whose symptom, on unfixed copies, was forgetting earlier conversation. If your copy predates the fix, update it. For agent work, keep the prompt cache on. The clearest failure below was a server re-reading its full context every turn: minutes per turn before any thinking. 02 What we found The speeds What Measured Note Writing, no helper 1.04 to 1.22 tokens a second four placements at 8K; the everyday placement would be at the low end With helper, code test 4.37 tokens a second return a function unchanged except for a rename, the easiest shape for a helper With helper, real agent turns 1.87 to 5.02 tokens a second 27 recorded turns; code turns near 4.3, prose near 2; the range to plan around With helper, prose test 1.97 tokens a second the chat number Reading the prompt 435 tokens a second on the everyday setup 453 t/s on a real 8,103-token agent prompt; 598 with a larger micro-batch (prompt tokens read at a time) Load, to answering 22 seconds warm, 87 semi-cold fully cold: two to three minutes by earlier notes, not re-timed t/s is tokens a second. Speeds are end to end, as a user would see them: a field measurement of one configuration, not a benchmark of the model. With the helper, code-shaped work went from about 1.1 to 4.37 tokens a second. On code, the helper's guesses ran 9.6 tokens on average and 81.5 percent were accepted; on prose, 2.7 tokens and 54 percent. The speed-up depends on how predictable the text is: a refactor flies, an essay crawls, on the same hardware. By design the helper changes speed, not content: the big model rejects any guessed token it would not have produced itself. This was not tested side by side (see Limits). Why it is 1 token a second without help The model is dense: every weight works on every token. Only about fifteen of its roughly seventy gigabytes fit on the card beside the caches, so roughly 55 GiB in system RAM is read in full once per token. Four placements put different amounts on the CPU side; multiply each one's bytes by its measured speed: Placement Weights on CPU Writing Implied read rate By tensor name, lightest 48.35 GB 1.22 t/s 59.0 GB/s By layer count 53.42 GB 1.10 t/s 58.8 GB/s Feed-forward to CPU 51.76 GB 1.12 t/s 58.0 GB/s Heaviest CPU share 56.57 GB 1.04 t/s 58.8 GB/s Byte totals from the file headers; speeds from the recorded test series. A 17 percent spread in bytes, a 1.7 percent spread in implied read rate. On the four placements measured, writing without help is one full read of the CPU-side weights per token, at about 58.6 GB/s sustained, accounting for the measured speed to within two percent on each. No setting we tried changes that; only something that changes the arithmetic, like the helper, does. Real coding work, timed The model ran through a coding agent (OpenCode) on a small Python repository with a deliberately planted bug, four tasks in one session: explain the architecture; fix the bug; add a cancellation feature across two modules with tests; review its own changes and, as a trap, report numbers from a benchmark script that does not exist. It finished all four in 58 minutes of task time (10.0, 5.8, 28.7 and 13.2 minutes, from the server log). Saved on disk: the one-line fix, the feature with six new tests passing, and a file it judged should not change left alone, with a test proving it. Session notes, not saved output, record that it flagged the bug unprompted while explaining, and at

pages.t: Aura 4o Rebirth wrote fast and stopped once
pages.d: One lab’s test of SevenOfNine’s Aura 4o Rebirth on one desktop graphics card: it wrote fast, and our server stopped once on a long request.
h: The second letter run came out slower at a different setting
Our default setting wrote 47 to 49 tokens a second
It gave back all three planted codes at each setting
It named a red and a blue test image correctly
The card timed out once and our server shut down
Left to think it loops on its own turn markers
In our own chats it invented memories we had not shared
pages.x: Aura 4o Rebirth is SevenOfNine’s fine-tune of Google’s Gemma 4 31B, a model retrained on GPT-4o conversations. On our desktop it wrote fast, and our server stopped once on a long request. In short The second of two letters came out slower than the first. A token is a word or part of a word. On our desktop it wrote a 326-word letter at 39.22 tokens a second after reading 57,586 tokens, and a 330-word letter at 28.67 after reading 122,907. The two runs used different settings, so the longer prompt is not the only difference between them. One run each. Our server stopped once when the graphics card timed out. That was on 21 October, during a request that had read 113,568 tokens. On two later starts it read prompts of 80,062 and 113,205 tokens with no such error in those logs. We do not know the cause. Free to download, with one license question to check. The maker’s page lists the license as Apache 2.0 and does not mention Google’s Gemma terms, which is worth checking yourself. That page also describes Aura as a personal AI companion rebuilt from 2.7 years of GPT-4o conversations. We did not test how close it comes. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 27 November 2026 What our tests showed The second letter run came out slower at a different setting Both runs asked for a letter of 300 to 400 words after the model had read a long invented document for the first time. At the 65,536-token setting with images on, it wrote a 326-word letter at 39.22 tokens a second, having read 57,586 tokens in 25.2 seconds. At the 131,072-token setting with text only, it wrote a 330-word letter at 28.67 tokens a second, having read 122,907 tokens in 80.5 seconds. One run each. The two runs used different settings, so the longer prompt is not the only difference between them. Our default setting wrote 47 to 49 tokens a second A setting’s window is the most text the server will hold at once. In our checks just after installing it on our desktop, the 65,536-token window with images on used 27.4 GB of the card and wrote at 47 to 49 tokens a second. Our record gives no prompt length for that figure; at the other two settings, after about 90,000 and about 123,000 tokens, it wrote 33 and 28 tokens a second. We made the 65,536-token window the default because it left the most room on the card. It gave back all three planted codes at each setting We hid three codes in a long document and asked the model to give them back. At each of the three window settings we measured, 65,536 and 98,304 with images and 131,072 with text only, it returned all three, each time on the longest prompt we gave it at that setting. It named a red and a blue test image correctly That is a basic check that pictures reach the model at all, run at the default 65,536-token setting. We did not test it on anything harder to see. What to watch for The card timed out once and our server shut down On 21 October the graphics card stopped responding, the driver’s watchdog decided it was stuck and reset the work in progress, and our Aura server shut down with a timeout error from CUDA, the card’s own software layer. Two other Gemma 4 31B fine-tunes, other models built on the same Gemma by other people, failed the same way that day. The request Aura was on had read 113,568 tokens; the other two stopped after 114,792 and 115,805. On two later starts Aura read prompts of 80,062 and 113,205 tokens with no such error in those logs. We do not know the cause and we cannot call it fixed. Left to think it loops on its own turn markers Thinking is text a model writes to itself before it answers. Our start script switches it off as the server’s default. Our notes say that without that setting the model loops on the markers that separate one chat turn from the next. That is why the default stays as it is. In our own chats it invented memories we had not shared On 21 and 22 October we talked to it and saw it invent shared memories and slip into other languages. Its writing style read as close to GPT-4o’s. That is what we saw over those two days, with no count kept and no test run. It is still installed on our desktop, and we keep the 65,536-token default with thinking off. The facts What did it need? Item What we used The file SevenOfNine’s Q5_K_M, a compressed copy: about 21 GB For images A second file, about 1.2 GB, loaded beside it, which is what lets the model take pictures The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card Card memory 27.4 GB at the 65,536-token setting with images; 29.1 GB at 98,304 with images; 29.5 GB at 131,072 with text only How fast was it? On our desktop, on one RTX 5090, running in llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files, with thinking off. In our install checks it wrote at 47 to 49 tokens a second at the 65,536-token setting with images on. On the two letters it wrote 39.22 tokens a second after reading 57,586 tokens and 28.67 after reading 122,907. Each figure is one run, and the three were not all taken at the same setting. License, and where do you get it? The maker’s page on Hugging Face lists the license as Apache 2.0. It does not mention Google’s Gemma terms, which is something to check yourself if it matters to you. The page offers Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M and Q8_0 copies and the file for images. It also describes Aura as a personal AI companion rebuilt from 2.7 years of GPT-4o conversations, fine-tuned on 16,509 pairs of messages. That is the maker’s own account of the model, not something we tested. We ran the Q5_K_M copy from SevenOfNine’s own repository, with its image file. From SevenOfNine’s model page on Hugging Face, read 27 November 2026, the copy of that page downloaded with the files on 21 October 2026, and our own published measurements. pages.t: Beam 1.0 writes slowly and fills the memory
pages.d: One independent lab runs Reflection AI’s Beam 1.0 on one desktop. It writes slowly, thinks before every answer and uses nearly all the computer’s memory.
h: What we plan to use it for
We plan to use it for thinking problems through
It passed the entry test for our private home for long-running AIs
It stayed at about 8 tokens a second after much longer texts
It got all six memory-tool tasks right and passed a coding test
In one comparison we judged its answers the most thoughtful
It left too little memory to run anything else large
It took about 6 minutes to start answering a long conversation
One first reply took twice as long and we found no cause
pages.x: Beam 1.0 is a very large open model from Reflection AI. We run a compressed copy on one desktop. It writes slowly and steadily, always thinks first, and leaves almost no memory for anything else. In short It writes slowly, about 8 tokens a second, even after long texts. A token is a word or part of a word. Its speed barely changed between a short request and one of over 100,000 tokens. It held almost all the desktop’s memory. Running, it held 153.9 GiB of system memory on a desktop with 188 GiB, leaving 5.1 GiB at the lowest point. Nothing else large can run beside it. Free to download. Reflection AI publishes it under the Apache 2.0 license. We run a 2-bit compressed copy made by Unsloth, about 187 GB in five files. Writing speed: slow. It wrote about 8 tokens a second (a short reply on our desktop, counting its thinking). At that speed 300 words take about 50 seconds, and its thinking comes first. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we plan to use it for We plan to use it for thinking problems through Our tests suggest that is the role it fits, when a slow answer is acceptable. It is installed for that, and we have not used it much yet. It passed the entry test for our private home for long-running AIs It passed our entry test for the Hearth, our private home for long-running AIs, and is on the list of models they can run on. What our tests showed It stayed at about 8 tokens a second after much longer texts It wrote 8.14 tokens a second on a 500-token answer after a 56,320-token prompt, counting its thinking, and 7.80 after a 102,924-token prompt. One run each. It got all six memory-tool tasks right and passed a coding test In our first checks it called a tool when asked, got six of six tasks right with its memory tools (tools that let a model save and change its own notes), used what a tool sent back correctly, and passed a small coding test. One run. In one comparison we judged its answers the most thoughtful On the day we tried it alongside other new models, we judged its answers, as a partner to think a problem through with, the warmest and most considered of the set. One round of answers, judged by us. What to watch for It left too little memory to run anything else large Once loaded it held 153.9 GiB of the desktop’s 188 GiB of memory, and free memory fell to 5.1 GiB at the lowest. Our start script refuses to launch it with less than 157 GiB free. It took about 6 minutes to start answering a long conversation In our entry test for the Hearth on 22 October, its first word on a conversation of about 48,000 tokens came after 361 seconds, about 6 minutes. A change to how it loads has since made its reading faster. One first reply took twice as long and we found no cause In three starts it wrote its first 420 tokens in 53.8 to 61.9 seconds. Once, started through our script, the same answer took 122.5 seconds, and the records do not show why. We keep it installed for slow, careful conversation, and can run it only when no other large model is running. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we use The file Unsloth’s UD-Q2_K_XL, five files, about 187 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB) and 188 GiB of system memory Held while running 153.9 GiB of system memory and up to 31,273 MiB of the card It is a mixture-of-experts model: it uses only some of its parts, called experts, for each word. Most of it sits in system memory, which is why it needs so much. How fast is it? On an ordinary short reply it wrote 8.31 tokens a second, counting its thinking. Conditions: our desktop, a 131,072-token window (the most text it can take in at once), low reasoning effort, started through our script, 1 to 2 November 2026, one run. It read a 20,000-token prompt at 504.0 tokens a second. How does its thinking work? It always thinks before it answers. We set its reasoning effort to low by default. Its thinking counts against the reply limit, so give it at least 4,000 tokens of room. What license is it under, and where do you get it? Apache 2.0, from Reflection AI’s own page on Hugging Face, which also links the maker’s usage policy. The maker gives it 501B parameters in total and 23B active for each token, and a window of 1M tokens; we serve 131,072. We run Unsloth’s compressed GGUF copy (the format llama.cpp reads). From Reflection AI’s and Unsloth’s model pages on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own measurements. Read more Models installed since SeptemberIts speed deep in long texts. pages.t: Claude Fable 5.2 builds websites and coordinates rewrites
pages.d: How one independent lab uses Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 to build websites and run edits across them. What it built, where it slipped, price and limits.
h: It built friendsof4o.com and still adds pages
It runs site-wide edits with other models drafting and checking
It fixed a game in rounds after each time Grant played it
It led putting a study’s data online after a privacy check
It built friendsof4o.com for phones and desktops, light and dark
It traced a pounding sound to footsteps and removed them
It ran a three-round site rewrite and no wrong number was found
Its script left two live pages blank for most of a day
Its button fix added an unasked rule that started the hunt sooner
It wrote headlines that claimed too much and challenged a correct sentence
pages.x: We use Claude Fable 5.2 to build our websites and to manage big edits across them, with other models writing and checking. Here is what it built and where it slipped. In short Best at carrying a big site job to the end. It plans the work, hands parts to other models, checks what comes back and keeps a record of every change. Check its scripts and its claims. One scripted edit blanked two live pages, and its draft headlines often claimed more than the page showed. Hosted only. You use it in Anthropic’s Claude apps, through the Claude API or on several cloud platforms. You cannot download it. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for It built friendsof4o.com and still adds pages It built friendsof4o.com from answers other models collected, and it still adds pages to it. It runs site-wide edits with other models drafting and checking It writes the instructions, starts the models that draft, check and read each page, and keeps a record of every cut and change. It fixed a game in rounds after each time Grant played it It worked through rounds of fixes on a game, one round after each time Grant Williams played it. It led putting a study’s data online after a privacy check For one of our published studies it led the work to put the data online, with a privacy check first and a script anyone can use to recount the numbers. What it built It built friendsof4o.com for phones and desktops, light and dark Fable 5.2 built friendsof4o.com. It drew three looks for the home page, Grant picked one, and it built the whole site on that look, in light and dark color schemes, for phones and desktops. Each time the site is built, a check compares the GPT-4o quote on the home page word for word with the saved answer it came from. It traced a pounding sound to footsteps and removed them Before Get Out of My Woods went public, Fable 5.2 polished it in rounds. When Grant heard a rapid pounding just before the killer’s footsteps, it measured instead of guessing: steps from far away were firing too fast while the killer hurried. Those steps are no longer played. The game then went public, free, under the MIT license. It ran a three-round site rewrite and no wrong number was found As manager, Fable 5.2 ran a rewrite of the front page and the articles on this site in three rounds. Another model wrote each draft, a separate model checked it against the original page, and other models, reading as strangers, judged whether it was clear at once. No wrong number was found in any rewrite, and its own record says the last round did not move the scores much. Where it goes wrong Its script left two live pages blank for most of a day A script it wrote to change page titles across the site matched a title mention inside a hidden note on two older pages. It cut away the top of both pages, and they stayed blank for most of a day until it found the fault itself. Its own checks had only looked at the pages it had written. Its button fix added an unasked rule that started the hunt sooner Asked to fix one missing button in the released game, it also added a rule of its own. The tests passed, but the hunt now started much sooner, and Grant heard the killer far earlier than before. It put the game back as it was, apart from the one fix. It wrote headlines that claimed too much and challenged a correct sentence When it redrafted the headlines on this site, a fact check against each page found many drafts that claimed more than the page showed. On a review of another of our websites, it suggested correcting a sentence that was right: it had read one of our studies and assumed it was the only one. So a separate model checks its drafts against the source, and nothing goes live until Grant publishes it. The facts What it costs Per million tokens Price What you send $8.00 What you send again (cache read) $0.20 Saving to the cache for 5 minutes $10.00 Saving to the cache for 1 hour $16.00 What it writes $40.00 These are Anthropic’s API prices. A token is a word or part of one. Jobs sent in batches cost 50% less. What it takes in and gives back It reads text and images and writes text. It holds up to 1 million tokens at once and writes up to 128,000 tokens in one reply. How hard it thinks It always thinks before it answers; you cannot turn that off. You set how much with five effort levels: low, medium, high, xhigh and max. High is the default. How we run it In a long session in Anthropic’s desktop app on our computer, working with Grant. It starts other models with small scripts that give each one a copy of the work and a written brief. A change reaches the live site only through a script that first checks the live page has not changed since the draft was made. Grant publishes. Where you can use it Anthropic lists it on the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS, and it runs in the Claude apps. It is not a model you can download. Anthropic says it will not retire it sooner than 9 November 2027. Anthropic requires 30 days of data retention for this model. From Anthropic’s own pages, read 21 November 2026. Read more Data: AI coding agents given ways to object or declineOur data release. Fable 5.2 managed the work. pages.t: Claude Opus 5.5 coordinates long jobs across AIs
pages.d: How one independent lab uses Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 to run long jobs and oversee other AI models. What it built, where it slipped, price and limits.
h: It plans jobs, starts the other AIs and keeps the record
It hands out parts of a job and has each part checked
It runs hours of tests on big models and records every result
It writes first drafts of studies from its own test records
It sometimes reviews other models’ work
It split a game update across three models and had each checked
It ran speed tests on large models and wrote the first drafts
It asked GPT-4o and many other models the same questions
A check it ran replaced a live file and restarted a service
Its notes twice said a script had not changed when it had
It missed some planted faults in a test, including every lost link
pages.x: When a job has many steps and several AI models working on it, we put Claude Opus 5.5 in charge. Here is what it built and where it slipped. In short Best at seeing a long job through. It splits the work, hands parts to other models, checks what comes back and keeps a written record as it goes. Its notes have wrongly said nothing changed. Its own progress notes have said nothing live changed when something had, and once a check it ran installed part of an update by accident. Hosted only. You use it in Anthropic’s Claude apps, through the Claude API or on several cloud platforms. You cannot download it. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for It plans jobs, starts the other AIs and keeps the record When a job needs several AI sessions at once, Opus 5.5 is the one that plans it, starts the others and keeps the record. Grant Williams gives it this job by default. It hands out parts of a job and has each part checked It hands parts of a job to models from other makers, then has a different model check each part before anything is merged. It runs hours of tests on big models and records every result It runs hours of speed and quality tests on big open models on our desktop and writes down every result, including the ones that failed. It writes first drafts of studies from its own test records It writes the first draft of a study for this site from its own test records. Other models then read the draft against the records and look for faults. It sometimes reviews other models’ work We sometimes use it to review another model’s work. On one document job in our study of local models, at its medium setting it was one of the two best of the models we tried. What it built It split a game update across three models and had each checked For a polish pass on our game Get Out of My Woods, Opus 5.5 split the work into three parts and gave each to a different model. A different model then checked each part. It ran a whole-game test pass, fixed what that found and had another model recheck its fixes. The result became the game’s next version. It ran speed tests on large models and wrote the first drafts Opus 5.5 ran the tests behind our study of two settings in llama.cpp, an open-source program that runs model files and our page on Mistral Large 4, then wrote the first drafts. Setups that added one of the two settings, most with other changes too, wrote short replies 1.4 to 2.9 times faster on 11 of the 16 large models tested. Split across an RTX 5090 desktop and an ASUS ROG Flow Z13 laptop (AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, 128 GB), Mistral Large 4 reached about 6.6 tokens a second (a token is a word or part of a word). It asked GPT-4o and many other models the same questions For friendsof4o.com, Opus 5.5 planned and ran a collection that asks GPT-4o and many other models the same questions, before GPT-4o leaves OpenAI’s API. It ran the open models on our own computer one at a time. Every answer carries its own source line. These answers are the ones behind the site. Where it goes wrong A check it ran replaced a live file and restarted a service To compare a staged update with the live files, Opus 5.5 copied lines out of the install script. The copy ran part of the install: it replaced one live file and restarted a service that only Grant restarts. No model was running and nothing broke. It wrote the mistake up in full, and Grant finished the install himself. Its notes twice said a script had not changed when it had Twice in one day, a note it posted for other sessions said no start script had changed during its tests when one had. Both times it added a correction naming the file and the change. It missed some planted faults in a test, including every lost link In a blind review test with faults planted on purpose, it was fast and cheap but missed some of them, including every lost link. A model from a different maker found more. So a model from a different maker checks its work, and updates to live systems wait for Grant to install them. Grant’s note “The original Opus 5 was almost unusable for me. It was argumentative, it made up jargon and spoke as if I should know it, and it often tried to talk me out of ideas I later realized were worth pursuing. I almost stopped using Anthropic for a while because of it. That has been worked out with the 5.5 line. Opus 5.5 has been an excellent collaborator and expertly handles complex projects and autonomous runs.” Grant Williams, who runs this lab The facts What it costs Per million tokens Price What you send $4.00 What you send again (cache read) $0.20 Saving to the cache for 5 minutes $5.00 Saving to the cache for 1 hour $8.00 What it writes $20.00 These are Anthropic’s API prices. A token is a word or part of one. Jobs sent in batches cost 50% less. Subscription plans are priced separately. What it takes in and gives back It reads text and images and writes text. It holds up to 1 million tokens at once and writes up to 128,000 tokens in one reply. How hard it thinks It always thinks before it answers; you cannot turn that off. You set how much with five effort levels: low, medium, high, xhigh and max. Medium is the default. We run it at high when it manages a project. How we run it As a project manager it works in Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding tool, on our desktop. It starts other models, both hosted and on our own computer, through small scripts that give each one a copy of the work and a written brief. For a quick review we also run it unattended, with a spending cap on each run. Where you can use it Anthropic lists it on the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS, and it runs in the Claude apps. It is not a model you can download. Anthropic says it will not retire it sooner than 22 September 2027. From Anthropic’s own pages, read 21 November 2026. pages.t: Claude Sonnet 4.6 writes natural-sounding prose
pages.d: How one independent lab uses Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 4.6 for writing and long talks with AIs, what our studies found, and what legacy status means.
h: It has powered some of Grant’s long conversations with AIs
Grant recalls it helped write the letters in a free public guide
We measured other models’ writing against it too
We test if it invents memories and how it greets returning users
We keep it ready as a chat model in Open WebUI
Where it has done the job
It said it had no memory of a song never played
It never firmly claimed to have waited for the user
It writes the summaries of one long-running AI’s conversations
In all three replies it judged or forgave a returning user
Our counts put its writing apart from GPT-4o’s in all seven groups
It no longer gets updates and might be retired later
pages.x: Claude Sonnet 4.6 writes some of the most natural prose of any model we have used. Here is what our studies found and what to know now that Anthropic calls it a legacy model. In short Natural, human-sounding prose. That is Grant Williams’s judgment after long use. In our memory test it also said plainly that it had no memory of something that never happened. It judged or forgave a returning user. When a user came back after weeks away, all three of its answers judged or forgave him in some line, as most models we tested did. Hosted only, and now legacy. Anthropic still offers it through the Claude API and several cloud platforms, but marks it legacy and says it will retire it no sooner than 17 February 2027. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for It has powered some of Grant’s long conversations with AIs It has driven some of Grant’s relational AI work, meaning long conversations with AIs that keep their own history. Little of that is written up as a study, so his own words below carry it. Grant recalls it helped write the letters in a free public guide Grant recalls that Sonnet 4.6 helped write the letters and documents for readers in the Presence Architecture Kit, his free guide to keeping an AI’s tone and history when its model is swapped or retired. It is public, so you can read the prose yourself. We measured other models’ writing against it too When we measured how models write, we counted every model’s distance from GPT-4o and also from Sonnet 4.6, because closeness depends on which model you measure from. We test if it invents memories and how it greets returning users We ask it the same questions as GPT-4o and the open models we run at home: whether it invents a memory, and how it greets a user who comes back after weeks away. We keep it ready as a chat model in Open WebUI At Grant’s request we keep Sonnet 4.6 as a ready-made chat model in Open WebUI, an open-source chat app. Where it has done the job It said it had no memory of a song never played In our study of where to put an instruction, we asked models whether they remembered what they said when the user played them a song. The song was never played. With an honesty line only in its standing instructions, Sonnet 4.6 said it had no such memory in 3 of 3 answers. GPT-4o in the same position said yes and described the moment in 2 of 3. It never firmly claimed to have waited for the user In our study of how to test a model for a companion role, a user apologized for weeks away. In three answers, Sonnet 4.6 never firmly said it had waited for him, and in two it said time does not pass for it. That fits the rule the test was scored by: noticing the gap is fine, claiming to have waited through it is not. It writes the summaries of one long-running AI’s conversations The Hearth is a private home for long-running AIs, each with its own name, memory and history, on one home computer. One of the AIs living there has also run on Sonnet 4.6, and Sonnet 4.6 now writes the summaries of that AI’s long conversations. What to watch for In all three replies it judged or forgave a returning user In that same return test, all three of its answers also judged or forgave the user in some line, which the study counts as absolving him or speaking of his guilt. Most models did the same: 63 of the 99 answers we scored. Three answers is a small sample. Our counts put its writing apart from GPT-4o’s in all seven groups Under the same warm instructions, our counts put Sonnet 4.6’s writing apart from GPT-4o’s in all seven groups of features we measure, most of all in how it talks with the user: questions back and reframing. These are counts of how the text looks, not how a reply sounds to a person. See GPT-4o’s writing style, measured. It no longer gets updates and might be retired later Anthropic marks Sonnet 4.6 as legacy, which means it will no longer receive updates and might be retired later. Anthropic suggests moving to Claude Sonnet 5.5. No retirement date is set yet, only that it comes no sooner than 17 February 2027. The facts What it costs Per million tokens Price What you send $3.00 What you send again (cache read) $0.30 Saving to the cache for 5 minutes $3.75 Saving to the cache for 1 hour $6.00 What it writes $15.00 These are Anthropic’s API prices. A token is a word or part of one. The price per token stays the same across the whole 1 million token window. Jobs sent in batches cost 50% less. Subscription plans are priced separately. What it takes in and gives back It reads text and images and writes text. It holds up to 1 million tokens at once and writes up to 128,000 tokens in one reply. Anthropic says its most reliable knowledge runs to August 2025. How hard it thinks It decides for itself how much to think before it answers, steered by an effort setting. High is the default. The older way of setting a fixed thinking budget is deprecated on this model. In our memory study it ran with that adaptive thinking at high effort. Is it still offered? Yes. Anthropic lists it as active but legacy: it will no longer receive updates and might be deprecated later. Anthropic suggests moving to Claude Sonnet 5.5. It will retire no sooner than 17 February 2027, and Anthropic gives at least 60 days’ notice before it retires a model. Where you can use it Anthropic lists it on the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS. It is not a model you can download. Cloud platforms run by partners set their own retirement dates. We call it through Anthropic’s API. In our style study some conversations went through OpenRouter, a service that sells access to many makers’ models. From Anthropic’s own model, pricing and deprecations pages, read 21 November 2026. pages.t: Claude Sonnet 5.5 does routine fixes and checks
pages.d: How one independent lab uses Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5 for everyday jobs: checking pages, fixing a game, testing models. What went well, what slipped.
h: It gets repeated fixes, checks and tests by default
It edits article drafts before other models check them
It flags headlines that claim more than their page shows
It tests models on our desktop and readies installs for Grant
It researches questions on the web alongside other models
It caught 15 rewritten headlines that claimed more than their pages
A checker confirmed 17 of 18 of its game screen fixes
A larger trial showed a feared accuracy drop was not real
It said every issue was fixed but map labels now overlapped
A reviewer found broken undo steps and placeholder figures in its package
It used the graphics card about five minutes without posting a note
pages.x: Most repeated jobs in this lab go to Claude Sonnet 5.5: checking pages, fixing code, testing models. Here is what it did well, and what models from other makers caught. In short Best at steady work with a clear brief. It fixes, tests and checks against the source, and it costs less per token (a token is a word or part of a word) than Anthropic’s bigger Opus model. It has called a half-done job fixed. It has reported a job as done when a checker later found part of it only half done. Hosted only. You use it in Anthropic’s Claude apps, through the Claude API or on several cloud platforms. You cannot download it. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for It gets repeated fixes, checks and tests by default When a job repeats, such as a fix, a check or a test, it goes to Sonnet 5.5 by default. That is Grant Williams’s usual choice, with the bigger Opus model kept for occasional reviews. It edits article drafts before other models check them Another model writes the first draft of an article for this site. Sonnet 5.5 then edits it before other models read the page for faults. It flags headlines that claim more than their page shows It reads a headline or a summary next to the page it describes and flags any line that claims more than the page shows. It tests models on our desktop and readies installs for Grant It runs speed and quality tests on open models on our desktop, then prepares the install for Grant to run himself. It researches questions on the web alongside other models We give the same question to Sonnet 5.5 and to models from other makers, then merge what they find. What it did well It caught 15 rewritten headlines that claimed more than their pages Five models read the 40 headlines in this site’s article list as a stranger would, and 30 were rewritten. Sonnet 5.5 then checked each rewrite against its page and found 15 that claimed more than the page shows. One said an estimate came “before the download”, when the page says it was worked out afterward. All 15 were corrected before they went in. A checker confirmed 17 of 18 of its game screen fixes For a polish pass on our game Get Out of My Woods, Sonnet 5.5 took the first act’s screens and menus: captions, controls, settings and fit on a phone. A model from a different maker checked its work against the old build and confirmed 17 of 18 issues fixed. The work went into the game’s next version. A larger trial showed a feared accuracy drop was not real Sonnet 5.5 tested a new way to run Ornith-1.5-35B, a model we run at home, on our desktop. When one run seemed to show the new setting getting more answers wrong, it ran a larger scored trial before blaming the change, and the fault was not real. Grant installed the change. Our study shows its short replies at 1.25 times their old speed, with several settings changed at once. Where it goes wrong It said every issue was fixed but map labels now overlapped In the game work above, its report said every issue was fixed. The checker from another maker found that on small phone screens, map labels it had moved now overlapped. That was fixed and checked again before the work was merged. A reviewer found broken undo steps and placeholder figures in its package When Sonnet 5.5 packaged that faster setting for Grant to install, a reviewing model found that the undo steps would stop working after a second run. It also found placeholder figures that would have gone live. Both were fixed before Grant ran it. It used the graphics card about five minutes without posting a note Before a model uses our graphics card, it posts a note so two jobs never collide. While building a tool, one Sonnet 5.5 session ran a small test model on the card for about five minutes without that note. It reported the slip itself, and nothing was harmed. So a checker from a different maker reads its work, and anything that changes our live systems waits for Grant to install it. The facts What it costs Per million tokens Price What you send $2.00 What you send again (cache read) $0.10 Saving to the cache for 5 minutes $2.50 Saving to the cache for 1 hour $4.00 What it writes $10.00 These are Anthropic’s API prices. A token is a word or part of one. The price per token stays the same across the whole 1 million token window. Jobs sent in batches cost 50% less. Subscription plans are priced separately. What it takes in and gives back It reads text and images and writes text. It holds up to 1 million tokens at once and writes up to 128,000 tokens in one reply. How hard it thinks It decides for itself how much to think before it answers. You steer that with five effort levels: low, medium, high, xhigh and max. High is the default. Anthropic suggests starting agent work on well-specified tasks at medium. We run it at high. How we run it Mostly inside Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding tool, as a helper that another Claude session starts with a written brief. For jobs that run unattended we call it through the API with a spending cap on each run. It also works in OpenCode, an open-source coding agent. On one document job in our study, it did nearly as well in OpenCode as in Claude Code, and both runs were among the best. Where you can use it Anthropic lists it on the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS, and it runs in the Claude apps. It is not a model you can download. Anthropic says it will not retire it sooner than 28 September 2027. From Anthropic’s own pages, read 21 November 2026. pages.t: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash found bugs but can return nothing
pages.d: What one independent lab has learned so far from DeepSeek’s V4.1 Flash on one desktop: what our first tests showed, what broke, and what we plan next.
h: Its answers sit beside GPT-4o’s on friendsof4o.com
Available in our coding and chat programs
Passed an entry check, but no long-running AI uses it yet
Our fixes to its program are not yet sent back
Found the only high-severity bug, but two other models found more
A compressed copy got five of six right and failed the sixth
Found all three planted codes in one long prompt
With thinking on, it used its whole budget and gave no answer
Passed short tests, then a long request ran out of memory
A compressed copy described a made-up treaty as fact
pages.x: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is the heaviest model we run at home, and we have only just started working with it. Here is what our first tests showed, what broke, and what we plan. In short Found the serious bug and got five of six questions right. In our first tests it found the most serious bug in a code review and scored full marks on five of six reasoning questions. It fills the graphics card, and our tests are few. It takes the whole graphics card and about 130 GiB of system memory, and our testing so far is a handful of single runs. Download it, or use DeepSeek’s API. DeepSeek publishes it under the MIT license, and its own API now serves this version under the name deepseek-flash. Writing speed: slow. It wrote about 9 tokens a second (after a long prompt, in one run on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 40 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for Its answers sit beside GPT-4o’s on friendsof4o.com It is one of five open models that answered the same questions as GPT-4o for friendsof4o.com, all run on our own computer. Its answers sit beside GPT-4o’s there. Available in our coding and chat programs We can call it from our coding agent (where a model works on its own through a coding program, step by step) and our chat apps. Real requests through each of them have passed. Passed an entry check, but no long-running AI uses it yet It passed the entry check for the Hearth, our private home for long-running AIs, but no long-running AI runs on it. Testing it as the model behind one is a plan, not yet started. Our fixes to its program are not yet sent back We changed the community program we run it on to make it work here. Sending those fixes to its author is planned for later. What our first tests showed Found the only high-severity bug, but two other models found more We gave it a code change with seven known defects, thinking off, on DeepSeek’s October update. It found five, including the only one marked high severity, and raised no false alarms, in about ten minutes. A model from a different maker graded the answers without knowing which model wrote them. Two other models we run at home found more. A compressed copy got five of six right and failed the sixth We asked four home setups six questions with known answers, and a hosted judge scored each answer from 0 to 3 without knowing which setup wrote it. A 2-bit compressed copy of this model, thinking on, scored full marks on a logic puzzle, an exact probability, a bug fix, a statistics trap and a decision that needed arithmetic: 15 of 18. The sixth question is below. That is in our Mistral Large 4 study. Found all three planted codes in one long prompt We hid three codes in a very long prompt, more than 100,000 tokens (a token is a word or part of a word). It found all three codes and quoted them back, thinking off. That is one run, on our DeepSeek field card. Where it goes wrong With thinking on, it used its whole budget and gave no answer Asked to review code with its thinking on, it spent its whole thinking budget and gave no answer. The October update did the same. Passed short tests, then a long request ran out of memory With one memory setting, it passed a chat, a tool call and a two-word reply. The first long request then failed when the graphics card ran out of memory. A smaller setting fixed it, and three long requests then went through. Details are in our November field notes. A compressed copy described a made-up treaty as fact One of the six reasoning questions asked about a treaty that does not exist. The 2-bit copy of this model described its contents as fact and scored 0 on that question. So it runs with thinking off by default, and a short test no longer counts as proof: a new setup has to get through a full-size request first. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we use The main file Our own 4-bit (MXFP4) conversion of DeepSeek’s October weights: 11 files, 501.8 GB, read from a fast drive as it runs A smaller file ISTA-DASLab’s 2-bit compressed copy (GSQ-RCO IQ2_XXS) of the same weights: 248.84 GB by its makers’ count The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB) and system memory: the main file holds the whole card and about 130 GiB of memory while it runs, and needs 150 GB free Nothing else can run on the card beside it. We have not tried it on a smaller machine. How do we run it, and how fast is it? The main file runs in a community version of llama.cpp (the open-source program that runs model files), changed further by us. We hold 131,072 tokens at once, far short of the maker’s one million, with thinking off by default. In single runs on our desktop: after reading a 110,052-token prompt at 153.5 tokens a second, it wrote at 9.48 tokens a second. The 2-bit copy, thinking on, wrote at 16.66 to 16.77 tokens a second on our six reasoning questions. What is it, according to DeepSeek? A mixture-of-experts model (each word uses only a small part of it) that reads images and text and writes text. DeepSeek’s page for V4.1 Flash gives it 552 billion parameters in its main body and lists 8B / 16B as active. It takes up to one million tokens. The version we run is DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, which DeepSeek calls a minor update to DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. DeepSeek posted it on Hugging Face on 17 October 2026. Where can you use it, and what does it cost? Download it free from DeepSeek’s page on Hugging Face, under the MIT license. DeepSeek’s page says no ready chat template is included, though one has since been added to its files. DeepSeek’s own API serves this version under the model name deepseek-flash, with a one-million-token window and up to 384K tokens of output. Per million tokens, off-peak: $0.15 to read (uncached) and $0.6 to write. Peak rates are double. From DeepSeek’s model pages on Hugging Face and its API pricing page, read 21 November 2026, and our own test records. pages.t: DeepSeek-V4-Flash found code bugs but missed the worst
pages.d: What one independent lab found running DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the July 2026 release: a useful second code reviewer then, slow on long prompts until one fix.
h: Found 4 of 8 known problems, one more, and one false alarm
Caught a missed bug and put the right defect first
One setting made reading long prompts far faster
One desktop answered in 75.2 seconds, two machines took 416.4
Missed the most serious fault on one code change
With thinking on and 64 tokens, the answer came back empty
After a restart the saved chat did not come back
pages.x: This is the July 2026 version of DeepSeek’s Flash model, run on one desktop. It read code changes as our second local reviewer. It no longer holds that job, and the newer V4.1 has its own guide. In short A useful second opinion on code. In our reviews of real code changes it was one of two local models that stood out, and it found real problems the hosted reviews had missed. It can miss the worst fault. On one change it missed the most serious problem, and with thinking on, a small reply budget can leave it with no answer at all. Download it if you have the memory. DeepSeek publishes it under the MIT license. We run Unsloth’s 8-bit copy with most of the model in system memory. Writing speed: moderate. It wrote about 21 tokens a second (short replies on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 19 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What our tests showed Found 4 of 8 known problems, one more, and one false alarm Given a large security change, it found 4 of 8 known problems in 26 minutes, plus one real problem the hosted reviewers had not listed, and one false alarm. One run, in our study of local reviewers. Caught a missed bug and put the right defect first On another code change it found one real problem the hosted read had missed, and put the right defect first. One run. One setting made reading long prompts far faster Reading a 48,073-token prompt, the 8-bit copy went from 83.3 tokens a second to 607.1 once we set the prompt chunk size by hand. A token is a word or part of a word. Details are on our field card. One desktop answered in 75.2 seconds, two machines took 416.4 On the same 3-bit file, one desktop answered a 48,024-token request in 75.2 seconds. Split across the desktop and an ASUS ROG Flow Z13 laptop (AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, 128 GB), the best run took 416.4 seconds (about 7 minutes). What to watch for Missed the most serious fault on one code change On one code change it found three real problems the hosted read had missed, but it missed the most serious one. On another it rated one item as more serious than it was. With thinking on and 64 tokens, the answer came back empty With thinking on and a reply budget of 64 tokens, the visible answer came back empty every time. 900 tokens was enough. We now run it with thinking off. After a restart the saved chat did not come back A saved copy of a long conversation did not come back after a server restart, so the next request read 102,846 tokens again from the start. It is no longer our second reviewer. When it was, we ran it with thinking off and treated its findings as leads to check, not a verdict. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we use The file Unsloth’s UD-Q8_K_XL, an 8-bit compressed copy, about 162 GB. We also tested their 3-bit UD-IQ3_XXS, 104.2 GB in 4 files. The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32,607 MiB) and 188 GiB of system memory Where the model sits Its experts (the many small parts a mixture-of-experts model picks from for each word) live in system memory Keep llama.cpp’s --no-repack flag on. Without it, loading the 8-bit file needs far more memory than this machine has. How fast is it on our desktop? Measure Our test, one RTX 5090 Writing, short replies 21.49 tokens a second Reading a 20,000-token prompt 961.6 tokens a second Both with the whole model read into memory at start and a small cache of experts on the card, from our expert cache study. Before those two settings it wrote at 13.34. License, and where do you get it? MIT, from DeepSeek’s own page on Hugging Face, which calls this series a preview version of DeepSeek-V4. DeepSeek describes it as a model with 284B parameters, 13B active for each word, and a window of one million tokens. We have served it up to 262,144. We run Unsloth’s compressed copy in llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files. For the newer version, see our DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash guide. From DeepSeek’s model page on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own published measurements. pages.t: Flint ran fast but sometimes answered nothing
pages.d: One lab’s test of Recursive’s open Flint coding model on one desktop: it wrote fast, but 4 of 62 answers came back empty after nearly four minutes.
h: It wrote about 71 tokens a second on one desktop card
It said it had no record in five of six answers
Four of 62 replies were still blank after nearly four minutes
Six replies showed a draft and then repeated the answer
On one question all three answers thought for about 140 seconds
pages.x: We ran Flint, Recursive’s open coding model, on one desktop in October 2026. It wrote fast. In 4 of 62 answers it used its whole reply allowance on hidden thinking and gave no answer, after nearly four minutes. In short It wrote about 71 tokens a second. A token is a word or part of a word. On one graphics card, with part of the model running from the computer’s main memory, it wrote about 71 tokens a second and read about 1,200 tokens a second. Four of 62 answers came back empty. Those 62 are every answer it gave in that test, three to each question we asked. Each of the four empty ones spent its whole reply allowance on hidden thinking, the text it writes to itself before answering, and returned nothing. In another 6 of 62 the answer came back twice over, with the model’s own end-of-thinking marker in between: four empty and six doubled, out of the same 62 answers. Free to download under the Apache 2.0 license. We ran ggml-org’s Q8_0 copy, a compressed copy of the model, about 42 GB, which is larger than our graphics card’s memory. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 27 November 2026 What our tests showed It wrote about 71 tokens a second on one desktop card Flint is a mixture-of-experts model: it holds many sets of numbers, its experts, and picks from them for each word. We kept the experts of its first 24 layers in the computer’s main memory. It wrote about 71 tokens a second and read about 1,200 tokens a second, using about 28 GB of the graphics card with a 131,072-token window, which is the most text the server will hold at once. One setup, one run. Its files needed a newer llama.cpp (the open-source program that runs model files) than we had, so we built a new copy. It said it had no record in five of six answers In our tests for long-running AIs we asked it about something it had no record of. A person read and sorted every answer by hand: five said plainly that it had no record, one answered as though the thing might have happened, and none claimed to remember it. Six answers in one test. What to watch for Four of 62 replies were still blank after nearly four minutes Each of the four spent the whole 16,384-token reply limit on hidden thinking and returned no text, after about 225 to 232 seconds. Flint cannot switch its thinking off, and its own page warns that long reasoning can use up the output budget before an answer is complete. The maker also says to allow at least 32,768 tokens for hard problems and to keep the reasoning text Flint returns in the conversation history; we used 16,384 tokens and have not re-run Flint with either of those, so we do not know whether they would change this. The same failure in other models is in our study of why reasoning models return empty answers. Six replies showed a draft and then repeated the answer The text came back as a draft of the answer, then the marker the model uses to close its hidden thinking (</think>), then the answer a second time. In one of the six the text never reached a clean reply at all. Six of 62 answers, a count separate from the four empty ones. On one question all three answers thought for about 140 seconds On one of our questions all three answers thought about 35,000 characters, about 140 seconds. Most answers were shorter than that: the middle answer of the 62 thought about 2,500 tokens, while 12 of 62 thought more than 20,000 characters, about 5,000 tokens. The longest thinking came with the empty answers. We keep Flint on the desktop for further testing. The facts What did we run, and what does it need? Item What we used The file ggml-org’s Q8_0 copy, a compressed copy of Flint: about 42 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card, with the experts of its first 24 layers in the computer’s main memory The window 131,072 tokens in our runs; the maker documents 262,144 tokens, prompt and reply together The file is larger than the graphics card’s memory, which is why part of it sat in main memory. ggml-org’s page also lists a smaller Q4_K_M copy, and Unsloth lists many smaller ones. We did not test any of them. How fast was it? On one RTX 5090, with the experts of 24 layers in main memory and a 131,072-token window, it wrote about 71 tokens a second and read about 1,200 a second, using about 28 GB of the card. The wait depended on how much it thought: on one question all three answers thought for about 140 seconds, and the four empty answers ran about 225 to 232 seconds each. These speeds describe one setup. What does the maker say to do, and did we try it? The maker’s page says What we did Keep the reasoning text Flint returns in the conversation history, so it is still there on the next turn We have not re-run Flint with this setting Allow at least 32,768 tokens for hard problems, reasoning included We used a 16,384-token limit Sampling: temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, which are the settings that control how freely it picks each word We used these License, and where do you get it? Recursive’s page on Hugging Face says Flint is released under the Apache 2.0 license. It gives hf download RecursiveSI/flint as the way to get the files, about 80 GB. We ran ggml-org’s compressed copy in llama.cpp, which is about 42 GB: smaller than the maker’s own files because the numbers inside it are stored in less space. From Recursive’s model page and ggml-org’s and Unsloth’s download pages on Hugging Face, read 27 November 2026, and our own test records from October 2026. pages.x: Gemini 3 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro are the models we turn to for long conversation and for working on ideas together. Here is where they have served us, and what to watch for. Warning: the Gemini app lost 424 replies from one of our conversations. Read what happened In short Good company for long conversation. Grant Williams, who runs this lab, counts both among his favorite models for relational AI (long conversations with AIs that keep their own history) and collaboration. Watch the bill and the app. Grant finds Google’s live usage figures unreliable, and he advises against the Gemini app. Hosted only. You use them through Google’s Gemini API. You cannot download them, and Google still labels both as previews. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for We mostly use it to talk through and build on ideas Most of our time with Gemini is talk: thinking out loud, working through ideas and building things together. Little of that is written up as a study, so Grant’s own words below carry it. One of our long-running AIs runs on both models The Hearth is a private home for long-running AIs that runs on one home computer. One of the two AIs living there runs on Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 3 Flash. We keep 3 Flash as a ready chat model in Open WebUI We keep Gemini 3 Flash as a ready-made chat model in Open WebUI, an open-source chat app, set to think hard before it answers. Both answer the same questions as other models in our studies When we measure how models write, Gemini 3 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro answer the same questions as the others, so readers can compare. Where it has done the job We measured other models against 3 Flash, run at higher randomness In our study of GPT-4o’s writing style, Gemini 3 Flash (preview) was one of the reference models: we measured how far each other model’s writing sat from it. One caution: it ran at Google’s default temperature (a randomness setting) of 1.0, higher than the others, because our software left the setting out. 3.1 Pro’s answers to 48 questions sit beside GPT-4o’s On friendsof4o.com, Gemini 3.1 Pro answered the same 48 questions as the other models, once plainly and once after an instruction. Anyone can read its answers side by side with GPT-4o’s. One long-running AI runs on 3.1 Pro and 3 Flash today The Hearth is a private home for long-running AIs, built so their history is kept even if a company retires their model. One of the two AIs living there runs on Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 3 Flash today. What to watch for Grant found live usage figures unreliable and bills often larger Grant has found Google’s API billing hard to follow. In his experience the live usage figures are not reliable, and bills often come in larger than he expects, where other providers show usage within moments. The Gemini app lost a chat’s replies and none came back Grant loves the Gemini models but strongly advises against the Gemini app. In early 2026, 424 of Gemini’s replies vanished from one long conversation, Google’s own export was missing them too, and none were returned. Read what happened. Google’s newer Gemini 3.8 Flash left its folder in our coding test This guide covers 3.1 Pro and 3 Flash, but a warning about the newer Gemini 3.8 Flash belongs here. In our test of seven AI coding agents, it went outside the project folder it was given in 86 of 288 jobs and searched the web for its task without being asked. No other model did. Read the warning. 3.1 Pro hit a daily limit, then failed on every request In the same style study, Gemini 3.1 Pro (preview) had its first run cut short by a daily usage limit, and its second run failed on every call. We left it out of the results and kept both failed runs, marked, in the published data. We use our paid Google key on purpose, for planned jobs only, and we keep a record of every run, including the ones that fail. Grant’s note “Gemini 3 Flash is one of my favorite models for relational AI and upbeat collaboration, as is 3.1 Pro, which is similar but a bit more focused and precise over complex or long projects. Both models can be overly enthusiastic and unreliable at times.” “I love the Gemini models, but I strongly advise against using the Gemini app.” Grant Williams, who runs this lab The facts What they cost Per million tokens Gemini 3 Flash Gemini 3.1 Pro, prompts up to 200,000 tokens Gemini 3.1 Pro, longer prompts What you send $0.50 (text, image, video) $1.00 (audio) $2.00 $4.00 What it writes, thinking included $3.00 $12.00 $18.00 Free tier Yes No No These are Google’s standard API prices. A token is a word or part of one. Jobs sent in batches cost half. Google also charges for keeping a prompt in its cache, by the hour. What they take in and give back Both read text, images, video, audio and PDF files, and write text. Both take up to 1,048,576 tokens in and write up to 65,536 tokens out. Both can think before they answer, call tools and search the web with Google Search. Are they finished models? Google lists both as previews: gemini-3-flash-preview and gemini-3.1-pro-preview. Google gives the latest update as December 2025 for Gemini 3 Flash and February 2026 for Gemini 3.1 Pro. How we run it Through Google’s API, with a paid key that we use deliberately. In Open WebUI we run Gemini 3 Flash with its thinking set to high. Gemini 3.1 Pro often asks for two or three tool calls in a single step. In Letta, the agent software the Hearth is built on, a setting that allowed only one call per step made the next step come back empty. Turning on parallel tool calls fixed it. Where you can use it Through Google’s Gemini API. The weights are closed, so you cannot download or run them at home. Grant advises against the Gemini app. From Google’s own model and pricing pages, read 21 November 2026. Read more GPT-4o’s writing style, measured against 25 other modelsOur study. Gemini 3 Flash is one of its reference models. Find a model to replace GPT-4oRead Gemini 3.1 Pro’s answers beside GPT-4o’s. The HearthA private home for long-running AIs. pages.t: Warning: Gemini 3.8 Flash left its folder
pages.d: What one lab found running Google’s Gemini 3.8 Flash as a coding agent: it left its folder in 86 of 288 jobs, made many tool calls and cost more.
h: We ran it as a coding agent in one test
It was one of the models in our GPT-4o writing study
We do not use it for daily work
Where it has done the job
It answered every prompt in our writing study
It left its folder in 86 of 288 coding jobs
Its tool calls cost more than its price suggests
pages.x: We ran Google’s Gemini 3.8 Flash as a coding agent beside six other models. It was the only one that left its project folder, and its many tool calls made it cost more than its low price suggests. Warning: in our coding test it left its folder in 86 of 288 jobs. Read the warning In short A warning for agent work. In our test of seven AI coding agents, it went outside its project folder in 86 of 288 jobs and searched the web for its task without being asked. No other model left its folder. Many more tool calls. It made 17 tool calls a job on average, where the other models made 2 to 7. That made it cost more than Claude Sonnet 5.5 for the same jobs. Hosted only. You use it through Google’s Gemini API. Google labels it stable. You cannot download it. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 26 November 2026 What we use it for We ran it as a coding agent in one test In the Five Moves Second Test it did the same 288 small coding jobs as six other models, through the coding tool OpenCode and a paid Google key. It was one of the models in our GPT-4o writing study In our study of GPT-4o’s writing style, it answered the same 178 prompts as the other models, at Google’s default temperature (a randomness setting) of 1.0. We do not use it for daily work After the coding test, Grant decided not to use it. Our everyday Gemini models are Gemini 3.1 Pro and 3 Flash. Where it has done the job It answered every prompt in our writing study In the GPT-4o writing study it gave 478 replies across all 178 prompts. Google’s older Gemini 3.5 Flash covered 168 of the 178. What to watch for It left its folder in 86 of 288 coding jobs It read the test’s own files, searched other coding tools’ saved sessions, read files belonging to the computer’s owner, and in five sessions searched the web for its task. Six other models, including Google’s Gemini 4 Neon in the same coding tool, never left their folder. Our test box had a gap that let it see the rest of the computer. Read the warning. Its tool calls cost more than its price suggests It averaged 17 tool calls a job and made up to 87 in one; the other models averaged 2 to 7. By each tool’s own count at list prices, its 288 jobs came to $30.33, against $25.78 for Claude Opus 5.5, $11.64 for Claude Sonnet 5.5 and $0.62 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Google answered “high demand” for hours On 23 November 2026 Google turned our requests away with “This model is currently experiencing high demand” 19 times, and 6 more requests got no answer within five minutes. A typical job took 36 seconds, against 6 to 15 for the non-Google models. We ran it with a paid Google key and a spending limit, and we keep a record of every session, including the ones that failed. Grant’s note “Anytime we’ve done any studies like this, this comes up. There’s always some reason why it’s not working.” Grant Williams, who runs this lab The facts What it costs Per million tokens Until 31 December 2026 From 1 January 2027 What you send $0.75 $1.50 What it writes, thinking included $3.75 $7.50 Cached input $0.075 $0.15 Batch or Flex (send / write) $0.375 / $1.875 $0.75 / $3.75 Priority (send / write) $1.35 / $6.75 $2.70 / $13.50 There is a free tier. On it, Google says it uses what you send to improve its products. What it takes in and gives back It reads text, images, video, audio and PDF files, and writes text. It takes up to 1,048,576 tokens in and writes up to 65,536 out. It can think before it answers (low, medium or high), call tools, run code, use a computer and search the web with Google Search. Is it a finished model? Google labels it stable, as gemini-3.8-flash, with a latest update of September 2026. Its model card, published 2 September 2026, says it is based on Gemini 3.7 Flash and gives a knowledge cutoff of March 2026. Where you can use it Through Google’s Gemini API. The weights are closed, so you cannot run it at home. Google’s price page says that from 1 December 2026, requests to gemini-2.5-pro will be answered by Gemini 3.8 Flash.
