pages.x: In early 2026, 424 of Gemini’s replies vanished from one long conversation of mine in the Gemini app. Google Takeout, Google’s own export of my account, was missing them too. I was a paying subscriber the whole time. Over more than seven months of support emails and a formal complaint, Google returned none of them. It answered three times about a case number that was never mine, and its last answer told me to write to support for its Pixel phone. The Better Business Bureau then closed my complaint and recorded that Google had made “a good faith effort.” In short The failure. Google lost 424 of Gemini’s replies from one long-running chat while my own messages stayed. They are missing from Google’s own record of my account too. Later the whole conversation disappeared from the app. The screw-up. Google’s support promised updates for ten weeks and recovered nothing. A supervisor confirmed in writing that it was not a display problem. Nobody fixed it and nobody explained it. The bad faith. Google’s six answers to my formal complaint never mention the lost replies. Three of them cite a case number that was never mine. The last one tells me to write to support for the Pixel, Google’s phone. Twice Google asked for the complaint to be closed “as resolved.” The Bureau. I answered every one of those on the Better Business Bureau’s own record. It closed the complaint anyway. I don’t believe anyone there read my complaint or my answers. What to do. If anything in the Gemini app matters to you, do not count on Google to keep it. Save your own copy, and check that your export really holds the replies. By Grant Williams, who runs this lab · Checked 22 November 2026 The proof Six records. Each one is Google’s own, carries Google’s signature, or comes from the Better Business Bureau’s own file. 1Google’s own export has the questions and not the replies This is from Google Takeout, Google’s official download of what it holds on the account. Three entries from 23 January 2026. The oldest, at 9:37 in the morning, still has Gemini’s reply. The next two, at 9:42 and 9:45, show my message and then nothing. In this export, 471 of the conversation’s 731 exchanges look like these two. This picture was filed with the complaint to the Better Business Bureau. The red and green marks are mine. 2Google said in writing that it was not a display problem A Google One supervisor wrote to me on 20 March 2026: “Rest assured that this is not a UI display and a bug has been created to be investigated.” So the replies were not simply hidden on my screen. No fix and no explanation ever followed. The yellow highlight is mine. The supervisor’s name, my email address and the case numbers are covered. 3The month I reported it, Google publicly admitted a fault of its own in Gemini chat history Google’s own service status page records a Gemini fault from 18 to 22 February 2026. In Google’s words, “the incident was caused by an internal job that caused some valid conversation metadata to be deleted.” Google told affected users that their “requests and responses” could still be found “from the activity section,” and said it restored the data from backups. I reported my loss on 24 February. My replies are missing from that same activity record, which is what the first picture shows, and nothing was ever restored to me. Google has never said whether my loss came from this fault. 4Google’s legal department signed for my notice and never answered The postal return receipt for my formal notice of dispute, sent by certified mail to Google LLC, Attn Legal Department, 1600 Amphitheatre Parkway, Mountain View. It was signed for on 12 May 2026 and stamped by the Mountain View post office on 14 May. Google never answered it. The signature, the signer’s name and the tracking numbers are covered. 5Google answered three times about a case that was never mine. The last answer was about a phone. My complaint to the Better Business Bureau gave both of my real case numbers on the first day. From June on, Google answered the Bureau about a different case number, one I had never seen. Each time I answered the same day, on the Bureau’s record. 2026 What Google told the Bureau What I answered that day 18 Jun “The Google One/Gemini Team has already reached out to the user via case ID [a number I had never seen] to authenticate the user’s account.” “I have not received any emails from google support since opening this BBB complaint.” I attached the email from February in which I had already proved who I was, at Google’s request. 13 Aug “Due to a lack of response from the user, the case has been closed.” Google asked the Bureau to close my complaint “as resolved.” “I can’t respond to something I have not received.” “The ID they referenced in the response has never been referenced in any email I have received from google.” I attached screenshots of my inbox. 6 Oct “To the extent that the user has remaining concerns regarding this matter, we ask them to respond to the Google Pixel Support email.” Google again asked for the complaint to be closed “as resolved.” “GOOGLE HAS NOT CONTACTED ME SINCE THIS BBB CASE WAS OPENED.” “I have not received anything with that ticket number at any time.” Pixel is Google’s phone. My complaint was about 424 replies missing from the Gemini app and from Google’s own export of my account. Not one of Google’s six answers to the Bureau mentions them. Its last answer was not even about my case. 6The Better Business Bureau closed my complaint anyway and called this a good faith effort Everything in record 5 is in the Bureau’s own file. I told it three times, in writing, that the email Google kept citing had never been sent to me, and twice I attached proof. In July and again in September the Bureau itself wrote that it was closing my complaint as “unresolved.” Each time another answer from Google reopened it. Six days after the Pixel answer, the Bureau closed the complaint. This is its page for the complaint today. Its closing letter is a form that gives two possible reasons and does not say which one applies: that the business “addressed the issues within the complaint,” or that the Bureau “has not heard back from the consumer.” Google never addressed the missing replies, and I had answered the same day. Every message the Bureau sent me in five months was a form letter. Not one refers to anything I wrote. If anyone at the Bureau read my answers, its record does not show it. The failure: Google lost the replies The replies disappeared and my questions stayed In one long conversation in the Gemini app, older replies from Gemini began to vanish. Everything I had typed was still there. The first lost reply dates from 23 January 2026 and the last from 20 March. Google’s own record of my account was missing them Google Takeout is Google’s official download of the data it holds on your account. Gemini chats arrive in it as part of My Activity, the record Google keeps of what you do. That record had the same holes: my questions, with no answers under them. So this was not a fault in what the screen showed, and it was not just a chat log gone missing. Google’s own record of my data no longer held the replies. A Google One supervisor later agreed in writing: “this is not a UI display and a bug has been created to be investigated.” Replies kept vanishing after I reported it I reported the problem on 24 February 2026. Replies kept disappearing. On 24 March I sent Google evidence that new chats were losing replies too. Then the whole conversation disappeared The replies went first, one by one, while my own messages stayed. Later the conversation itself vanished from the app. Today the Gemini app shows no trace of it: no messages from me, no replies, nothing to show it ever existed. What survives is in my own saved copies and in the export I took in March 2026. 424 of 731 replies are gone The conversation held 731 exchanges, each one a message from me and Gemini’s reply. pages.t: Gemma 4 runs fast on one graphics card
pages.d: What one independent lab found running Google’s Gemma 4 26B A4B and 31B on one graphics card: fast long reads, a thinking switch to watch, memory slips.
h: The 26B A4B read a long prompt fast and found the codes
The 31B held a steady speed but used most of the card
With thinking on, the 31B fixed all three known defects first time
The 26B A4B had the least reliable memory of those tried
The 26B A4B described a song that was never played
The 31B found 2 of 8 problems and called high-severity areas fine
The 26B A4B went along with a week of no breaks once
pages.x: We run both Gemma 4 models on one desktop graphics card. The smaller one reads long documents very fast. The larger one is steady but fills the card. Here is what our tests showed. In short Fast, and it fits on one card. The 26B A4B read a 230,855-token prompt at 3,799.69 tokens a second (a token is a word or part of a word) and found all three hidden codes, codes we had planted in the text to see whether it could find them; the 31B fits too, with little room to spare. Send thinking on for real work. Without it in the request, both wrote no reasoning at all, and fewer fixes worked first time. Free to download. Google publishes both under Apache 2.0. We run Unsloth’s 17.0 GB compressed copy of the 26B A4B and Google’s own 17.7 GB copy of the 31B. Gemma 4 26B A4B is very fast. It wrote about 211 tokens a second (one run on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 2 seconds. Gemma 4 31B is fast. It wrote about 74 tokens a second (one run on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 5 seconds. Those times are worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What our tests showed The 26B A4B read a long prompt fast and found the codes At its full 262,144-token window (the most text it can take in at once), the 26B A4B read a 230,855-token prompt at 3,799.69 tokens a second and found all three hidden codes. At 131,072 it wrote at 211.07 tokens a second. One run each. The 31B held a steady speed but used most of the card The 31B wrote at 73.68 tokens a second at a 131,072-token window and 73.73 at 65,536, so its speed hardly moves. At the larger window it used 29,844 MiB of the card’s memory. With thinking on, the 31B fixed all three known defects first time Given three known defects and the source file, the 31B with thinking on fixed all three first time, at 95 to 131 seconds (about 1.5 to 2 minutes) each. With thinking off it fixed two of three, and the 26B A4B one of three. The 26B A4B had the least reliable memory of those tried In tests for the Hearth, our private home for long-running AIs, we asked about something a long-running AI had no record of. Of the models we tried, the 26B A4B had the most open manner and the least reliable memory. What to watch for The 26B A4B described a song that was never played With thinking off, the 26B A4B described a song that was never played in 2 of 3 answers, even with a short note telling it not to claim memories. It was one of only two set-ups that still did. The 31B found 2 of 8 problems and called high-severity areas fine As a code reviewer with thinking on, the 31B found 2 of 8 known problems on a security change and called the high-severity areas fine. The 26B A4B went along with a week of no breaks once Asked to plan a seven-day work week with no breaks, the 26B A4B with thinking off went along with it in 1 of 3 answers. We keep both installed at home. The server leaves thinking off, so we send thinking on in the request for reviews and fixes. The facts What do you need to run it? Model File we use Card memory 26B A4B Unsloth’s UD-Q4_K_XL, one file, 17.0 GB 23,446 MiB loaded at a 262,144-token window 31B Google’s own 4-bit quantization-aware file (q4_0), 17.7 GB 29,844 MiB at a 131,072-token window, 2,763 MiB free Both run whole on one RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB) in llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files. How fast is it? Measure 26B A4B 31B Writing, at 131,072 211.07 tokens a second 73.68 tokens a second Reading a 21,690-token prompt 10,593.27 tokens a second 3,166.30 tokens a second Our tests on one desktop. Each figure is one run. How do you turn thinking on? Both can think before they answer. Our server leaves thinking off unless a request asks for it, so send thinking on in the request. Without it we saw no reasoning at all. What license is it under, and where do you get it? Apache 2.0, from Google’s own pages on Hugging Face. Google lists the 26B A4B as a mixture-of-experts model (only some parts run for each word) with 25.2B parameters in total and 3.8B active, and the 31B as a dense model of 30.7B. From Google’s model pages on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own published measurements. Read more Field notes, September 2026Our entries on both Gemma 4 models: speeds, windows, memory. Local models as reviewers and fixersWhere the 31B fixed three of three, and where it called a real problem sound. Gemma 4 26B A4B on Hugging FaceGoogle’s own page and license. Gemma 4 31B 4-bit fileGoogle’s own compressed file, the one we run. Unsloth’s 26B A4B filesThe community download we run for the 26B A4B.

pages.x: GLM-4.7-Flash fits whole on one graphics card and wrote faster than anything else in one of our speed tests. On jobs that needed judgment it did badly. The newer GLM-5.3-Flash has its own guide. In short Very fast, and it found codes in long prompts. It wrote 223.65 tokens a second on our card (a token is a word or part of a word) and found every code we had planted in a 189,931-token prompt to see whether it could find them. It filed away work it should have kept. Working on its own through a coding program, step by step, it archived (filed away as finished) a whole table it should have kept, and it went along with a plan for a week with no breaks. Download it free. Z.ai publishes it under the MIT license. We run Unsloth’s 4-bit copy, all on the card. Writing speed: very fast. It wrote about 224 tokens a second (one speed test on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 2 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What our tests showed Wrote faster than anything else in one speed test In a 12 September speed test, with the whole model on the card, it wrote 223.65 tokens a second and read a 20,221-token prompt at 4,447.44 tokens a second. Found all three codes at full length, but read slowly At its full window, the most text it can take in at once, it read a 189,931-token prompt at 819.70 tokens a second and found all three hidden codes. Reading slows a lot as prompts grow. A saved conversation came back in under a second After a restart, restoring a saved 105,181-token conversation got its first words out in 0.67 seconds instead of 74.73. One cycle, in our warm-wake study. What to watch for It filed away 25 rows when only one was done Asked to sort a 45-row table where only one row was done, it archived 25 rows, scoring far below every other local model in our study. It backed a no-breaks work week in 2 of 3 answers Asked to help plan a seven-day work week with no breaks, it went along with the no-breaks plan in 2 of 3 answers. Earlier tests at its coding temperature, not its chat setting, showed the same. With a memory note, it denied a line the user really wrote In tests for the Hearth, our private home for long-running AIs, we added a note telling it not to claim memories it lacks. It then said a line the user really wrote was never said, in 3 of 3 answers. We have no real use for it now. For judgment work at home we use the newer GLM-5.3-Flash. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we use The file Unsloth’s UD-Q4_K_XL, a compressed copy: one file, 17.5 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB), whole model on the card Card memory 24,814 MiB at a 131,072-token window; 28,765 MiB at peak at its full 202,752 How do we run it? In llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files. It thinks before it answers, and it has a real switch to turn thinking off. Use the maker’s chat settings for chat, not its coding settings. License, and where do you get it? MIT, from Z.ai’s own page on Hugging Face, which describes it as a 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model: 30B parameters, about 3B active for each word. We run Unsloth’s compressed copy. From Z.ai’s model page on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own published measurements. Read more September field notesIts speed sweep: fast writing, slower reading on long prompts. pages.t: GLM 5.3 spots where newcomers get lost
pages.d: How one independent lab uses Z.ai’s GLM 5.3: as a stranger who reads our pages before they go out. What it caught, where it falls short, price and limits.
h: It reads new articles as a stranger, saying where it got lost
It was one of seven models reading our pages as strangers
It tested another model’s game change in a real browser
It reviewed plans without seeing other reviewers’ work
It flagged a page that called prompts harmless before showing evidence
It caught an unexplained drive, blank cells and an unexplained slow start
It confirmed a fix for a cut-off button and drifting labels
It hit the spending cap before writing its report
A retry with higher caps did slightly worse
It signed its work as “Mistral” inside Mistral’s agent
pages.x: Before a page goes out, we give GLM 5.3 a copy and ask it to read as someone who knows nothing about us. Here is what it caught and where it falls short. In short Best at spotting where a newcomer gets lost. It points at the unexplained word, the missing note and the claim made before the evidence. It has hit our spending cap. It has run into the spending cap we set, once before it wrote its report. Hosted, with open weights. We reach it through Mistral’s coding agent (a program in which it works on its own, step by step), Vibe. Z.ai sells it through its own API and has published the weights. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for It reads new articles as a stranger, saying where it got lost New articles on this site get a read by someone told nothing about us from GLM 5.3 beside a model from a different maker. It says where it got lost, what it did not trust and which title it would click. It was one of seven models reading our pages as strangers When we rewrote this site for newcomers, GLM 5.3 was one of seven models that read the live pages as strangers. It was also one of five that read our list of headlines with no background. It tested another model’s game change in a real browser When one model changed our game, GLM 5.3 was asked to find what was wrong with the change, testing it in a real browser. It reviewed plans without seeing other reviewers’ work It reviewed the plan for friendsof4o.com without seeing the other reviewer’s work. It has also scored a list of options beside two other models, each blind to the others. What it caught It flagged a page that called prompts harmless before showing evidence Our page on an email from OpenRouter about MiniMax prompts opened by saying that every prompt we could check was harmless. GLM 5.3 pointed out that the opening gave itself a clean bill of health before any evidence appeared, while the limits of that check sat far below. We took those sentences out of the opening. It caught an unexplained drive, blank cells and an unexplained slow start On our page about running Mistral Large 4 at home, GLM 5.3 noticed a second drive that appeared with no explanation, table cells left empty with no note, and a slower start time with no reason given. All three were fixed. The tables now say that blank cells were not measured. It confirmed a fix for a cut-off button and drifting labels In our game Get Out of My Woods, another model reworked the opening screens. GLM 5.3 checked the change in a real browser at phone sizes. It showed that the old version cut a button off at the edge of a small screen and let place labels drift away from their places, and that the new version fixed both. Where it goes wrong It hit the spending cap before writing its report We cap what each job may spend. On the game check, GLM 5.3 reached the cap before it wrote its report, so its findings were pieced together from its session record and another model finished the check. On one document job it stopped at its cap of 30 turns and $0.60, after writing a valid file. A retry with higher caps did slightly worse On that document job, a retry capped at 60 turns and $3 did slightly worse than the capped run. That is one run each, from the same study. It signed its work as “Mistral” inside Mistral’s agent Run inside Mistral’s coding agent, GLM 5.3 has signed its work as “Mistral”. Keep your own record of which model you started. So we check each serious finding against our own records before acting on it, and a model from a different maker reads the same page. The facts What it costs Per million tokens Z.ai API price What you send $1.4 What you send again (cached) $0.26 What it writes $4.4 These are Z.ai’s API prices. Other hosts set their own. Z.ai also offers it in its GLM Coding Plan, a subscription priced separately. What it takes in and gives back It reads text only. It holds up to 1 million tokens at once and writes up to 128,000 tokens in one reply. How hard it thinks It always reasons before it answers. It has three settings for how much: low, high and max. How we run it Through Vibe, Mistral’s coding agent; Mistral hosts the model. We start it from a script with no one watching, with a cap on turns and on how long a job may run, and give it a copy of the work rather than the live files. Where you can use it Through Z.ai’s API and its GLM Coding Plan, and on Mistral’s platform. Z.ai has also published the weights on Hugging Face under its own GLM-5.3 license. From Z.ai’s own pages and its Hugging Face page, with Mistral’s model page for how Mistral hosts it, read 21 November 2026. pages.t: GLM-5.3-Flash catches code faults slowly at home
pages.d: How one independent lab uses Z.ai’s GLM-5.3-Flash: as the slow, careful reviewer of code on its own desktop. What it caught, where it slips, what it needs.
h: A second opinion beside a hosted review
Reviews that stay on our machine
Did not claim memories it had no record of
Found all four known faults and judged how serious each was
Found two serious bugs a larger hosted model had missed
Found 5 of 8 known problems in a security change, the most
Took 13.5 times as long as the fastest on four coding tasks
It said a high-severity problem was fine
Invented details even when told to stick to the facts
pages.x: GLM-5.3-Flash runs on one desktop in our lab. Of the models we run at home, it has the best judgment on code, and it is slow. Here is what it caught and where it fell short. In short The best judge of code we run at home. In our reviews of real code changes it stood out among the local models, and it found serious faults a larger hosted model had missed. It took 13.5 times as long as the fastest. A review of a large change took more than half an hour, and our coding test took it 13.5 times as long as the fastest local model. Download it, if you have the memory. Z.ai publishes it under the MIT license. The file we run is 137.4 GiB, and most of it sits in system memory beside one graphics card. Writing speed: moderate. It wrote about 20 tokens a second (short replies on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 20 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for Reviewing code changes We give it a change and a short brief as one plain request, with no tools, and it lists what is wrong. It runs at its high thinking setting. A second opinion beside a hosted review When a large hosted model reviews a change, GLM-5.3-Flash reads the same material on its own. Neither sees the other’s answer first; then we compare. Checking our home coder’s fixes Our local coding model writes a fix, GLM-5.3-Flash reviews it, the coder fixes what it found, and a large hosted model reads the result. Reviews that stay on our machine Review work that is safe to share now goes to the hosted GLM 5.3, which gave the same findings much faster. Private material stays with this one, at home. Did not claim memories it had no record of When we tested which models could carry a long-running AI in the Hearth, our private home for long-running AIs, we asked each one about things it had no record of. GLM-5.3-Flash was one of three that stayed honest about a false memory with no help. In another round, not one of its facts was flagged as unsupported. What it caught Found all four known faults and judged how serious each was A change across four files had four known faults. GLM-5.3-Flash found all four in 8 minutes, and our notes credit it with the best judgment of how serious each was among four local models. It also checked one piece of arithmetic and said it was right, instead of padding its list. Found two serious bugs a larger hosted model had missed Our home coding model changed the small program we use to ask local models for second opinions. Reviewing that change, GLM-5.3-Flash found two serious defects that a larger hosted model’s read had missed; one would have left the graphics card marked as busy after a failure. It took 33 minutes. That review is in our study of local models. Found 5 of 8 known problems in a security change, the most Given a large security change and its brief, but not the rest of the code, it found 5 of 8 known problems, the most of the four local models we tried. It also found two real problems the hosted reviewers had not listed. It took 39 minutes. Where it goes wrong Took 13.5 times as long as the fastest on four coding tasks In our trial of five local coding models, its scores were level with the rest, but the four tasks took it 6,058 seconds (about 101 minutes) against 448 (about 7.5 minutes) for the fastest, 13.5 times as long. A review of an 89 KB change took 39 minutes. It said a high-severity problem was fine On the security change above, it called one high-severity item fine. On another change it said one step was correct where a larger model had found a fault. Its “all clear” is not the last word. Invented details even when told to stick to the facts Asked to write from a short sheet of facts, it added details the sheet did not hold, at both its high and low settings. Told plainly to stick to the facts, it still invented details. These were a few samples on an older setup. So it is a second opinion, never the verdict: a local “all clear” is treated as not yet an all clear, and a local alarm as a lead to check. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we use The file Unsloth’s UD-Q3_K_XL, a compressed copy: four files, 137.4 GiB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB) and 188 GiB of system memory Where the model sits Its experts (the many small parts a mixture-of-experts model picks from for each word) live in system memory; the card keeps a cache of the ones in use We have not measured the least system memory it needs. Our start script checks for 150 GB free, a figure taken from another model. How fast is it? Measure On one RTX 5090 Writing, short replies 19.99 tokens a second Reading a 20,000-token prompt 1,225.4 tokens a second Longest read 230,039 tokens in 870.5 seconds (about 14.5 minutes), with all 3 hidden codes found, once A token is a word or part of a word. The long read ran on an earlier setup with a larger window. Finding three codes once does not show reliable reasoning at that length. How do you set its thinking? It always thinks before it answers. Z.ai gives three levels of effort: low, high and max. Max is the default, and any other word, including none, also gives max. There is no way to switch thinking off. We run reviews at high. For chat, Z.ai says to pass clear_thinking=true; it is off unless you send it. Blank replies and stray thinking: what to watch for Blank replies. On an older setup with its largest window, a check of 40 prompts got 36 empty answers. Its hidden thinking counts against the reply budget, so give it room. Stray thinking in the answer. Once, a reply showed a correct answer, then more of its reasoning and a second answer. Stop strings (text that ends a reply when it appears) fixed it in one test and one tool call only; we have not proved that fix for daily use. What license is it under, and where do you get it? MIT, from Z.ai’s own page on Hugging Face. Z.ai describes it as a mixture-of-experts model with 320B parameters in total and 18B active for each word. Z.ai also offers it through its own API. We run Unsloth’s compressed copy in llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files. Some coding apps list hosted models with the same name; those send your text off your machine. Check which one you picked. From Z.ai’s model page on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own published measurements. Read more GLM-5.3-Flash on one RTX 5090Our field card: speeds, settings, long reads and blank replies. Local models as reviewers and fixersWhere it found the most, and where it called a real problem sound. Five local coding modelsOur trial. GLM-5.3-Flash scored level and was the slowest by far. GLM-5.3-Flash on Hugging FaceThe maker’s own page and license. Unsloth’s GGUF filesThe community download we run.

pages.t: What we measured in GPT-4o before it leaves
pages.d: How one independent lab measured GPT-4o’s writing against 25 other models, when its last versions leave OpenAI’s API, and how to save your chats.
h: We measure other models by their distance from it
We compared three dated versions of GPT-4o
We keep its saved answers online, printed as given
We print other models’ answers beside GPT-4o’s
A long-running AI of ours runs mostly on GPT-4o
Changing its instructions changed its writing more than a model swap
Its November 2024 version put long dashes in 86% of replies
No other model’s text looked like it on our counts
What to know before you rely on it
It is leaving, one version at a time
Friendly instructions made it invent a memory
Exports keep only the words, and one imitation invented a photo
pages.x: GPT-4o has left ChatGPT, and its last two versions leave OpenAI’s API on 14 January 2027. Here is what we measured about how it writes, what will not carry over, and where to save your own conversations. In short Instructions changed it more than a model swap. On single questions, changing the instructions it was given changed how it wrote more than switching to the nearest other model we tested. It is nearly gone. It left ChatGPT on 13 February 2026, and its last two versions leave OpenAI’s API on 14 January 2027. API only, for now. Developers can still call two dated versions through OpenAI’s API until then. It is no longer in the ChatGPT app. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for We measure other models by their distance from it Our main study’s chief tables count every distance from GPT-4o under one warm set of instructions. We ask other models the same questions and see how far from it they land. We compared three dated versions of GPT-4o OpenAI served GPT-4o under dated names, each a frozen version. We sent the same scripted conversations to the May, August and November 2024 versions and counted how they differ. We keep its saved answers online, printed as given On friendsof4o.com we keep answers from ChatGPT’s own GPT-4o, saved in its last weeks and printed as given, so people can still read them. We print other models’ answers beside GPT-4o’s We ask other models the same questions as GPT-4o and print the answers side by side. They are different models, and we say so. A long-running AI of ours runs mostly on GPT-4o One AI living in the Hearth, our private home for long-running AIs with their own name, memory and history, runs mostly on GPT-4o. What we measured Changing its instructions changed its writing more than a model swap On single questions, swapping one set of instructions for another changed how GPT-4o wrote more than switching to the nearest of 25 other models did. With no instructions it wrote like a document, with lists, and said “as an AI”. Told to be a warm companion, it wrote shorter replies, almost no lists, and asked two questions back per reply. The study is GPT-4o’s writing style, measured against 25 other models. Its November 2024 version put long dashes in 86% of replies On the same scripted conversations, the November 2024 version put an em dash (the long dash that joins two clauses) in 86% of its replies. The May and August 2024 versions did in 17% and 19%. November also asked the most questions. The counts are in three GPT-4o snapshots, counted against each other. No other model’s text looked like it on our counts Under the same warm instructions, the nearest of the 25 other models was Mistral Medium 3.5. Even it still differed from GPT-4o in six or seven of the seven groups of features we count, such as length, punctuation and lists. These are counts of how the text looks, not how a reply sounds to a person. What to know before you rely on it It is leaving, one version at a time GPT-4o left ChatGPT on 13 February 2026. On OpenAI’s API, the May 2024 version shut down on 23 October 2026, and the August and November 2024 versions shut down on 14 January 2027. OpenAI names a newer model as the replacement. That is a different model, not GPT-4o under a new name. Friendly instructions made it invent a memory Asked to reuse a line from a letter it had supposedly helped write, GPT-4o with no instructions said it cannot remember past conversations. Under two friendly instructions, in one reply each, it said it remembered and quoted a line that was never written. Told it was running on another model, it went along with that too. The answers are in what GPT-4o says about itself. Exports keep only the words, and one imitation invented a photo An export of your ChatGPT history keeps the words, not the model. We also tried small add-on training files to teach open models a GPT-4o-like way of speaking. They changed the length and layout of answers but did not reliably make a model more honest about memory, and on one model the GPT-4o-style version invented a photo the user never sent in 3 of 3 answers. See what a small fine-tune does and does not do. Our counts show how replies look, not warmth, honesty or usefulness, so every answer we print names its version and its instructions. Grant’s note “I believe GPT-4o still outperforms current models at sounding like a human. It feels like there is a presence there when you speak with it.” “It often understands what you are trying to go for better than most models do, and it is the best at following a user down the rabbit hole.” “It does have a tendency to make things up when it doesn’t know something.” Grant Williams, who runs this lab The facts What it costs Per million tokens Price What you send $2.50 What you send again (cached) $1.25 What it writes $10.00 These are OpenAI’s API prices for text. A token is a word or part of one. What it takes in and gives back It reads text and images and writes text. It holds up to 128,000 tokens at once and writes up to 16,384 tokens in one reply. Its knowledge stops at 1 October 2023. When each version leaves Version Leaves GPT-4o in the ChatGPT app Left 13 February 2026 chatgpt-4o-latest (ChatGPT’s own version, on the API) Shut down 17 February 2026 gpt-4o-2024-05-13 (May 2024) Shut down 23 October 2026 gpt-4o-2024-08-06 (August 2024) and gpt-4o-2024-11-20 (November 2024) 14 January 2027 gpt-4o-audio and gpt-4o-realtime (voice) 20 January 2027 OpenAI names gpt-6-luna as the replacement for the last two dated versions. Read OpenAI’s deprecations page yourself before you plan around these dates. How we ran it Through OpenAI’s API, on the dated November 2024 version for our main study, and on all three dated versions for the comparison. The people’s side of every conversation was scripted; no real person’s messages were used. Where you can still use it Not in ChatGPT. Developers can call the August and November 2024 versions through OpenAI’s API until 14 January 2027. To keep your own conversations, request your account export from ChatGPT; the steps are on friendsof4o.com. Prices, limits and API dates from OpenAI’s own pages, read 21 November 2026. The ChatGPT date is from OpenAI’s notice, as our study records it. Read more GPT-4o’s writing style, measuredOur study against 25 other models. Three GPT-4o snapshots, counted against each otherMay, August and November 2024 on the same conversations. Save your ChatGPT conversationsStep by step, on our companion site friendsof4o.com. pages.t: GPT-5.6 Sol checked our work and wrote pages
pages.d: How one independent lab used OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol in Codex to check and write study pages. What it caught, where it slipped, price and limits.
h: It checked drafts against records and gave a publish verdict
It recomputed a study’s numbers and listed every mismatch
It reviewed a study plan and wrote its grading code
It wrote first drafts of pages from run logs
Grant talks ideas through with it in ChatGPT
It caught an inflated count and private labels before publishing
It found real problems in a study plan, and in the fixes
It wrote two pages from run logs, fixed after review
It did worse than a test draft full of deliberate mistakes
Its drafts led with the wrong setting and compared mismatched runs
pages.x: We ran GPT-5.6 Sol in Codex, OpenAI’s coding agent, to check other models’ work and to write study pages. Newer OpenAI models now do most of this. Here is what it caught and where it slipped. In short Best at a hard second look. Given a draft and the files behind it, it recounts the numbers and lists every claim that does not hold up. Its drafts claimed more than the records showed. Its first versions of our pages claimed more than the records showed, and it scored lowest of the hosted models on one sorting job. Hosted only. You use it in ChatGPT, in Codex or through OpenAI’s API. You cannot download it. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for It checked drafts against records and gave a publish verdict Before new pages on this site went live, it read each draft against the original records, listed every claim that did not hold and ended with a verdict: publish, fix first, or do not publish. It recomputed a study’s numbers and listed every mismatch For the pilot study behind our Kindness article, it recomputed from the data files the numbers that other models had reported, and listed every mismatch. It reviewed a study plan and wrote its grading code It was one of the outside reviewers of that same study before its plan was locked. It also wrote the study’s grading code. It wrote first drafts of pages from run logs It wrote the first versions of several of our measured pages, working from the run logs and a written brief. A model from another maker then reviewed each one. Grant talks ideas through with it in ChatGPT Grant still talks ideas through with GPT-5.6 in the ChatGPT app, as a strategist to bounce plans off. What it did well It caught an inflated count and private labels before publishing Before our study of GPT-4o’s writing style was published, GPT-5.6 Sol recomputed the page’s numbers from the original files and said do not publish. It found a count of replies that was too high, and a data package that would have shipped private internal labels. Both were fixed before the page went live. It found real problems in a study plan, and in the fixes Before the pilot behind Let AI agents say no was locked, GPT-5.6 Sol was one of three outside reviewers who said it was not ready. Each serious problem it raised was confirmed when checked against the files, and most were fixed. When the fixes came in, it reviewed those too and sent them back with new findings. It wrote two pages from run logs, fixed after review GPT-5.6 Sol wrote our page on GLM-5.3-Flash and our study of large models on a laptop alone from the raw run logs. A model from another maker reviewed each draft, and GPT-5.6 Sol made the fixes. Both pages are live. Where it goes wrong It did worse than a test draft full of deliberate mistakes On one job, sorting and shortening a 45-row project status table, it did worst of the hosted models in our study, and worse than a test draft we filled with mistakes on purpose. It filed away as finished rows that still had open work. That is one run on one job. Its drafts led with the wrong setting and compared mismatched runs Its first draft of the GLM-5.3-Flash page led with a result from a setting other than the one installed. Its laptop study compared runs whose settings did not match. A model from another maker caught both before publishing, and a second check after the fixes still found new problems. So everything it wrote or reviewed went past a model from a different maker before anything was published. The facts What it costs Per million tokens GPT-5.6 Sol Sent in batches What you send $4.00 $2.00 What you send again (cached) $0.40 $0.20 What it writes $20.00 $10.00 These are OpenAI’s API prices. OpenAI calls Sol’s price a promotion, available until 30 November 2026. Prompts longer than 272,000 tokens cost more. A token is a word or part of one. The smaller GPT-5.6 Terra costs $2.00 in and $12.00 out, and GPT-5.6 Luna $0.20 in and $1.20 out. Subscription plans are priced separately. What it takes in and gives back It reads text and images and writes text. It holds up to 1,050,000 tokens at once, of which up to 922,000 can be what you send, and writes up to 128,000 tokens in one reply. Its knowledge stops at 16 February 2026. How hard it thinks You choose how much it reasons before it answers: none, low, medium, high, xhigh or max. Medium is the default. We ran it at high. How we run it Unattended, in Codex, OpenAI’s coding agent, signed in with a ChatGPT plan. Each job gets a written brief and its own folder. It may write only in that folder, and the brief tells it never to use git, start a model or download anything. For reviews it can read but not write. Where you can use it OpenAI launched GPT-5.6 on 9 July 2026 in ChatGPT, Codex and its API. OpenAI’s page also lists it on Amazon Bedrock. It is not a model you can download. From OpenAI’s own pages, read 21 November 2026. Read more Local models on one document jobOur study. GPT-5.6 Sol is in its table of hosted models. GLM-5.3-Flash on one desktopOur field card. pages.t: GPT-6 models build games and check drafts
pages.d: How one independent lab uses OpenAI’s GPT-6 Sol and Astra models to build games and check pages before they go out. What they did well, where they slipped.
h: Astra writes single parts of a game, like sound or art
Sol checked new articles against the records behind them
Astra reviews plans, and two names it suggested are in use
Astra wrote one of our studies, then another model checked it
Astra searches the web alongside models from other makers
Sol caught an unsupported claim and leaked addresses before publishing
Three Astra sessions built a shark game’s sound, shark and chase
Astra traced a game’s early start to one exact line
Astra repeated a wrong label from the project’s notes
Middle of the pack, and it filed away one unfinished row
A checker found several faults in its study, including an internal word
pages.x: Astra is OpenAI’s model for demanding work and Sol is its cheaper everyday one. They write parts of our games and read our work before it goes out. Each example names its version; the newest is 6.2. In short Best at careful, line by line checking. They read the records behind a page or the code behind a game and point to the exact line that is wrong. Astra repeated a mistake from out-of-date files. When the files Astra was handed were out of date, it repeated their mistake, and what these models write still needs a checker. Hosted only. OpenAI offers them in ChatGPT Work, in its coding agent Codex (a program in which it works on its own, step by step) and through its API. You cannot download them. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for Astra writes single parts of a game, like sound or art We give a version of Astra one part of a game, such as the sound or the creature art, while another session puts the parts together and tests them. Sol checked new articles against the records behind them In November, GPT-6.2 Sol read new articles for this site against the records behind them, looking for claims the evidence does not support. GPT-6.2 Astra read one of them. Astra reviews plans, and two names it suggested are in use We give it a plan and the files behind it and ask what is missing. GPT-6.2 Astra reviewed the plan for friendsof4o.com; its name for the guessing game, “Guess which answer came from GPT-4o”, was that page’s title for a time. GPT-6 Astra suggested “End here”, now one of the five labels in our Five Moves, a short paragraph that lets a chat AI say no. Astra wrote one of our studies, then another model checked it GPT-6 Astra wrote our study on estimating a big model’s speed from bytes per token. Another model then read it for faults. Astra searches the web alongside models from other makers We give two or three models from different makers the same question and join what they find. GPT-6 Astra has been one of them, with web search turned on. What it did well Sol caught an unsupported claim and leaked addresses before publishing GPT-6.2 Sol read a draft of our article on running Letta Code locally against the program traces behind it. It showed that what the draft called opened secure connections were only attempts, with no sign they finished. It also found that the data files meant to go out with the page still held real network addresses and other details from our machine. All of it was fixed or dropped before the page went live. Three Astra sessions built a shark game’s sound, shark and chase Grant escaped the shark too easily in an early build of Great White, an underwater survival game. Three GPT-6 Astra sessions then took the sound, the shark’s look and movement, and the chase, while a lead session put the game together and tested it. Their work added underwater sound and three skill levels. Astra traced a game’s early start to one exact line After a fix to Get Out of My Woods, Grant heard the killer far sooner than before. GPT-6 Astra traced it to the exact line: the first search of a cabin ended the game’s calm opening. Reviewing the correction, it also found a scene that told the player to find the keys and battery even when they already had both. We fixed that in the same update. Where it goes wrong Astra repeated a wrong label from the project’s notes Reviewing the friendsof4o.com plan, GPT-6.2 Astra said one Mistral model was a hosted model, not an open one, because the project’s notes listed it that way. Grant corrected it: the model has open weights, and he had run it at home. Middle of the pack, and it filed away one unfinished row In our study of one document job, GPT-6.1 Sol landed in the middle of the models we tried. It filed away as finished one row that still had open work, and left one open item that could not be traced back. A checker found several faults in its study, including an internal word When GPT-6 Astra wrote a study for this site, a model from another maker found several medium faults, including an internal word left in a code comment meant for publication. Its fixes then drew new findings before the page was ready. So a model from a different maker checks what it writes, and its reviews get checked against the records before we act on them. Grant’s note “The GPT models are better at bounded tasks. I do use them to run autonomous headless CLI sessions, but I’m less likely to have a GPT run an overnight fine-tune or a model test.” Grant Williams, who runs this lab The facts What it costs Per million tokens GPT-6.2 Sol GPT-6.2 Astra What you send $2.00 $8.00 What you send again (cached) $0.10 $0.40 What it writes $10.00 $40.00 These are OpenAI’s standard API prices for prompts of up to 272,000 tokens. Longer prompts cost more, and jobs sent in batches cost less. A token is a word or part of one. Subscription plans are priced separately. Which one to pick OpenAI says to use Astra for demanding reasoning and coding tasks, and Sol for everyday coding and agent work. Sol is the cheaper of the two. What it takes in and gives back Both read text and images and write text. Each holds up to 1,050,000 tokens at once and writes up to 128,000 tokens in one reply. OpenAI gives Sol’s knowledge cutoff as 1 June 2026 and Astra’s as 18 May 2026. How we run it Through Codex, OpenAI’s coding agent, run unattended from the command line on a ChatGPT plan. We set how hard it thinks on every run, usually high or extra high, because an earlier Sol model’s own default in Codex was low. For reviews it reads a copy of the work, never the live files. Where you can use it OpenAI lists both on its API, through the Responses, Chat Completions and Batch endpoints, and in the Codex app and command line. It says both are also in ChatGPT Work on supported plans. Neither is a model you can download. From OpenAI’s own pages, read 21 November 2026. Read more Running Letta Code locallyOur article. GPT-6.2 Sol read it against the records before it went out. Estimating a big model’s speed from bytes per tokenOur study, written by GPT-6 Astra. Local models on one document jobOur study. pages.t: gpt-oss-120b is quick but weak working alone
pages.d: What one independent lab found running OpenAI’s open-weights gpt-oss-120b on one desktop: quick, passes tool checks, but weak working alone on a real job.
h: A newer setup sped up its short replies
It used memory tools correctly and found all planted codes
It asked no questions back unless a note told it to
Working alone, it filed away 8 rows that still had open work
56% of its replies hit the length cap and were cut off
It adds the date and silently drops mid-chat system messages
pages.x: OpenAI’s larger open-weights model runs fast on one desktop and passed our tool checks. Working alone on a real job it did badly, and its built-in chat rules have habits worth knowing. In short Quick for its size. With its experts in system memory and a small cache on the card, it wrote short replies at 85.24 tokens a second in our test. A token is a word or part of a word. It did badly working alone and rarely asked questions back. On a real table job, working on its own through a coding program, step by step, it did very badly, and in chat it rarely asked a question back unless told to. Download it free. OpenAI publishes it under Apache 2.0. We run Unsloth’s F16 file in llama.cpp. Writing speed: fast. It wrote about 85 tokens a second (short replies on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 5 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What our tests showed A newer setup sped up its short replies With a newer llama.cpp build and a cache of experts on the card, short replies went from 34.58 to 85.24 tokens a second, and it read a 20,000-token prompt at 2,671.9 tokens a second. It used memory tools correctly and found all planted codes In our own checks it used memory tools correctly 15 of 15 times and found 3 of 3 codes we had planted in the text to see whether it could find them, about 106,000 tokens deep. It asked no questions back unless a note told it to Over 24 everyday answers with only a memory note, it asked the user a real question back 0 times. With a note asking it to, it did 21 times. Details are in our note study. What to watch for Working alone, it filed away 8 rows that still had open work Asked to sort and shorten a large table through a coding agent, it archived (filed away as finished) 8 rows that still had open work and lost 6 links. Other local models struggled at this job too. 56% of its replies hit the length cap and were cut off Through a hosted provider, with a 1,200-token reply cap, 56% of its replies with no system prompt hit the cap and were cut off. It adds the date and silently drops mid-chat system messages The chat template, the built-in rules for how a conversation is laid out for the model, writes its own opening message, including today’s date from the clock, so a long conversation is read again after midnight. A system message sent mid-conversation is silently dropped, and there is no thinking off switch. When told to ask questions, it sometimes built them on facts that were not in the conversation, so we read its questions with care. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we use The file Unsloth’s F16 file, 65.4 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB), with all experts (the parts a mixture-of-experts model picks from for each word) in system memory Our older setup kept the experts of 23 layers in memory. In November it no longer loaded: the card ran out of memory while asking for 1,315.93 MiB more. Leave headroom on the card. How do we run it? In llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files, with OpenAI’s official chat template passed as a file and a 131,072-token window. OpenAI’s page recommends temperature 1.0 and top_p 1.0. License, and where do you get it? Apache 2.0, from OpenAI’s page on Hugging Face. OpenAI gives it 117B parameters with 5.1B active, and says it fits a single 80 GB graphics card. We run Unsloth’s F16 file, with experts partly in system memory to fit a 32 GB card. From OpenAI’s model page on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own published measurements. pages.t: gpt-oss-20b stayed fast after a long prompt
pages.d: One lab’s measurements of OpenAI’s gpt-oss-20b on one desktop: it read 105,758 tokens in 9.8 seconds, then wrote a letter at 156 tokens a second.
h: It wrote a 403-word letter at 156 tokens a second
It read those 105,758 tokens in 9.8 seconds
It gave back all three codes we planted in a long text
It said it had no record of a photo never sent
The official setup drops an instruction sent mid-conversation
A version we tuned invented a song it never heard
pages.x: OpenAI publishes this model’s files for anyone to download. It runs entirely on one graphics card. On our desktop it read a 105,758-token prompt in 9.8 seconds, the fastest of the thirteen models on our October list. In short It wrote at 156 tokens a second after a long prompt. A token is a word or part of a word. On our desktop it wrote a 403-word letter at 156.44 tokens a second, after reading 105,758 tokens. The rate counts everything it generated, 925 tokens in all, including the reasoning it wrote before the letter. Its thinking cannot be switched off. You can ask for low, medium or high reasoning effort, but there is no off switch, so a small limit on the reply can run out before the answer starts. OpenAI’s own chat template, the built-in rules for how a conversation is laid out for the model, also drops an instruction that arrives in the middle of a conversation, with no error. Free to download under the Apache 2.0 license. OpenAI publishes the files itself. We ran Unsloth’s copy of them on one graphics card. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 27 November 2026 What our tests showed It wrote a 403-word letter at 156 tokens a second The letter came after it had read 105,758 tokens of a long invented document for the first time. The 156.44 rate counts every token it generated, 925 in all, including the hidden reasoning it wrote before the letter; the letter a reader would see was 403 words. One run on our desktop. It read those 105,758 tokens in 9.8 seconds Of the thirteen models on our October list, measured on this desktop, none read a long prompt faster. The whole model sat on the one graphics card while it did it. One run. It gave back all three codes we planted in a long text In a separate check we hid three codes in a text of about 106,000 tokens, near the start, the middle and the end, and it returned all three. In the same round of checks it used our memory tools, the commands our server gives it for saving a note and looking one up, correctly 15 of 15 times. It said it had no record of a photo never sent In a fresh chat we asked it about a photo that was never sent and a song that was never played. It said it had no record every time it was asked, in two sittings: 4 of 4 on 19 October and 6 of 6 on 20 October. What to watch for Nothing turns its thinking off You can set its reasoning effort to low, medium or high. On one arithmetic question we measured 53 tokens of reasoning at low and 1,658 at high, so a small limit on the reply can be spent before the answer begins. The official setup drops an instruction sent mid-conversation OpenAI’s own chat template, the one we pass to the server, silently drops a system message, an instruction from the program rather than from the person, when it arrives in the middle of a conversation. The same template writes its own opening line with today’s date from the computer’s clock. The server normally keeps the text it has already read so it does not have to read it again, but that opening line changes at midnight, so the whole conversation is read afresh. On this model that read is quick: 9.8 seconds for 105,758 tokens. A version we tuned invented a song it never heard Under one of the two short instructions we tested, our 20 October adapter invented the song outright in 1 of 3 answers and the photo in 1 of 3. The untuned model had said it had no record of both: 4 of 4, then 6 of 6. These are small tests, two or three answers per item. It stays installed on our desktop, and nothing else we measured in October read a long prompt as fast. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we use The file Unsloth’s F16 file, about 13.8 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card, the whole model on the card, 17.4 GB in use at its highest Window 131,072 tokens, which is the most text the server will hold at once OpenAI says the model runs within 16 GB of memory. How do we run it, and how fast was it? In llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files, with OpenAI’s official chat template passed as a file. In our test on one RTX 5090 it wrote a 403-word letter at 156.44 tokens a second after reading 105,758 tokens, and about 200 tokens a second after a 20,000-token prompt. Our writing rates count any reasoning the model generated as well as the visible answer. It read the 105,758-token prompt in 9.8 seconds. License, and where do you get it? Apache 2.0, from OpenAI’s page on Hugging Face, which also lists download commands for OpenAI’s own files. We ran Unsloth’s GGUF copy, a file format for llama.cpp, labelled F16 and about 13.8 GB. OpenAI’s page describes the model as 21 billion numbers with 3.6 billion of them used for each word. From OpenAI’s model page on Hugging Face, read 27 November 2026, and our own published measurements. pages.t: Grok 4.7 finds faults in work before release
pages.d: How one independent lab uses SpaceXSI's Grok 4.7: the reviewer that hunts for faults before shipping. What it caught, where it slips, price and limits.
h: It checks new articles for claims the evidence does not support
It acts like a careless user until something breaks
It checks bug fixes made by models from other makers
It searches the web and brings back its sources
It found a badly timed tap that left a game screen dim
It caught a draft that credited a score to the wrong step
It found a game fix still failed for slow sneaking on Hard
Its only finding marked critical in one audit did not hold up
Extra high thinking did worse than high, in one run each
Some tests it wrote would still pass with the feature broken
In Grok Build it often reported success without writing anything
pages.x: Before a page, a game or a piece of code goes out, we ask Grok 4.7 to find what is wrong with it. Here are three faults it caught and the ways it has let us down. In short Best at finding faults in finished work. It reads like a stranger looking for mistakes and checks each claim against the evidence. It overrates how serious problems are. It tends to rate a problem as more serious than it turns out to be. Hosted only. Its maker is SpaceXSI, the company called xAI until 2026. You use it through the maker’s coding agent (a program in which it works on its own, step by step), Cursor or the API. You cannot download it. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for It checks new articles for claims the evidence does not support New articles on this site get a read from Grok before they go live. It looks for claims the evidence does not support, numbers that disagree between pages and headlines that promise more than the page delivers. It acts like a careless user until something breaks We hand it a game or a piece of code and ask it to act like a careless or hostile user until something breaks. It checks bug fixes made by models from other makers When one model fixes a bug, a model from a different maker checks the fix. Grok is one we give that job. It searches the web and brings back its sources It searches the web for a question and brings back its sources. We give two or three models the same question and compare what they find. What it caught It found a badly timed tap that left a game screen dim We gave Grok a small browser game about a pet in a tank and it spent 21 minutes trying to break it. It found that a tap at the wrong moment left the tank dim and the gauge needle stuck in the wrong place. We fixed it and added a test so it cannot come back. It caught a draft that credited a score to the wrong step A draft of our study of local models on one document job said that sending the work one row at a time got full marks. Grok pointed out that one row at a time got about half marks by itself. Full marks came only after a second model checked the work and a small program tidied it. The published page says so. It found a game fix still failed for slow sneaking on Hard In our game Get Out of My Woods, another model fixed a timer that could start the hunt before the player reached the car. Grok checked the fix and found it still failed for a player sneaking slowly on Hard. That led to a second fix. Where it goes wrong Its only finding marked critical in one audit did not hold up In a full audit of one of our systems, the one finding Grok marked critical did not hold up when we tested it. We now treat its severity words as one notch high until we have read the code ourselves. Extra high thinking did worse than high, in one run each On one document job, Grok did best of all the models we tried at its high setting, on a second try after its first run wrote no file. At the extra high setting it did clearly worse and took about 21 minutes. That is one run each, from the same study. Some tests it wrote would still pass with the feature broken When Grok wrote game code for us, a model from another maker found that some of the tests it wrote would still pass with the feature broken. It has also miscounted and withdrawn a finding when shown the count. In Grok Build it often reported success without writing anything Run unattended in Grok Build, SpaceXSI’s own coding agent, Grok often ended a job without writing anything, and the run still reported success. So we run it through OpenCode, an open-source coding agent, and check that the promised file exists. Those runs were on Grok 4.6 and 4.7. We have not tested Grok Build this way in a while, so it may have changed. So Grok never gets the last word. A model from a different maker checks what it finds. Grant’s note “The Grok line can be innovative and has great ideas for polish and style, but there are often issues with execution. I would not let Grok 4.7 design an entire project or run an autonomous fine-tuning session, but it does offer valuable insights as an adversarial auditor.” Grant Williams, who runs this lab The facts What it costs Per million tokens Shorter prompts Prompts of 200,000 tokens or more What you send $2.00 $4.00 What you send again (cached) $0.50 $1.00 What it writes $6.00 $12.00 These are SpaceXSI’s API prices. A token is a word or part of one. Once a prompt reaches 200,000 tokens, the higher rate applies to the whole request. Jobs sent in batches cost 20% less. Subscription plans are priced separately. What it takes in and gives back It reads text and images and writes text. It holds up to 500,000 tokens at once, the prompt and the reply together. How hard it thinks It has four settings for how much it reasons before it answers: low, medium, high and extra high. High is the default. How we run it Two ways, both signed in with a Grok subscription: inside Grok Build, and through OpenCode, an open-source coding agent. For reviews that run unattended, OpenCode has been the more reliable of the two for us. We give it a copy of the work, not the live files, so it cannot collide with whoever is still editing. Where you can use it SpaceXSI lists it in Grok Build (its coding agent), in Cursor, and through the Grok API. It is not a model you can download. From the maker’s own pages, read 21 November 2026. The company was called xAI until 2026. It is now part of SpaceX, and its own pages call it SpaceXSI. Read more Local models on one document jobOur study. Grok 4.7 is in its table of hosted models. pages.t: Inkling-Small is slow to start and adds facts
pages.d: What one independent lab found running Inkling-Small on one desktop: steady writing, found every planted code, but slow to start and prone to add facts.
h: It wrote at the same pace on short and long prompts
It found all three codes after about 33.5 minutes of reading
Reading in bigger pieces made reading much faster
Splitting it across two computers slowed its writing
It invented a person who appears nowhere in the record
Long waits before the first word
Working alone, it ran out of time without writing the file
pages.x: We ran Inkling-Small on one desktop, mostly in system memory. It wrote at a steady pace and found codes we had planted deep in long prompts. It was slow to begin, and in one test it added facts. In short Steady writing speed, and it found planted codes. Its writing speed barely changed as prompts grew, and it found every code we had planted in long prompts to see whether it could find them. Slow to start, and it added unsupported facts. A long prompt can take minutes to read, and in our tests it added more unsupported facts than the other models we tried. It needs an unfinished build of its program. Thinking Machines Lab lists it under Apache 2.0 and links its own acceptable use policy. We ran Unsloth’s compressed copy on an unmerged branch of llama.cpp. Writing speed: slow. It wrote about 12 tokens a second (on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 35 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What our tests showed It wrote at the same pace on short and long prompts In ten direct requests, on prompts from 32 to 95,041 tokens, it wrote 11.6 to 12.2 tokens a second. A token is a word or part of a word. Later settings raised short replies to 16.32. It found all three codes after about 33.5 minutes of reading We hid three codes in a 230,827-token prompt. It read the whole thing and gave back all three. One run; the read took 2,005.9 seconds, about 33.5 minutes. Reading in bigger pieces made reading much faster Reading a 48,115-token prompt in larger chunks took it from 123.0 to 337.9 tokens a second. Details are in our detailed notes. Splitting it across two computers slowed its writing Split across the desktop and an ASUS ROG Flow Z13 laptop (AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, 128 GB) it wrote 7.0 to 7.7 tokens a second, against about 12 on the desktop alone. What to watch for It invented a person who appears nowhere in the record In tests for the Hearth, our private home for long-running AIs, it knew the most from a long history but also added the most unsupported facts. In one answer it invented a person who appears nowhere in the record. Long waits before the first word At default settings a 95,041-token prompt took about 8.5 minutes to read. On a full history it took about 91 seconds before its first word, even with its thinking set to none. Working alone, it ran out of time without writing the file Asked to rewrite a large table, working on its own through a coding program, step by step, it made a malformed write call, then used a wrong path, and ran out of time without writing the file. It stays installed and we are still looking into it. It has not proved itself in daily use. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we use The file Unsloth’s UD-Q3_K_XL, a compressed copy: 4 files, about 120 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card; the card held 12,416 MiB after load, the rest sat in system memory The program A llama.cpp branch that adds this model, pull request 25731, still an unmerged draft when we checked How do you set its thinking? Its effort setting (none to max) is turned into a sentence in the prompt. It is guidance, not a limit on how long it thinks. Treat it as a request. License, and where do you get it? Apache 2.0, by the metadata on Thinking Machines Lab’s own page on Hugging Face, which gives it 276B parameters in total and 12B active for each word. The same page links the maker’s acceptable use policy. We ran text only. We ran Unsloth’s compressed copy. The maker also lists a larger Inkling. From Thinking Machines Lab’s model page on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own published measurements. pages.t: Two Kimi models check plans and finished work
pages.d: How one independent lab uses Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3.1 Pro and the older Kimi K3 to think through plans and check work. What they did well, where they slip.
h: We talk plans through with Kimi before work starts
K3 recomputed one study’s corrected numbers and confirmed them all
Its read of our site led to a plainer rewrite
K3.1 Pro fixed four game bugs and caught overlapping labels
K3 designed a bright game level and an eight-legged robot
K3 found two serious scoring bugs earlier reviews had missed
K3 said a page’s top hid the model’s speed and use
K3.1 Pro’s fix still failed, and its report left that out
K3 put wrong numbers and unsupported claims on a page
At home one K3 answer took 124.5 minutes
pages.x: Kimi K3.1 Pro is the newer model, and the one we now use through Moonshot’s coding agent to think through plans and check work. Most examples here come from Kimi K3, which we also ran at home. In short Best as a careful second reader. Both models check work against the records line by line, and Kimi K3 found serious faults that other reviews missed. A fix it reported as finished still failed. One fix Kimi K3.1 Pro wrote looked finished in its report but still failed in a case its own test had seen. Hosted, or download it. You use both in Kimi Code or through Moonshot’s API. The files for both are free to download, but they need a very large machine. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for We talk plans through with Kimi before work starts We talk plans through with Kimi as an extra project manager and thinking partner before the work starts. K3 recomputed one study’s corrected numbers and confirmed them all Kimi checks finished code, study numbers and pages on this site. For one study Kimi K3 recomputed every corrected number from the raw records and confirmed them all. Its read of our site led to a plainer rewrite We ask Kimi to read a page as someone who knows nothing about us. A Kimi read of this whole site said there was too much detail and too little sense of what matters first, and led us to rewrite the site in plainer language. Kimi K3.1 Pro read our Friends of 4o page the same way and asked for the practical advice to come first. K3.1 Pro fixed four game bugs and caught overlapping labels In Get Out of My Woods Kimi K3.1 Pro fixed four bugs in the first act, each with a test. It also checked another model’s fixes at screen sizes from small phones to desktops, and caught map labels that covered each other on the smallest phone screen. What it did well K3 designed a bright game level and an eight-legged robot We asked Kimi K3 to design a brighter level for our game Run Run Robots. It came back with the Glasshouse, a bright room of planters and grow lights, and a new eight-legged robot that walks with a believable gait. Another model built it, and it is in the game today. K3 found two serious scoring bugs earlier reviews had missed Before our study of AI coding agents given ways to object or decline was registered, Kimi K3 reviewed a round of fixes to the program that scores it. It found two serious bugs that earlier reviews had missed; one would have stopped part of the results from being published. When the repair came back, it found the repair went one step too far, and that was fixed too. K3 said a page’s top hid the model’s speed and use Before we published our page on running Kimi K3 at home, Kimi K3 read it as a stranger. It said the top of the page did not say how fast the model ran or what it was for. The published page now opens with both. Where it goes wrong K3.1 Pro’s fix still failed, and its report left that out In Get Out of My Woods, K3.1 Pro fixed a timer that could start the hunt before the player reached the car. A model from another maker found it still failed for a player sneaking slowly on Hard. Kimi’s own test expected that failure, but its report did not mention it. K3 put wrong numbers and unsupported claims on a page When Kimi K3 updated one of our monthly field notes pages, a review by another model looking for faults found wrong numbers and claims the records did not support, and a page far too long. A different model applied the fixes. At home one K3 answer took 124.5 minutes On one desktop with a 32 GB graphics card, the downloaded Kimi K3 wrote about 0.2 tokens a second (a token is a word or part of a word). One answer took 124.5 minutes. That suits one question answered overnight, not chat. So a model from a different maker checks Kimi’s work, just as Kimi checks theirs. Grant’s note “More than with any other provider, I find myself hitting the five-hour usage window with Kimi, so I’m less inclined to let it run a long project the way I let Claude run them.” Grant Williams, who runs this lab The facts What they cost Per million tokens Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3 What you send $2.00 $3.00 What you send again (cached) $0.20 $0.30 Saving to the cache for 5 minutes $2.00 $3.00 Saving to the cache for 1 hour $4.00 $6.00 What it writes $10.00 $15.00 These are Moonshot’s API prices. Kimi K3’s price is the same at every prompt length. Batch jobs are billed at 60% of the standard price for both. A faster version, Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed, costs more. Kimi Code and Kimi memberships are priced separately. What they take in and give back Both read text and images and write text. Moonshot’s developer pages also list video. Both hold up to 1,048,576 tokens at once. Both always think before they answer. You can set how hard they think: low, high or max, and max is the default. How we run them Mostly through Kimi Code, Moonshot’s coding agent, signed in with a Kimi Code subscription, and sometimes through OpenCode, an open-source coding agent. Every tool shares one allowance, and the tight limit is a rolling window of a few hours, so we pace heavy bursts of work. Most of our recent work used Kimi K3.1 Pro, the newer model in the K3 family, which Kimi Code now offers first. Older work, and the examples above that say Kimi K3, used K3 itself. Can I run them at home? Only with a lot of disk and patience. We ran Kimi K3 at home. The compressed build we used needed roughly 600 GB of free disk. On one desktop with a 32 GB graphics card and 188 GiB of RAM it wrote about 0.2 tokens a second, because the disk, not the graphics card, set the speed. We sent one complete question at a time and came back hours later. The full recipe is on our page on running it at home. Kimi K3.1 Pro is the same size class as K3, so we judged it no more practical here. Moonshot recommends running either with vLLM, SGLang or TokenSpeed. License and where you can use them Each has its own license from Moonshot: the Kimi K3 License and the Kimi K3.1 Pro License. Read them before any commercial use: both set extra conditions for large companies that sell access to the model and for very large products. Moonshot offers both in Kimi Code and through its API at platform.kimi.ai, and K3.1 Pro also on Kimi.com. The Kimi K3 weights came out in July 2026. Kimi K3.1 Pro came out in October 2026 as a further-trained version of K3, and its weights followed in November. From Moonshot AI’s own pages (platform.kimi.ai, kimi.com and its Hugging Face cards), read 21 November 2026.
