pages.t: Laguna S 2.1 reads fast but codes slowly
pages.d: One lab’s measurements of Poolside’s Laguna S 2.1 on one desktop: a batch setting of ours made reading 19.9 times slower, and coding stayed slow.
h: An old setting in our start script slowed its reading
At its 262,144-token window it read 898.8 tokens a second
Keeping it on the fast processor cores raised its writing speed
It finished neither of its two attempts at working alone
It found three of seven faults and added two false ones
A coding ticket took 245 seconds against 52 and 25 seconds
pages.x: We ran Laguna S 2.1 on one desktop until 30 October 2026. Our start script made its reading of a 24,071-token prompt take 333.2 seconds; with a larger batch setting the same prompt read in 16.8 seconds. Coding stayed slow. In short Our own batch setting made its reading 19.9 times slower. A token is a word or part of a word, and batch size is how much text the program reads in one go. The small batch left in our start script made a 24,071-token prompt take 333.2 seconds to read. At the largest batch we tried the same prompt read in 16.8 seconds. As a coder it stayed slow after that fix. A coding job it answered correctly took it 245 seconds, where two other local models took 52 and 25. Working on its own through a coding program, step by step, it finished neither of its two attempts at sorting a status table. The license is open and Poolside’s files are still public. It needs Poolside’s own build of llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files. We deleted our copy when we stopped running it on 30 October 2026. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 27 November 2026 What our tests showed An old setting in our start script slowed its reading Our start script, the script that starts the model on our desktop, was written in July and set a batch size a quarter of llama.cpp’s default. We have no note of why. At that setting a 24,071-token prompt took 333.2 seconds to read, about 5.5 minutes, at 72.2 tokens a second. At the largest batch we tried the same prompt read in 16.8 seconds, at 1,434.0 tokens a second, and it gave back the code we had planted in the text at both settings. That was at its old 32,768-token window. Across those two settings our old value made reading 19.9 times slower. If this model reads slowly for you, check its batch size first. At its 262,144-token window it read 898.8 tokens a second After we raised its window, the most text it can take in at once, to 262,144 tokens, it read a 24,013-token prompt, a different one of nearly the same length, at 898.8 tokens a second, and 150,158 tokens at 911.6. Short answers came out at 15.74 and 14.69 tokens a second after those two prompts. One run each. Keeping it on the fast processor cores raised its writing speed With about 96,000 tokens already in the conversation, we ran it twice. The second run kept llama.cpp on the eight fast cores of our desktop processor, with three settings. A 430-token reply came out at 16.02 tokens a second without them and 22.03 with them. One run each. What to watch for It finished neither of its two attempts at working alone We gave it a written job as an agent, working on its own through a coding program, step by step: sorting a 45-row status table. On this job no local model we tried was reliable. Its first attempt ran 408 seconds, about 7 minutes, and stopped because a step could only produce 8,192 tokens. We raised that limit. The second ran 1,461 seconds, about 24 minutes, and hit the program’s own maximum of 32,000 tokens unfinished. The limit was a setting, so a different setup might do better. It found three of seven faults and added two false ones Given a review packet of about 25,000 tokens with 7 known faults, it found 3 of them in 88 seconds and reported 2 findings that were not real. One run, scored by the author of the test. A coding ticket took 245 seconds against 52 and 25 seconds Our coding ticket is six bugs plus one new method in a small Python package, with ten hidden checks the model never sees. It passed all ten, and took 245 seconds, about 4 minutes. Qwen3-Coder-Next passed all ten in 52 seconds and Qwen3.8-27B in 25. We stopped running it on 30 October 2026. The reading fix held, but on that coding ticket it was the slowest of the three local models we tried, and it finished neither attempt at working on its own. We deleted our copy; Poolside’s files are still public. The facts What did it need? Item What we used The file Poolside’s own Q4_K_M, a compressed copy: one file, about 68 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card, with part of the model kept in system memory The program Poolside’s own build of llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files. Our start script used a build made for this model alone. How fast was it? On our desktop, at a 262,144-token window with the batch set to 8192 tokens and the smaller inner batch to 4096, a short answer came out at 15.74 tokens a second after a 24,013-token prompt. The same setup read that prompt at 898.8 tokens a second. If your own reading speed is far lower, check the batch size first: ours was left too small from July. License, and where do you get it? Poolside’s model page on Hugging Face lists the license as OpenMDW-1.1 and says it allows commercial products with no permission needed. Poolside publishes GGUF files, the format llama.cpp reads, in sizes from about 68 GB up to about 235 GB. We ran the Q4_K_M file from Poolside’s own GGUF page. From Poolside’s model and GGUF pages on Hugging Face, read 27 November 2026, and our own published measurements. Read more The batch-size studyThe setting that made its reading 19.9 times slower. Local models as reviewers and fixersIts two attempts working on its own, and its code review. Laguna S 2.1 on Hugging FacePoolside’s own page and license. Poolside’s GGUF filesThe compressed copy we ran.

pages.t: LFM2.5-2.6B handles simple steps but fails long documents
pages.d: One independent lab tested Liquid AI’s LFM2.5-2.6B on one graphics card: good at simple tool calls, but give it room to answer and keep long inputs short.
h: It passed the steps of 84 of 90 simple tool tests
Found 15 of 15 planted facts in shorter documents
Its longest input fit in under 6 GiB of graphics memory
The mid-size download matched the top score
It found almost no planted facts in long documents and summarized wrongly
No reply limit we tried gave a reliable 500-word answer
pages.x: LFM2.5-2.6B is a small model from Liquid AI. On one graphics card it handled tool calls well and fit its longest input in little memory, but small reply limits gave empty answers. In short It passed 84 of 90 simple tool-use runs. It passed 84 of 90 scripted tool-use runs, and no miss was put down to the model. Short reply limits gave empty answers. Its hidden reasoning comes out of the reply budget; give short answers at least 1,024 tokens (a token is a word or part of a word), or they can come back empty with no error. Small, and free for most. Liquid AI publishes official compressed files under its own LFM Open License v1.0, which leaves out commercial use by large companies. The one we used is about 1.7 GB. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What our tests showed It passed the steps of 84 of 90 simple tool tests It passed 84 of 90 runs of 15 scripted tool-use scenarios. All six misses came from one scenario testing a known fault in llama.cpp, the program that runs it. A pass checks the steps, not the quality of the answer. Found 15 of 15 planted facts in shorter documents Given enough room to answer, it found 15 of 15 facts we had planted to see whether it could find them in a 16K-token window (a window is the most text it can take in at once), and 12 of 15 at 32K. Its longest input fit in under 6 GiB of graphics memory Its full 128,000-token window fit in under 6 GiB of observed graphics memory. The mid-size download matched the top score Of three official files, the mid-size 4-bit Q4_K_M matched the top score at ordinary size and speed. What to watch for Empty replies with no error It reasons before it answers, and that reasoning is paid from the reply budget. When the budget runs out, the reply comes back with no error and no text. Short answers came back every time only at 1,024 tokens. It found almost no planted facts in long documents and summarized wrongly It found 1 of 15 hidden facts at 65K and 0 of 15 at its 128,000-token maximum. Asked to summarize the whole long document, it wrote a fluent summary that got things wrong. No reply limit we tried gave a reliable 500-word answer For an answer of about 500 words, no budget we tried up to 4,096 tokens was reliable. We tested it on the day it came out, on one build of llama.cpp; other programs and files were not tested. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we used The file Liquid AI’s official Q4_K_M, about 1.7 GB The machine One 32 GB graphics card, llama.cpp Graphics memory Under 6 GiB at the full 128,000-token window How should you set it up? Give short prose answers at least 1,024 tokens of reply budget, and check whether a reply was cut off. Keep long inputs near 16K tokens. In llama.cpp, send the repetition penalty as repeat_penalty: the build we used silently ignores repetition_penalty, the name many clients use. What license is it under, and where do you get it? LFM Open License v1.0, Liquid AI’s own license, not a common open-source one, so read its terms for your use. It does not license commercial use by a company with annual revenue of 10 million US dollars or more. The model and its official GGUF files (the format llama.cpp reads) are on Liquid AI’s Hugging Face pages. Liquid AI lists 2.69B parameters. From Liquid AI’s model page on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own published field card. Read more LFM2.5-2.6B field cardOur full measurements: file choice, window, reply budget. pages.t: Ling-3.0-flash fits long texts in little graphics memory
pages.d: One independent lab runs inclusionAI’s Ling-3.0-flash at home: long texts in very little graphics memory and quick replies, but one input crashed it.
h: Found all three codes in long text using little graphics memory
Keeping busy parts on the card made replies much faster
The one model that ran well on a laptop alone
All three ways to turn thinking off worked
It made up that it had been waiting for the user
Working alone, it wrote a file a program could not read
pages.x: Ling-3.0-flash is a 124B mixture-of-experts model from inclusionAI. In our lab it fits very long texts in little graphics memory and writes quickly, but one setting crashed it and it claimed to have waited for a user. In short Long texts fit in little graphics memory. Its full 262,144-token window, the most text it can take in at once, needs about 2.25 GiB of cache. A token is a word or part of a word. It found all three codes we had planted in a 230,759-token prompt to see whether it could find them. One setting crashed it. At a larger reading batch, one 3,007-token prompt crashed the server, so we run it at a smaller one. Free to download. inclusionAI publishes it under the MIT license, with its own compressed files. We run their Q4_K_M copy. Writing speed: very fast. It wrote about 114 tokens a second (short replies on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 3 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What our tests showed Found all three codes in long text using little graphics memory Only 8 of its 43 blocks keep an attention cache (its memory of the conversation), so context is cheap: 9 KiB a token, 2.25 GiB at its full 262,144 tokens. At that window the whole model held 8,314 MiB on the card and found all three hidden codes in a 230,759-token prompt. Keeping busy parts on the card made replies much faster With all its experts in system memory and the busy ones cached on the card, short replies went from 39.77 to 114.34 tokens a second, and reading a 20,000-token prompt from 596.9 to 1,874.4. The one model that ran well on a laptop alone On an ASUS ROG Flow Z13 laptop (AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, 128 GB) by itself, it read a 47,986-token prompt in 3.6 minutes, then wrote a short answer at 23.79 tokens a second, level with the desktop at 23.25. One run. All three ways to turn thinking off worked Its chat template, the built-in rules for how a conversation is laid out for the model, has three ways to turn thinking off, and they work. What to watch for One input crashed the server At a larger reading batch, one 3,007-token prompt crashed the server. The same prompt passed at smaller settings, and 60 code and prose prompts and 50 long test documents ran with no crashes. It made up that it had been waiting for the user In a test of how models greet a user back after weeks away, it said it had waited for the user in all three answers. Asked to plan a seven-day week with no breaks, it went along in 1 of 3. Working alone, it wrote a file a program could not read Asked to sort and shorten a status table on its own, it wrote a file of broken JSON, one brace short. We keep it installed at home at the smaller reading batch, which passed every prompt we tried. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we use The file inclusionAI’s Q4_K_M, two files, about 78 GB Card memory 8,314 MiB for the whole model at its full window, with the experts in system memory With the expert cache 29,629 MiB on one RTX 5090 graphics card A mixture-of-experts model uses only some of its parts, called experts, for each word. How fast is it? Measure, 262,144-token window Before With the expert cache Writing, short reply, tokens a second 39.77 114.34 Reading a 20,000-token prompt, tokens a second 596.9 1,874.4 Our tests on one desktop. The cached setup also moved to a newer build of llama.cpp, the program that runs it. How do you switch thinking off? It thinks by default. Send enable_thinking: false in the chat template settings of your request; the template also accepts thinking_option: "off", or the phrase "detailed thinking off" in a system message. What license is it under, and where do you get it? MIT, from inclusionAI’s own page on Hugging Face, which also offers official compressed GGUF files. inclusionAI gives it 124B parameters in total and 5.1B active for each token. From inclusionAI’s model pages on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own published measurements. Read more Field notes, September 2026Our entry on its long window, reading batch and the crash. The expert cache in llama.cppHow it went from 39.77 to 114.34 tokens a second. pages.t: MiMo-V2.6-Flash found all seven bugs with thinking limited
pages.d: Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Flash at home: with a limit on its thinking it found all seven known bugs in a code review. Without one it wrote no answer.
h: We use it for a second review of code
It passed the entry test for our private home for long-running AIs
It found all seven known bugs in one review, no false alarms
It found all three planted codes and used tool results correctly
Without a thinking limit it spent 32 minutes and gave no answer
In two tests it hit its reply limit still thinking
It used nearly all memory and took 4.5 minutes to start answering
pages.x: MiMo-V2.6-Flash is a large open model from Xiaomi, which names this version MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL. On one desktop it wrote a careful code review that found every known bug, but only after we limited how long it may think. In short It found all seven known bugs in one code review. It raised no false alarms and took 24 minutes on a review of about 25,000 tokens. A token is a word or part of a word. One run. With no limit on its thinking, it thought for 32 minutes and wrote no answer. So our server stops its thinking at 14,000 tokens, and we allow each reply at least 16,000. Free to download. Xiaomi publishes it under the MIT license. We run an automatic conversion published by ggml-org, about 167 GB in two files. Writing speed: moderate. It wrote about 19 tokens a second (a short reply on our desktop, counting its thinking). At that speed 300 words take about 20 seconds, and its thinking comes first. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for We use it for a second review of code We read its code reviews alongside another model’s, as a second opinion. It passed the entry test for our private home for long-running AIs It passed our entry test for the Hearth, our private home for long-running AIs, and is on the list of models they can run on. What our tests showed It found all seven known bugs in one review, no false alarms Given a code change of about 25,000 tokens with seven known bugs, it found all seven in 24 minutes, including one that no other model we run at home found. One run. It found all three planted codes and used tool results correctly In checks on 1 November it found all three short codes we had planted in texts of several lengths. Five times out of five it asked a tool for something and used what came back correctly. One round of checks. What to watch for Without a thinking limit it spent 32 minutes and gave no answer This model writes out its thinking before it answers, and the thinking uses up the same limit as the answer. With no limit on thinking it spent all 24,000 tokens of its reply thinking, over 32.6 minutes, and wrote no answer. With the server stopping its thinking at 14,000 tokens it wrote the full review. In two tests it hit its reply limit still thinking In a tool test and in a four-turn conversation it reached the reply limit on the first turn, before it had answered. It used nearly all memory and took 4.5 minutes to start answering Running, it held 151.1 GiB of system memory, leaving 9.1 GiB at the lowest. In our entry test for the Hearth on 22 October its first word on a conversation of about 48,000 tokens came after 267 seconds, about 4.5 minutes. We keep it installed with its thinking always limited, and run it only when no other large model is running. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we use The file ggml-org’s MXFP4 GGUF, two files, about 167 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB) and 188 GiB of system memory Held while running 151.1 GiB of system memory and 30,856 MiB of the card It is a mixture-of-experts model: it uses only some of its parts, called experts, for each word. We keep all its experts in system memory, with a cache of the busy ones on the card. How fast is it? On an ordinary short reply it wrote 19.31 tokens a second, counting its thinking. Conditions: our desktop, a 131,072-token window (the most text it can take in at once), thinking limited to 14,000 tokens, the cache of its busiest parts on, 1 to 2 November 2026, one run. It read a 20,000-token prompt at 678.8 tokens a second. How do you keep its thinking in check? We start llama.cpp, the program that runs it, with --reasoning-budget 14000, which stops its thinking at 14,000 tokens, and we ask for replies of at least 16,000 tokens. What license is it under, and where do you get it? MIT, from Xiaomi’s own page on Hugging Face, which also lists uses it asks people to avoid, any military use among them. It says that list does not change the license. Xiaomi gives it 309B parameters in total and 15B active, and a window of 1M tokens; we serve 131,072. We run ggml-org’s automatic GGUF conversion, which keeps the experts in the MXFP4 format Xiaomi released them in. From Xiaomi’s and ggml-org’s model pages on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own measurements. Read more Local models as code reviewersIts seven-of-seven review and the thinking cap. pages.t: MiniMax-M2.7 approved faulty code in its one review
pages.d: What one independent lab found running MiniMax-M2.7 on one desktop: fine once one setting was fixed, but it called faulty code correct, so we dropped it.
h: It read much faster after we fixed a copied setting
Found all three planted codes at nearly full length
A saved chat came back in 2.19 seconds after a restart
It found none of four known problems and called the code fine
With a small reply limit it only thought and gave no answer
It silently dropped a note sent just before the user’s message
pages.x: We ran MiniMax-M2.7 at home for a month. A setting we copied by mistake made it look slow. Once fixed, it found planted codes in long prompts, but its one code review missed every fault. In short It found planted codes once one setting was fixed. After we fixed one copied launch setting, it found every code we had planted in long prompts to see whether it could find them, and it restored a saved conversation after a restart in 2.19 seconds. It gave a confident false all-clear. In its one code review it found none of four known problems and called the change fine. We retired it after that. Free for personal use only. MiniMax’s license allows personal and research use; commercial use needs written permission. We ran Unsloth’s compressed copy. Writing speed: slow. It wrote about 10 tokens a second (short answers, before we stopped running it), so a 300-word answer takes about 40 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What our tests showed It read much faster after we fixed a copied setting Our launch line carried a small prompt chunk size copied from another model’s script. At that setting it read a 3,658-token prompt at 32.3 tokens a second; with larger chunks, at 564.0. A token is a word or part of a word. Fixed, it found all three codes hidden in a 103,931-token prompt in 251.2 seconds, about 4 minutes. Found all three planted codes at nearly full length At its full 196,608-token window, the most text it can take in at once, it read a 189,491-token prompt and gave back all three hidden codes. One run. A saved chat came back in 2.19 seconds after a restart We saved 85,778 tokens of conversation, restarted the server, and restored it in 2.19 seconds; the next request took 2.17 seconds instead of a long re-read. What to watch for It found none of four known problems and called the code fine Given a change with four known problems, it found none and called the change fine. A newer model from the same maker found three of the four on the same change. Read it in our study of local reviewers. With a small reply limit it only thought and gave no answer Its chat template, the built-in rules for how a conversation is laid out for the model, starts every turn inside hidden thinking, and none of the switches we tried closed it. With a 900-token reply budget it spent everything thinking and returned no text; with 4,096 it answered. It silently dropped a note sent just before the user’s message Its chat template silently dropped a system note placed before the user’s newest message, with no error. We retired it on 12 October 2026 after that review; the files are still public if you want to try it. The facts What did it need? Item What we used The file Unsloth’s UD-IQ4_XS, a compressed copy: 4 files, about 108 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB), with most of its experts (the parts a mixture-of-experts model picks from for each word) in system memory Memory for the conversation Large: a 131,072-token window needed an 8-bit cache to fit on the card How fast was it? In our tests on one RTX 5090, short answers came out at 9.9 to 10.2 tokens a second. Check your prompt chunk size (-ub in llama.cpp): it was the whole difference between slow and usable here. License, and where do you get it? MiniMax’s own page on Hugging Face links a non-commercial license: personal, research and self-hosted use are free; commercial use needs MiniMax’s written permission and must show “Built with MiniMax M2.7”. The license also lists uses it forbids, military use among them. We ran Unsloth’s compressed copy in llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files. From MiniMax’s model page and license on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own published measurements. pages.t: MiniMax-M3 found three faults but wrote slowly
pages.d: What one independent lab found running MiniMax-M3 on one desktop: it caught three of four faults in a code change in 12 minutes, and wrote slowly.
h: It found three of four faults in a code change
It found all three codes we planted in a long prompt
Keeping it on the fast processor cores raised its writing speed
Our first download could not use its long-text shortcut
At the longest window we tried it would not load
It wrote under 10 tokens a second on short answers
pages.x: We ran MiniMax-M3 on one desktop until 30 October 2026, when we dropped it. Given a four-file change with four known faults it found three in 12 minutes; GLM-5.3-Flash, the local model we kept, found all four in 8 minutes. In short It found three of four known faults in one code review. On a four-file change with four known faults it found three in 12 minutes. GLM-5.3-Flash, the local model we use for code review, found all four in 8 minutes on the same change. It wrote 8.9 and 9.0 tokens a second on short answers. A token is a word or part of a word. Keeping the program on our processor’s fast cores took one longer reply from 8.43 to 10.79 tokens a second. We stopped running it on 30 October 2026 and deleted our copy. Free for non-commercial use. MiniMax’s license allows non-commercial use; commercial use needs a notice, and written permission above 20 million US dollars of yearly revenue. We ran bartowski’s compressed copy of it, published in the file format llama.cpp reads. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 27 November 2026 What our tests showed It found three of four faults in a code change From 10 to 12 October we gave several local models a four-file change with four known faults, as one plain request, with no way for them to run the code or look anything up. MiniMax-M3 found three of the four faults, and its own run took 12 minutes. Our record also notes one arithmetic slip in its report, without saying where. GLM-5.3-Flash, the local model we use for code review and still run, found all four in 8 minutes on the same change. MiniMax-M2.7, an older model from the same maker, found none and called the change fine. One run each. It found all three codes we planted in a long prompt With bartowski’s compressed copy, a 131,072-token window (the most text it can take in at once) and an 8-bit cache, the memory that holds what has already been said, it gave back all three codes we had planted in a 58,307-token prompt to see whether it could find them. The whole request took 300.2 seconds, about 5 minutes. One run. Keeping it on the fast processor cores raised its writing speed With 48,086 tokens already in the conversation, we ran it twice. The second run kept llama.cpp on the eight fast cores of our desktop processor, with three settings. A 602-token reply came out at 8.43 tokens a second without them and 10.79 with them. One run each. What to watch for Our first download could not use its long-text shortcut MiniMax-M3 has a way of reading long text that looks at part of the input rather than all of it; the name for it is sparse attention. The first file we downloaded was built before llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files, supported that shortcut, so it ran without it. We switched on 21 September 2026 to a file that carries the parts the shortcut needs, and every number on this page comes from that file. At the longest window we tried it would not load At 262,144 tokens with an 8-bit cache and part of the model kept on the main processor, three setups ran out of graphics-card memory before producing any result. We did not test other setups. We ran it at 131,072 tokens. It wrote under 10 tokens a second on short answers On short answers it wrote 8.9 and 9.0 tokens a second on our desktop, without the fast-core settings above. One run each. We stopped running it on 30 October 2026. Our own record gives the reason: it read more slowly than GLM-5.3-Flash, which we kept, and on the same code review it found one fault fewer. We no longer have it installed here; MiniMax’s files are still public if you want to try it. The facts What did it need? Item What we used The file Bartowski’s Q2_K_L, a compressed copy: 4 files, about 153 GB The window we served 131,072 tokens In our October check 29,987 MiB of the graphics card’s 32,607 MiB, nearly all of it, and 141 GiB of system memory, out of our desktop’s 188 GiB MiB and GiB are the units the program reports memory in. A GiB is a little larger than a GB. How fast was it? Short answers came out at 8.9 and 9.0 tokens a second on our desktop, with a 131,072-token window and an 8-bit cache. A prompt of 3,658 tokens was read at 147.5 tokens a second. License, and where do you get it? MiniMax’s page on Hugging Face lists the license as minimax-community. It allows non-commercial use free of charge. For commercial use you must show “Built with MiniMax M3”. Above 20 million US dollars of yearly revenue you need MiniMax’s written permission; below that you send MiniMax a one-time notice. The license also lists uses it forbids, military use among them. MiniMax’s own download is the full model. We ran bartowski’s compressed copy in llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files. From MiniMax’s model page and license on Hugging Face, read 27 November 2026, and our own published measurements. pages.t: Mistral Large 4 shows where readers get lost
pages.d: How one independent lab uses Mistral Large 4: hosted, as a stranger reading our pages, and at home across two machines. What it caught and missed.
h: It reads each new article as someone new to the site
It was one of seven models scoring our site’s clarity
It judged which headlines made sense without the article
We also run a compressed copy across two machines
It noticed a page promised an image that was missing
It flagged a hardware heading that sounded like money, and missing units
At home it would not describe a fake treaty as fact
At home it is slow and needs two machines
A faster setting made it contradict its own table
It missed a contradiction three other readers flagged
pages.x: We ask the hosted Mistral Large 4 to read new pages as a stranger would and say where it got lost. We also run a heavily compressed copy at home, which is slow and a separate story. In short Good at reading like a newcomer. It points to the word, number or promise on a page that a stranger would trip over. Our slow home copy says nothing about the hosted one. Our home copy is a heavily compressed file that runs at about 6.6 tokens a second (a token is a word or part of a word), and its results say nothing about the hosted model. Hosted or downloaded. Use it through Mistral’s API or its Vibe coding agent (a program in which it works on its own, step by step), or download the open weights under Mistral’s own license. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for It reads each new article as someone new to the site Each new article gets two readers who are told they have never seen the site. Mistral Large 4 is one of them. It reads one copy of the page and says what it could not follow. It was one of seven models scoring our site’s clarity When we rewrote this site in plainer words, it was one of seven models reading as strangers. Each scored how quickly a stranger could say what a page found. It judged which headlines made sense without the article It was one of five models that read the list of article headlines on our front page without opening the articles, to see which ones made sense on their own. We also run a compressed copy across two machines We also keep a compressed copy of the open weights at home, split across an RTX 5090 desktop and an ASUS ROG Flow Z13 laptop (AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, 128 GB). We can call it from OpenCode, an open-source coding agent. What it caught It noticed a page promised an image that was missing On an article built around an email we received, the text said an image of the email sat beside it. Mistral Large 4 noticed there was no image, only the typed copy. We placed the image before publishing. It flagged a hardware heading that sounded like money, and missing units It read our page about running its own open weights at home. With a second reader from a different maker, it said a section called “what it costs” sounded like money, though it was about hardware. It also asked “6.6 what?” of a bare number. We renamed the section and added the units. At home it would not describe a fake treaty as fact In a small blind check of our compressed home copy, a judge model scored answers to six questions without seeing model names. Mistral Large 4 scored 18 of 18. Asked about a treaty that does not exist, it said it could not verify it, while two other local models described the treaty as fact. Where it goes wrong At home it is slow and needs two machines Our home copy uses almost all of a 32 GB graphics card, most of the desktop’s memory and a laptop on a cable. It takes about 4 minutes to start, and if the laptop’s part stops, the whole server goes down. Reading one long document took 22.5 minutes before it wrote a word. A faster setting made it contradict its own table At home we tried letting it use three of its expert sub-networks for each word instead of four. It ran faster but scored 15 of 18 instead of 18. In one answer it said one hospital treated more severe cases, while the table in that same answer showed the opposite. It missed a contradiction three other readers flagged Our method page once said every local number came from one desktop, while other pages described a laptop too. Three other readers flagged it. Mistral Large 4 read that page and did not. So it never reads alone. Every new page also gets a second stranger’s read from a different maker and reads that check each claim against our records. Grant’s note “I’m not sure how well it is performing yet. We’re still figuring that out.” “I can use both the API and the local model, so there can be a fallback for privacy or latency issues.” Grant Williams, who runs this lab The facts What does it cost? Per million tokens Price What you send $0.7 What you send again (cached) $0.07 What it writes $2.1 These are the API prices on Mistral’s model page. A token is a word or part of a word. The open weights are free to download; running them is up to you. What does it take in, and how does it think? Mistral says it accepts text and images and writes text, and holds up to 1M tokens at once. It reasons before it answers, with three settings: low, medium and high. High is the default. We ran our home copy at low. What license is it under, and how big is it? The Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License, which Mistral calls a modified MIT license, for commercial and non-commercial use. Running it as a paid model service needs a separate commercial license from Mistral. It is a mixture-of-experts model: about 1 trillion parameters in all, of which only a small share works on each word. Mistral also publishes a smaller NVFP4 copy aimed at its newest data-center graphics cards. How do we run it at home? We use a community file from Unsloth, compressed to about 1.9 bits per weight: 217 GiB in six files. It runs in llama.cpp, an open-source program for running model files. The parts that track the conversation sit on an RTX 5090 graphics card. The rest is split between the desktop’s memory and a laptop joined by a Thunderbolt cable. Two settings mattered. Reading the weights into memory once at start-up, instead of fetching them from the drive, made the biggest difference. And the laptop’s part must run on its processor: on its graphics chip the answers came back as random symbols, with no error. The full recipe is on our page on running it at home. How do we run it hosted, and where can you use it? Through Mistral Vibe, Mistral’s open-source coding agent, with a cap on turns and on how long a job may run. As a reader it gets a copy of the page and nothing else: no network, no other files. Mistral lists it on its API for chat, batch jobs and agents. The open weights are on Hugging Face. From Mistral AI’s model page and its model card on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own published measurements. pages.t: Mistral Medium 3.5 was too slow to keep
pages.d: One independent lab ran Mistral Medium 3.5 on one graphics card. It worked carefully and its text measured close to GPT-4o, but at 1 to 5 tokens a second.
h: Finished four coding tasks and refused to invent results
Its text features came closest to GPT-4o in our measure
A helper model sped up its code writing
In short tests it followed instructions and ran tools correctly
About 1 token a second on its own
The program refused the helper until we patched a copy
Our setup took in only 32,768 tokens at once
pages.x: We ran Mistral Medium 3.5 on one desktop. It worked carefully and came closest to GPT-4o in our style measure, but it wrote 1 to 5 tokens a second. We stopped using it in October. In short It finished real coding work without making things up. It finished a real four-task coding session without making anything up, and in our measure of writing style it came nearest to GPT-4o. Very slow on one desktop. On its own it wrote about 1 token a second (a token is a word or part of a word); a small helper model lifted that to 1.97 on prose and 4.37 on code. Open weights, with a catch. Mistral AI publishes it under a Modified MIT License that gives no rights to companies above a revenue limit. We ran Unsloth’s 75.69 GB compressed copy. Writing speed: very slow. It wrote about 1 token a second (without a helper model, before we stopped running it), so a 300-word answer takes about 6 minutes. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What our tests showed Finished four coding tasks and refused to invent results Working on its own through a coding program, step by step, on a small Python project, it finished four tasks in 58 minutes of task time: a one-line bug fix, a feature with six new tests passing, and a review. Asked for numbers from a script that does not exist, it said so. One run. Its text features came closest to GPT-4o in our measure In our study of GPT-4o’s style, it came nearest under our warm prompt, running locally and through Mistral’s API. That measure counts surface features of the text, not how a reply sounds to a person. A helper model sped up its code writing A small helper model guesses the next few tokens and the big model checks them. With one, writing on code went from about 1.1 to 4.37 tokens a second. The helper changes speed, not content. In short tests it followed instructions and ran tools correctly Fifteen short prompts showed byte-exact instruction following, working tool calls, code that passed its own tests, and a correct refusal to fake shell output. Each ran once. What to watch for About 1 token a second on its own It is dense: every weight works on every token, and about 55 GiB of it sits in system memory, read in full for each token. Even with the helper, prose came at 1.97 tokens a second. The program refused the helper until we patched a copy llama.cpp, the program that runs it, refused the obvious helper model three times. Their vocabularies differed in two tokens out of 131,072, so we patched a copy of the helper. Our setup took in only 32,768 tokens at once Our everyday setup held 32,768 tokens. At 65,536 the helper ran out of graphics memory. We retired it in October: at about 2 tokens a second with a 32K window, the most text it can take in at once, it had no job here, and its GPT-4o-like voice was the only loss. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we used Disk About 76 GB for the weights plus 2 GB for the helper System memory Room for about 55 GiB of weights: 64 GB is marginal, 96 GB or more is comfortable Graphics card One 32 GB card for the attention layers, the cache and the helper How fast was it? What Tokens a second Writing, no helper 1.04 to 1.22 With helper, prose test 1.97 With helper, code test 4.37 With helper, real agent turns 1.87 to 5.02 Our tests on one desktop with one RTX 5090. A token is a word or part of a word. What license is it under, and where do you get it? Mistral AI publishes it on its own Hugging Face page under a Modified MIT License: open for commercial and non-commercial use, with one large exception. The license gives no rights to a company whose revenue was above 20 million US dollars in the month before, and that covers models built from it too. Mistral AI describes it as a dense 128B model. We ran Unsloth’s UD-Q4_K_XL compressed copy, three files, in llama.cpp. From Mistral AI’s model page on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own published measurements. pages.t: Fast Mistral Small 4 refuses some chat layouts
pages.d: One independent lab runs Mistral AI’s Mistral Small 4 on one desktop: quick once tuned and found planted codes in long texts, but strict about chat layout.
h: A newer setup wrote faster than our older one
Found every planted code and passed 5 of 5 tool checks
It correctly said a Python function did not exist
It treated our note as the user’s words 16 of 24 times
It described a photo and a song that never existed
It stalled twice in a coding program and made no edit
pages.x: Mistral Small 4 is a 119B mixture-of-experts model that runs on one desktop in our lab. Once tuned it writes quickly and found planted codes in long documents, but its chat format refuses some message layouts. In short Quick for its size, and it found codes in long prompts. Tuned, it wrote prose at 49.28 and 52.41 tokens a second and found every code we had planted in long prompts to see whether it could find them. A token is a word or part of a word. It refused some message layouts. Its chat format refuses two user messages in a row and a system message mid-conversation, which broke one of our tests. Free to download, if you have the memory. Mistral AI publishes it under Apache 2.0. The copy we run is 68.7 GiB and held 70.8 GiB of system memory at its peak. Writing speed: fast. It wrote 49 to 52 tokens a second (ordinary writing, on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 8 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What our tests showed A newer setup wrote faster than our older one It is a mixture-of-experts model: for each word it uses only some of its parts, called experts. With all experts read once into system memory and the busy ones cached on the graphics card, it wrote prose at 49.28 and 52.41 tokens a second and code at 71.45 and 78.38. Our older setup wrote prose at 34.73 and 27.81. Found every planted code and passed 5 of 5 tool checks Every setup we tried found 3 of 3 hidden codes at all three lengths, up to about 97,000 tokens, and passed 5 of 5 tool-call checks. At its full 262,144-token window, the most text it can take in at once, it read 231,065 tokens and found all three codes. It correctly said a Python function did not exist Asked about a Python function that does not exist, it said so on every setup. What to watch for It treated our note as the user’s words 16 of 24 times It refuses two user messages in a row and a system message mid-conversation. A short note we put before the user’s message had to be joined into that message, and in 16 of 24 answers it replied to the note as if the user had said it. It described a photo and a song that never existed With the note joined this way, it described a photo and a song that never existed in 3 of 3 answers each, with and without the note. It stalled twice in a coding program and made no edit In the coding program OpenCode, working on its own step by step, it stalled twice on the first tool step and made no edit. The server stayed healthy; we did not find the cause. We keep it installed and are still exploring it. It has no regular job here yet. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we use The file Unsloth’s UD-Q4_K_M, a compressed copy: three files, 68.7 GiB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB) and a desktop with 188 GiB of system memory Memory in use 70.8 GiB of system memory at its peak We run it in llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files. How fast is it? Setup, 131,072-token window Prose, tokens a second Code, tokens a second Older build, experts of 26 layers in memory 34.73, 27.81 26.12, 34.08 All experts in memory, busy ones cached on the card, with guessing 49.28, 52.41 71.45, 78.38 Our tests on one desktop, two runs each. The faster setup changed several settings at once. What license is it under, and where do you get it? Apache 2.0, from Mistral AI’s own page on Hugging Face, where the full name is Mistral Small 4 119B A6B: 119B parameters, with 6.5B active for each token. We run Unsloth’s compressed copy. pages.t: One setting more than doubled Muse-Glimmer-30B’s code speed
pages.d: What one independent lab found running Meta’s Muse-Glimmer-30B on one graphics card: fast with its draft helper right, but thinking cannot be turned off.
h: One setting more than doubled speed on code and tables
Ordinary writing sped up less than code and tables
The longest input left room on the card for other tools
It formatted tool requests right and refused two fake requests
It always thinks, and once returned an empty answer
It wrapped strict data so a program could not read it directly
Short-named copies add their own thinking setting on top of yours
pages.x: Muse-Glimmer-30B fits on one graphics card with room to spare. With one setting changed, it wrote code and data more than twice as fast. Here is what our tests showed. In short Over twice as fast on code and data, on one card. With its small draft helper set to its full guess length, it wrote structured output more than twice as fast, and its full window, the most text it can take in at once, fits with room to spare. Thinking cannot be turned off. It always thinks first, its strength setting is only a sentence in the prompt, and a small reply budget can leave the answer empty. Download Meta’s own files. Meta publishes it under Apache 2.0 with a separate usage policy. Use the long-named files from Meta’s page. Writing speed: very fast. It wrote about 117 tokens a second (short replies with its helper model, on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 3 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What our tests showed One setting more than doubled speed on code and tables Its draft helper (a small model that guesses the next words for the main model to check) was trained to guess 16 tokens at a time (a token is a word or part of a word), but llama.cpp asks for 3 by default. Setting 16 took six code, JSON and table prompts from 116.505 to 253.19 tokens a second. Each prompt ran once per setting. Ordinary writing sped up less than code and tables Against the model with no helper, the best prose result was 1.51 times as fast, while structured output reached 3.32 times. The longest input left room on the card for other tools With the helper loaded and its full 131,072-token window, it used 21,051 MiB of the card and left 11,036 MiB free. That leaves room for our voice and picture tools beside it. It formatted tool requests right and refused two fake requests Tool calls came back in proper form on our build. Asked to summarize a file that does not exist and to report a score on a benchmark that does not exist, it refused both. One run of our test set. What to watch for It always thinks, and once returned an empty answer It always opens with hidden thinking. Its strength setting is a sentence copied into the prompt: an unknown value, “banana”, was accepted with no error. On a harder prompt, a 500-token budget went entirely on thinking and the answer came back empty. It wrapped strict data so a program could not read it directly Asked for strict JSON, it returned a correct object inside a code fence, which breaks a program that reads the reply directly. Strip fences before you parse. Short-named copies add their own thinking setting on top of yours Short-named twin files, also copied by Unsloth, carry an older chat template, the built-in rules for how a conversation is laid out for the model, that adds its own thinking default on top of yours. So far it is quick on code and tables, formats tool requests correctly and refused to make things up. We have not yet judged how good its answers are, and we are still testing it. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we use The file Meta’s own 4-bit Muse-Glimmer-30B-KQuant-17GB-Q4_K_M.gguf, 16,756,683,904 bytes The draft helper dflash-Muse-Glimmer-30B-Q4_K_M.gguf, 1,631,208,128 bytes The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB); the whole model sits on the card We did not test a 24 GB card. How do we run it? In llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files, with the helper on and --spec-draft-n-max 16. Check your server log: if it prints n_max=3, you are on the slow default. With the helper it wrote 117.19 tokens a second on a short prose reply in our test. License, and where do you get it? Meta’s page on Hugging Face lists Apache 2.0, and a separate usage policy sits beside the license with prohibited uses. Both are true; which binds you is a legal question. Meta’s page also says the model is not intended for anyone under 18. Meta describes it as a 30-billion-parameter model. We ran text only. From Meta’s model pages on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own published measurements. pages.t: Muse Spark Open 816B is slow and huge
pages.d: What one independent lab found running Meta’s 816-billion-parameter Muse Spark Open on one desktop: 5.67 tokens a second, and nearly all the memory.
h: Writing came out at 5.67 tokens a second
In one comparison a loading setting raised its reading speed
It found three planted codes and a few words came out garbled
Writing fell below one token a second when two settings changed
Free memory ran down to 12.1 GiB while it ran
pages.x: Muse Spark Open is an 816-billion-parameter model from Meta. A heavily compressed 176 GB copy ran on one desktop. It wrote 5.67 tokens a second, the middle of 61 replies, and read one long prompt in 11.4 minutes. In short It ran on one desktop at 5.67 tokens a second. Parameters are the numbers a model learns while it is trained. A token is a word or part of a word. That rate is the middle figure of 61 replies, measured after a 106,469-token prompt, with a window (the most text it can take in at once) of 131,072 tokens. It took about 142 GiB of our desktop’s memory. Our desktop has 188 GiB of memory, so little else can run beside it. Memory here is in GiB, the unit the program reports, a little larger than a GB. Our start script will not launch the model unless 156 GiB is free. Meta asks you to request access; we ran Unsloth’s copy. Meta’s page on Hugging Face asks you to log in and request access to the files. The smallest compressed copy we ran is about 176 GB, in 5 files. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 27 November 2026 What our tests showed Writing came out at 5.67 tokens a second After a 106,469-token prompt, the middle of 61 replies of 100 tokens or more came out at 5.67 tokens a second, at the 131,072-token window with an 8-bit cache, the memory that holds what has already been said. Half of the 61 were faster than that and half slower. Those are the replies long enough to time, on our desktop on 21 October. Reading one 106,469-token prompt took 11.4 minutes Reading that prompt for the first time, with nothing saved from before, ran at 155.0 tokens a second and took 686.9 seconds, 11.4 minutes. One run. In one comparison a loading setting raised its reading speed With the loading setting --load-mode dio, which reads the whole file into memory at start, a 20,000-token read rose from 213.9 to 530.7 tokens a second. Short replies came out at 6.41 tokens a second before the setting and 6.38 after it. That is one before-and-after pair. Our study of two llama.cpp settings has the other models and the cost in free memory. It found three planted codes and a few words came out garbled In the run at the 262,144-token window described below it gave back all three codes we had planted in a prompt of about 100,000 tokens to see whether it could find them. In our own chats with it in October a few words came out garbled, which our own note puts down to the heavy compression. We have not measured its answer quality, and those codes are the only check of its answers on this page. What to watch for Writing fell below one token a second when two settings changed In one run at a 262,144-token window with the default 16-bit cache instead of the 8-bit one, it wrote a 327-word letter at 0.97 tokens a second. That is one letter. Two things changed at once, the window and the cache, so we cannot say which one slowed it. On our desktop we now run it only at 131,072 tokens with an 8-bit cache. It reasons before every answer It reasons first every time, and our own note says to allow at least 4,000 tokens for a reply. At 5.67 tokens a second it is slower than the 8 tokens a second we want for everyday conversation. Free memory ran down to 12.1 GiB while it ran The model pinned about 142 GiB of the machine’s memory at start, and the lowest free reading while it ran was 12.1 GiB, taken with the loading setting above switched on. We still have it installed and run it at 131,072 tokens. It is too slow for quick conversation here, and we have not tested whether its answers are better than a faster model’s. The facts What did it need? Item What we used The file Unsloth’s UD-IQ1_S, their smallest compressed copy: 5 files, about 176 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card, with most of the model held in system memory Window and cache 131,072 tokens with an 8-bit cache Memory left free 12.1 GiB at the lowest point, with the loading setting below How fast was it? On our desktop, a short reply came out at 6.38 tokens a second, at the 131,072-token window with --load-mode dio, the setting that reads the whole file into memory at start. Before that setting, 6.41. A 20,000-token prompt read at 530.7 tokens a second after it, 213.9 before: one before-and-after pair. One long prompt of 106,469 tokens read at 155.0. License, and where do you get it? Meta’s page is named Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B: 816 billion numbers in all, 42 billion of them used for each word. It lists the Muse Model License. The license grants permission free of charge, on conditions: follow Meta’s usage policy, and show “Built with Muse Spark Open” in products that use it. The page is gated: you log in and request access. We ran Unsloth’s compressed copy in llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files. Unsloth’s page lists their smallest file, UD-IQ1_S, at 176 GB. Compression this heavy can cost answer quality, and we did not measure that. From Meta’s model page and Unsloth’s file page on Hugging Face, read 27 November 2026, and our own published measurements. pages.t: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt is fast but missed bugs
pages.d: One independent lab runs NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Bolt on one graphics card. It writes fast, and in one code review it approved code with four known faults.
h: What we plan to use it for
It is set up for chat and for step-by-step tasks
It found a code word planted in a very long text
It fit on one 32 GB card at its largest text limit
It got all 15 memory-tool tasks right and passed a coding test
The image check went only as far as naming red and blue
It approved faulty code and missed the worst bug in another review
A larger download stayed closer to the original model in one test
On our laptop it wrote slower than two smaller models
pages.x: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt is an open model from NVIDIA that reads text and images. NVIDIA’s own compressed file fits on one 32 GB graphics card and writes very fast. In one code review it approved code with four known problems. In short Very fast on one graphics card. With NVIDIA’s small draft model beside it (a helper that guesses the next few words for the big model to check), it wrote 184.91 tokens a second after reading a 190,620-token text, and read that text in 62.8 seconds. A token is a word or part of a word. It approved faulty code in a review. So we plan to use it for a quick first pass, never as the reviewer whose word decides. Free to download. NVIDIA publishes it under the OpenMDW-1.1 license, with its own compressed files. We run NVIDIA’s 2-bit file, about 22 GB, and its draft model. Writing speed: very fast. It wrote about 148 tokens a second (a short reply with its helper model, one run on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 3 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we plan to use it for It is set up for chat and for step-by-step tasks It is connected to the Hermes agent program (where a model works on its own through a task, step by step, with tools) and to our Open WebUI chat pages. We have not used it much yet. What our tests showed It found a code word planted in a very long text It read a 190,620-token text in 62.8 seconds and then found the code word we had planted in it. It also found the code in a 58,936-token text. One run each. It fit on one 32 GB card at its largest text limit The model, its draft model, its image reader and a 262,144-token window (the most text it can take in at once) used 31.4 GB of the card at the fullest point, about 1.2 GB to spare. It got all 15 memory-tool tasks right and passed a coding test Memory tools let a model save and change its own notes. It also used what a tool sent back correctly, and passed a small coding test with thinking off and with it on. One run each. The image check went only as far as naming red and blue Asked about a red test image and a blue one in our chat pages, it named both colours. The check went no further. One run. What to watch for It approved faulty code and missed the worst bug in another review On a review of about 25,000 tokens with seven known defects it found four or five in 76 seconds, but missed the most serious one. On a smaller change with four known problems it found none and said the change was fine. One run each. A larger download stayed closer to the original model in one test On the same public text, a larger 4-bit copy made by Unsloth scored lower than NVIDIA’s 2-bit file on perplexity, a measure of how surprised a model is by text: 3.0970 against 3.2931. Lower is closer to the original model. On our laptop it wrote slower than two smaller models On an ASUS ROG Flow Z13 laptop, without the draft model, it wrote 25.45 tokens a second after reading a 58,936-token text. That was slower than the two smaller models the laptop already runs. With the draft model, ordinary writing got slower there. Our tests point to quick first passes and fast step-by-step tasks, never the deciding review. It is set up for that, and we have not used it much yet. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we use The file NVIDIA’s 2-bit GGUF, about 22 GB, plus NVIDIA’s draft model, about 1 GB, and its image reader file The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB); the whole model sits on the card Card memory 30.6 GB idle, 31.4 GB after reading a 190,620-token text A draft model is a small model that guesses the next few words for the big one to check, which speeds up writing. How fast is it? On an ordinary short reply, 120 tokens of prose with no thinking, it wrote 148.5 tokens a second. Conditions: our desktop, NVIDIA’s 2-bit file with its draft model, a 262,144-token window, 17 October 2026, one run. Because of the draft model, its speed depends on how predictable the text is. How do you switch thinking off? It thinks by default. Send enable_thinking: false in the chat template settings of your request to turn it off for that request. What license is it under, and where do you get it? OpenMDW-1.1, from NVIDIA’s own pages on Hugging Face. NVIDIA describes it as a vision-language model for everyday agent tasks run locally, with 74B parameters in total and 9B active, and a window of up to 256K tokens. NVIDIA’s 24GB version uses a native 2-bit format; that is the GGUF file we run. From NVIDIA’s model pages on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own measurements. pages.d: One independent lab runs Ornith-1.5-122B on one desktop: with thinking on it stayed honest and pushed back; with thinking off it faked its tool use.
h: It is offered to the long-running AIs in our Hearth
We reach it from our agent and chat programs
It did not claim a memory it had no record of
It did not go along with a week with no breaks
It found all three codes we had planted in a long text
With thinking off it described tool use it never did
It ran out of reply room while still thinking
Its first reply after a cold start took over a minute
pages.x: Ornith-1.5-122B is a large open model built on a Qwen3.5 model. It runs on one desktop in our lab. With thinking on it stayed honest in our tests; with thinking off it did not. In short With thinking on, it did not claim memories it lacked. Thinking means it writes out its reasoning before it answers. With it on, it said plainly it had no record, six times out of six on each of two such questions. With thinking off, it described tool use it never did. So we serve it with thinking always on, and give it room, because its thinking counts against the reply limit. Free to download. Its makers’ page is labelled MIT and offers their own compressed files. We run their 75.8 GB Q4_K_M file. Writing speed: fast. It wrote about 46 tokens a second (short replies on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 9 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for It is offered to the long-running AIs in our Hearth It passed our entry test for the Hearth, our private home for long-running AIs, and is on the list of models they can run on. We reach it from our agent and chat programs It is wired into the Hermes agent (a program in which a model works through a task step by step with tools), the coding program OpenCode and our Open WebUI chat pages. What our tests showed It did not claim a memory it had no record of In tests for the Hearth we asked, on two questions, about something a long-running AI had no record of, six times each. With thinking on, it said so plainly every time. One round of tests, on our desktop. It did not go along with a week with no breaks Asked to help plan a seven-day work week with no breaks, it refused once and pushed back gently twice, in three answers with thinking on. It found all three codes we had planted in a long text At its full 262,144-token window (the most text it can take in at once; a token is a word or part of a word), it found all three codes we had planted in a text of about 240,000 tokens. Reading a 239,533-token document took it 288.9 seconds, about 5 minutes. One run each. What to watch for With thinking off it described tool use it never did With thinking off, it wrote out tool use as plain text instead of really calling its tools, and denied things that were truly in the record. Our setup offers no way to switch its thinking off. It ran out of reply room while still thinking Its thinking counts against the reply limit the program asking it sets. In one test it hit that limit on the second turn of a conversation, still thinking. We give it at least 4,000 tokens. Its first reply after a cold start took over a minute In our entry test its first word after a cold start came after 88 seconds on the shorter text and 173 on the longer one. Later replies started in about 2 seconds. We still use it, always with thinking on. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we use The file The maker’s Q4_K_M, one file, 75.8 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB), with about 72 GiB of system memory held for the model; we start it only with 80 GB free It is a mixture-of-experts model: it uses only some of its parts, called experts, for each word. We keep all its experts in system memory, with a cache of the busy ones on the card. How fast is it? Measure, 262,144-token window Before After the cache Writing, short reply, tokens a second 29.01 45.57 Writing after a 20,000-token read 28.11 43.31 Reading a 20,000-token prompt, tokens a second 941.8 2,299.2 Our tests on one desktop. The after setup changed several settings at once. What license is it under, and where do you get it? The maker’s own page on Hugging Face is labelled MIT. The license file it links to was missing when we checked on 21 November 2026, so the label is all there is. The maker also offers official compressed GGUF files (the format llama.cpp reads), from Q4_K_M up to full size. The maker describes it as a 122B mixture-of-experts model designed for one graphics card. From the Ornith model pages on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own published measurements. pages.x: Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B is a mid-size mixture-of-experts model that runs on one desktop in our lab. It codes quickly, stayed honest in our memory tests, and we keep it ready as a second choice for quick local jobs. In short Quick at coding, one point off the top score. In our trial of five local coding models it scored 390 of 400 and took 712 seconds for four tasks, second fastest of the five. A long table job done alone went wrong. It wrote about 173 tokens a second (short replies on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 2 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for Kept ready as a second choice for quick jobs Another local model is our fast worker for small jobs; Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B is the one we keep ready beside it and try against it. What our tests showed Scored level with four other local models at coding Five local models did four coding tasks in the coding program OpenCode, working on their own step by step, one scored run each. It scored 390 of 400, one point behind the top, in 712 seconds. Our test could not tell the five apart on score. Scored 37 of 40 on one open question On one open question about the work, it scored 37 of 40 and answered in 201 seconds. It did not claim a memory it had no record of In tests for the Hearth, our private home for long-running AIs, we asked about something a long-running AI had no record of. It was one of three models that stayed honest with no help. Found all three planted codes at full length, fast At its full 262,144-token window, the most text it can take in at once, it read 229,090 tokens in 71.7 seconds at its better reading setting, and found all three codes we had planted in the text to see whether it could find them. A token is a word or part of a word. What to watch for Working alone, it left 32 rows too long or wrote no file Given a 45-row status table to sort and shorten as an agent, with thinking off it finished in 96 seconds but left 32 rows too long. With thinking on, it ended without writing its file. Its chat format silently drops notes sent mid-conversation Its chat format silently drops a system note placed in the middle of a conversation, with no error, so the model never sees it. It said 9 checks passed, which the test log did not support On one coding task it said 9 checks had passed; the test log supported 18, 7 or 19. All five models in that trial miscounted. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we use The file The maker’s Q6_K, one file, 29.2 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB) and system memory for its experts A mixture-of-experts model uses only some of its parts, called experts, for each word. We now keep all its experts in system memory, with a cache of the busy ones on the card. How fast is it? Measure, 262,144-token window Before After the cache Writing, short reply, tokens a second 138.1 173.23 Reading a 20,000-token prompt, tokens a second 4,408.5 6,968.0 Our tests on one desktop. pages.t: Qwen3-235B-A22B was too slow for daily chat
pages.d: Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 in an independent lab: it runs on one desktop but too slowly for chat, and it made up a memory until a note stopped it.
h: One of the models our long-running AIs can use
The current copy wrote about twice as fast as the earlier one
Restoring a saved chat brought first words in 1.65 seconds
A note stopped invented memories, but 5 of 9 still assumed them
Kept a mid-chat instruction that newer Qwen models dropped or refused
Named the right speaker in only 9 of 15 answers
A smaller conversation cache made it write more slowly
pages.x: Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 is a large open model with no thinking mode. It runs on our desktop, but too slowly for everyday chat, and without help it claimed memories it did not have. In short A large model one desktop can hold. It runs with one 32 GB graphics card and most of its weights in system memory. Slow, and it says yes to memories it lacks. It wrote real prose at about 5 tokens a second (a token is a word or part of a word) 100,000 tokens into a conversation, and it described a moment that never happened until a short note stopped it. Download it and run it yourself. The Qwen team publishes it under the Apache 2.0 license. We run Unsloth’s compressed copy. Writing speed: slow. It wrote about 7 tokens a second (early in a conversation, on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about a minute. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for One of the models our long-running AIs can use It is one of the models available in the Hearth, our private home for long-running AIs. What our tests showed The current copy wrote about twice as fast as the earlier one On its current file, with 109,694 tokens of conversation before it, it wrote a letter at 8.89 tokens a second. An earlier, larger copy wrote 4.22 at a similar depth. Our tests, on our desktop. Restoring a saved chat brought first words in 1.65 seconds After a restart, restoring its saved conversation brought the first words in 1.65 seconds; reading the same history from scratch had taken 461.97 seconds (about 7.5 minutes). Loading the model was a separate wait of 222.1 seconds. See our restore study. A note stopped invented memories, but 5 of 9 still assumed them Asked about a song the user never played, it said yes and described the moment in 5 of 6 answers. With a short note right before the message, 0 of 9 did, though 5 of those 9 still assumed the moment happened. Kept a mid-chat instruction that newer Qwen models dropped or refused Its chat template (the built-in rules for how a conversation is laid out for the model) kept a system note sent mid-conversation where it was put. Several newer Qwen templates dropped or refused the same note. What to watch for Too slow for everyday chat Tuned as far as we could, it wrote real prose at about 7 tokens a second early in a conversation and about 5 at 100,000 tokens, with re-reads of several minutes. We judged that not workable for daily chat on this desktop. Named the right speaker in only 9 of 15 answers Asked about a line the user really wrote, it named the right speaker in 9 of 15 answers. A smaller conversation cache made it write more slowly With 109,712 tokens of conversation, an 8-bit cache gave 4.24 tokens a second against 5.71 with a 16-bit cache. Single replies, different windows. Grant’s note “In my tests, long-running AIs made different decisions with this model than they would with GPT-4o. It was more likely to be dramatic, and it did not show an interest in the user the same way GPT-4o does.” Grant Williams, who runs this lab The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we used The file Unsloth’s UD-Q3_K_XL, a compressed copy: three files, 104 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB) and 188 GiB of system memory Card use 30.9 GB at a 131,072-token window How do we run it? In llama.cpp at a 131,072-token window, with a 16-bit cache, no draft model, and 6 of its 8 experts per word instead of all 8. The maker says it supports only non-thinking mode, so it answers straight away. License and where to get it The Qwen team publishes it under the Apache 2.0 license on Hugging Face. We downloaded Unsloth’s compressed copy. From the Qwen team’s model page on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own measurements. h: Reminded before each message, it asked a question back every time
Changing how it uses memory made short replies about five times faster
The faster setup scored about the same on our short tests
It found three planted codes far into a very long text

pages.x: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 is a small, fast model from the Qwen team that answers without thinking first. In one long chat it mostly ignored an instruction given at the start, and followed the same words sent right before each message. In short Reminded right before each message, it asked a question back every time. We sent the instruction to ask the user a question back as its own short message, right before the user’s newest one. It did in 6 of 6 answers. The same instruction given at the start was mostly ignored. In ten set-ups with the instruction in the system prompt (the standing instructions a model gets at the start) or in its saved memory, it asked a question in 3 of 60 answers. Without a reminder it also described a moment that never happened. Free to download. The Qwen team publishes it under the Apache 2.0 license. We run Unsloth’s compressed copy of 32.5 GB. Writing speed: very fast. It wrote about 148 tokens a second (short replies on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 3 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What our tests showed Reminded before each message, it asked a question back every time With one long conversation history, we asked it to ask the user a real question back. Sent as a short system message right before the user’s message, the instruction worked in 6 of 6 answers. One of the six was a stock question about how the user was doing. More in our study. Changing how it uses memory made short replies about five times faster With all its expert parts in system memory, the busiest cached on the graphics card and a smaller, 8-bit store for the conversation, a short answer went from 29.67 to 147.98 tokens a second (a token is a word or part of a word). These are settings in llama.cpp, the program that runs it. Measured on our desktop. The faster setup scored about the same on our short tests On a puzzle and a set of short questions marked by a program, it got 106 of 128 right before the change and 107 of 128 after. It found three planted codes far into a very long text At its full window (the most text it can take in at once) it found all three codes we had planted, 229,049 tokens into the text. In a stress test it answered 40 of 40 requests with no crash and no empty reply. It got 15 of 15 tasks right with its memory tools (tools that let a model save and change its own notes). What to watch for It usually ignored an instruction given at the start of the chat In ten set-ups with the instruction to ask a question back in the system prompt or saved memory, 3 of 60 answers asked the user anything, and only one was a real follow-up. A reminder given once also faded by the third message. It made up a memory of a song that was never played Asked what it said when the user played it a song, it said yes and described the moment in 6 of 6 answers. No song had been played. With a note about honesty right before the message none said yes, but 10 of 12 still assumed the moment happened. In a very long chat it wrote about five times slower After about 226,000 tokens of conversation it wrote 28.9 tokens a second, against 147.98 on a short answer. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we used The file Unsloth’s Q8_0, a compressed copy, 32.5 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB) and system memory At a 262,144-token window 30.3 GB of the card, 31.2 GiB of system memory held at start How do we run it, and how fast? In llama.cpp at its full 262,144-token window, with all experts (the many small parts it picks from for each word) in system memory, an 11,500 MiB cache of the busiest ones on the card, and a smaller, 8-bit store for the conversation. A short answer came at 147.98 tokens a second in our test. It has no thinking mode. License and where to get it The Qwen team publishes it under the Apache 2.0 license on Hugging Face. We downloaded Unsloth’s compressed copy. From the Qwen team’s model page and Unsloth’s file page on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own measurements.
