pages.t: Two large Qwen3.5 models for conversation and reasoning
pages.d: Two large open Qwen3.5 models on one home desktop: how fast they wrote, the guessing setting that slowed creative text, and where they fell short.
h: The 122B is offered to the long-running AIs in our Hearth
The 122B wrote faster than the 397B on our desktop
Without a cutoff, its word guessing slowed creative writing
Both found all three planted codes in one long prompt
The 122B solved a hard puzzle when it had room to think
The 122B came back empty three times at a 700-token limit
Sorting a table alone, both did very badly
Both silently dropped an instruction placed before the user’s message
pages.x: We ran the Qwen3.5 122B and 397B on one desktop with a 32 GB graphics card and a lot of system memory. Both worked. Here is what our tests showed, and what to set first. In short Large open models you can run at home. On our desktop the 122B wrote about 26 to 38 tokens a second and the 397B about 14 to 20. A token is a word or part of a word. Without two settings, replies came back slower or empty. Give the built-in guessing feature a confidence cutoff, and give thinking plenty of room, or replies can come back slower or empty. Download them, if you have the memory. The Qwen team publishes both under Apache 2.0. Our compressed copies were 73.43 GB and 149.84 GB, held in system memory beside one graphics card. Qwen3.5-122B is moderate. It wrote 26 to 38 tokens a second (on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 12 seconds. Qwen3.5-397B is moderate. It wrote 14 to 20 tokens a second (on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 25 seconds. Those times are worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for The 122B is offered to the long-running AIs in our Hearth The 122B passed our entry test for the Hearth, our private home for long-running AIs, and it is on the list of models they can run on. We keep the 122B for fast everyday deep conversation and the 397B for hard reasoning. What our tests showed The 122B wrote faster than the 397B on our desktop With one RTX 5090 and 188 GiB of system memory, the 122B wrote about 26 to 38 tokens a second and the 397B about 14 to 20. One setup each, measured in August; the details are on our field card. Without a cutoff, its word guessing slowed creative writing Both files carry a small built-in part that guesses the next few words for the model to check. Without a confidence cutoff, the 122B wrote two creative prompts more slowly than with guessing off. With the cutoff at 0.75, 88 to 95 percent of guesses were kept on every shape we measured. Both found all three planted codes in one long prompt At their full 262,144-token window (the most text they can take in at once), both found all three hidden codes (codes we had planted in the text to see whether they could find them) in a prompt of about 230,000 tokens. One run each. The 122B solved a hard puzzle when it had room to think On a puzzle about timing 15 minutes with two hourglasses, the 122B ran out of room at 8,192 tokens and finished in 9,719 tokens with a 16,384 limit. We judged its answer correct. One run. What to watch for The 122B came back empty three times at a 700-token limit Both think before they answer, and the thinking counts against the reply limit. When the limit is too low, the request still succeeds and the answer is empty. The 122B came back empty three times in one evening at a 700-token limit. Sorting a table alone, both did very badly Asked as agents (working on their own through a coding program, step by step) to sort a 45-row status table, both did far worse than a test draft we had filled with mistakes on purpose, with rows wrongly archived (filed away as finished) and rows left too long. One run each, in our study of local models. Both silently dropped an instruction placed before the user’s message Their chat templates (the built-in rules for how a conversation is laid out for the model) silently dropped a system note placed right before the user’s message, with no error. Check where your note lands before you rely on it. The facts What do you need to run them? Item What we used 122B file Unsloth’s UD-Q4_K_S, a compressed copy: three files, 73.43 GB 397B file Unsloth’s UD-IQ3_XXS: four files, 149.84 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB) and 188 GiB of system memory The weights must fit in system memory. With less, they stream from disk and every number here changes, in ways we did not measure. How do we run them, and how fast? In llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files, with the guessing feature on and its cutoff at 0.75, and the weights copied into memory rather than read from disk as needed. Reading from disk as needed cut the 397B’s prompt reading by 82 percent. Model Writing, tokens a second 122B about 26 to 38 397B about 14 to 20 Our test, on our desktop, one request at a time. License and where to get them The Qwen team publishes both under the Apache 2.0 license on Hugging Face. We run Unsloth’s compressed copies that keep the built-in guessing part. From the Qwen team’s model pages on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own published measurements. pages.x: Qwen3.5-27B is a dense open model that fits whole on one 32 GB graphics card. We tested it for long conversations at home. It found planted codes and did not invent a memory, but it is strict about instructions. In short Found planted codes deep in long chats on one card. With a 262,144-token window on one 32 GB card, it found hidden codes at about 229,000 and 250,000 tokens. The window is the most text it can take in at once, a token is a word or part of a word, and the hidden codes were codes we had planted in the text to see whether it could find them. It refuses a second instruction with an error. Its chat template (the built-in rules for how a conversation is laid out for the model) refuses a second system message with an error, so notes have to go in as user messages. Download it and run it yourself. The Qwen team publishes it under the Apache 2.0 license. We run Unsloth’s compressed copy. Writing speed: fast. It wrote about 45 tokens a second (deep in a long conversation, on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 9 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for Grant uses it to give a long-running AI its voice It is one of the models Grant uses to carry the personality of a long-running AI in conversation. He finds both 27B Qwen models good for conversation and for holding a character. What our tests showed Took in a long chat in under a minute, all on one card With 106,129 tokens of conversation before it and thinking off, it wrote a reply at 45.24 tokens a second and read that prompt in 54.7 seconds. Our test, on our desktop. Found all three planted codes at about 229,000 and 250,000 tokens At its full window it found all three hidden codes at about 229,000 and 250,000 tokens, and a crash check passed 40 of 40. Never described a photo that was not sent, in a small test After a long conversation history, we asked about a photo the user never sent. With no memory note it never described one; with a short note it said plainly there was none in 3 of 3 answers. Three answers each: a small test. What to watch for Rejects a second system instruction with an error, and developer messages It refuses a system message after the first one with an error (HTTP 500), and its template also refuses a developer message. A note in mid-conversation has to go in as a user message. Without a note, two answers still assumed the photo moment happened Without the note, two of its three answers about the photo hedged: they did not describe it, but still assumed the moment happened. Two lightly retrained copies invented the photo, unlike the original Two small adapters (light extra training on our own examples) invented the photo that the untuned model never did. See our adapter study. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we used The file Unsloth’s UD-Q5_K_XL, a compressed copy, about 20 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB) Card use at the full window 30.3 GB, with an 8-bit cache The cache is the model’s memory of the conversation; at this window a 16-bit cache does not fit. How do we run it? In llama.cpp at a 262,144-token window. Thinking is off by default and can be switched on per request. The server sends the maker’s suggested settings for each mode, including a presence penalty of 1.5. License and where to get it The Qwen team publishes it under the Apache 2.0 license on Hugging Face. We downloaded Unsloth’s compressed copy. From the Qwen team’s model page on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own measurements. h: Grant uses it to give a long-running AI its voice
Wrote more slowly deep into a long chat
Found all planted codes at both lengths and passed 40 crash checks
Told to be curious, it asked back in 18 of 24 answers
Shortlisted as one of two local models for long-running AIs

pages.x: Qwen3.6-27B is a dense open model that fits on one 32 GB graphics card. We tested it for long conversations at home. It found codes we planted in long chats, but working alone on one job it did poorly. In short Found planted codes in long chats on one card. With a 262,144-token window on one 32 GB card, it found hidden codes in prompts of about 53,000 and 103,000 tokens. The window is the most text it can take in at once, a token is a word or part of a word, and the hidden codes were codes we had planted in the text to see whether it could find them. It silently drops some instructions, and one copy would not load. Its chat template (the built-in rules for how a conversation is laid out for the model) silently drops a system note sent mid-conversation, and the copy in Ollama’s library would not load in llama.cpp. Download it and run it yourself. The Qwen team publishes it under the Apache 2.0 license. We run Unsloth’s compressed copy, which keeps a built-in guessing part. Writing speed: fast. It wrote about 61 tokens a second (with a 20,000-token conversation before it, on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 7 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for Grant uses it to give a long-running AI its voice It is one of the models Grant uses to carry the personality of a long-running AI in conversation. He finds both 27B Qwen models good for conversation and for holding a character. What our tests showed Wrote more slowly deep into a long chat In July, through Ollama, a 4-bit copy wrote 72 tokens a second fully on our card. With our current file in llama.cpp at its full window, it wrote 60.9 tokens a second with 20,000 tokens of conversation before it, and 34.6 at 230,000. Our test, on our desktop. Found all planted codes at both lengths and passed 40 crash checks At its full window it passed our long-conversation check: all three hidden codes at about 53,000 and 103,000 tokens, and tool calls at about 206,000. A crash check passed 40 of 40. Told to be curious, it asked back in 18 of 24 answers We counted how often it asked the user a real question back. With thinking off and a memory note alone it did so in 9 of 24 answers; when the note also asked for curiosity, 18 of 24. Shortlisted as one of two local models for long-running AIs In tests for the Hearth, our private home for long-running AIs, it was one of two local models we kept as contenders. What to watch for Sorting a table alone, it invented 4 rows and misfiled 4 Asked as an agent (working on its own through a coding program, step by step) to sort a 45-row status table, it did very badly, with 4 rows wrongly archived (filed away as finished) and 4 invented rows. One run, in our study of local models. It silently drops an instruction sent just before the user’s message Its chat template silently drops a system note placed right before the user’s message. The server answers as normal and the instruction never arrives. The Ollama library copy would not load in llama.cpp The copy in Ollama’s model library is missing one value in its header, and every llama.cpp build here refused it in under a second. Unsloth’s file loaded. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we used The file Unsloth’s UD-Q5_K_XL with a built-in guessing part, about 20 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB) Card use at the full window 29.9 GB, with an 8-bit cache The window is how much text the model holds at once; the cache is its memory of the conversation. How do we run it? In llama.cpp at a 262,144-token window. At that window the guessing part is turned off, because it does not load there. Thinking is off by default and can be switched on per request; with it off we use temperature 0.7, top_p 0.8 and top_k 20. License and where to get it The Qwen team publishes it under the Apache 2.0 license on Hugging Face. We downloaded Unsloth’s compressed copy, not the copy in Ollama’s library. pages.t: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B handles small jobs fast but needs checking
pages.d: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B in an independent lab: very fast on one graphics card, good at small jobs one at a time, poor when left alone as an agent on a long job.
h: Handling many small items, one at a time
Pulled quotes from records, but only six in ten were exact
Wrote very fast, and stayed fast in a long chat
One row at a time got half marks, full marks once checked
Fixed three known defects with thinking on, one after a retry
Told to be curious, it asked back in 13 of 24 answers
Working alone on the whole table, it invented rows and lost links
With thinking on, it needed a 16,384-token reply limit to pass
With thinking on, 10 of 24 answers asked a generic welfare question
pages.x: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B is a mixture-of-experts model: large in total, small for each word. It is the fastest model we run at home for small, many-item jobs. Alone on a long job, it did poorly. In short Fast on small jobs when another model checks it. Sent one item at a time by a script, with another model checking and plain code fixing slips, it did a table job with full marks. Do not leave it alone on a long job. As a lone agent (working on its own through a coding program, step by step) on the same job it did very badly. Download it and run it yourself. The Qwen team publishes it under the Apache 2.0 license. We run Unsloth’s compressed copy of 29.3 GB. Writing speed: very fast. It wrote about 175 tokens a second (short replies on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 2 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for Handling many small items, one at a time A script sends it one item at a time and checks each reply. A different model checks its work, and plain code fixes small slips. Pulled quotes from records, but only six in ten were exact In an older job it pulled facts and quotes out of long records for our private archive, one bounded batch at a time. Only six quotes in ten came back word for word, so a script now checks every quote it gives. What our tests showed Wrote very fast, and stayed fast in a long chat Through Ollama in July it wrote 227 tokens a second (a token is a word or part of a word) fully on our card. In llama.cpp at its full window (the most text it can take in at once), with its most-used parts cached on the card, it wrote 162 to 174 tokens a second on prose and 124 with about 229,000 tokens of conversation before it. Our test, on our desktop. One row at a time got half marks, full marks once checked On a 45-row table job, sent one row per call by a script, it got about half marks. With a different model checking its done rows and plain code fixing slips, the chain got full marks. One run of each step, on one table. Fixed three known defects with thinking on, one after a retry Given three real defects and the source file, with no tools, it fixed all three, one after a retry, in 58 to 115 seconds each, with thinking on. Told to be curious, it asked back in 13 of 24 answers With thinking off and a memory note alone it asked the user a real question back in 0 of 24 answers; when the note also asked for curiosity, 13 of 24. What to watch for Working alone on the whole table, it invented rows and lost links Asked as an agent to sort the whole 45-row table at once, it did very badly: 5 rows wrongly archived (filed away as finished), 2 invented rows and 4 lost links. One run. With thinking on, it needed a 16,384-token reply limit to pass With thinking on, it needed a 16,384-token reply allowance to pass our memory-tool check every time. With thinking on, 10 of 24 answers asked a generic welfare question With thinking on and the curiosity note, 10 of 24 answers carried a question about rest, a welfare question that could be asked in any conversation. It stays our fast worker for small jobs, always with a check after it. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we used The file Unsloth’s UD-Q6_K, a compressed copy, 29.3 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB) and system memory At a 262,144-token window 30.0 GB of the card, about 28 GB of system memory held How do we run it, and how fast? In llama.cpp, with all of its experts (the many small parts it picks from for each word) in system memory and an 18,000 MiB cache of the busiest ones on the card. That setup took short replies from 131.06 to 175.30 tokens a second in our test. Thinking is switched with enable_thinking in each request. License and where to get it The Qwen team publishes it under the Apache 2.0 license on Hugging Face. We downloaded Unsloth’s compressed copy. pages.t: Qwen3.8-27B writes and fixes our code at home
pages.d: How one independent lab uses Qwen’s Qwen3.8-27B: as its coder and everyday model on one graphics card. What it built, where it slips, what it needs.
h: Writing code on its own in OpenCode
Fixing what another model’s review finds
Default model in our everyday Hermes agent
Also run from a second computer in the house
Finished fastest of five, with scores too close to rank
Fixed two defects, then five faults the tests had missed
Refused to summarize a missing file or invent a test score
With thinking on, it thought through whole steps and made no edit
Found 3 of 8 known problems and said no changes were required
Gave no visible answer with a 60-token budget
pages.x: Qwen3.8-27B runs on one graphics card in our lab. It writes and fixes our code and handles everyday work. Here is what it did well and where it let us down. In short Scored level with four others and finished fastest. In our test of five local coding models it scored level with the rest and finished the tasks fastest. Turn its thinking off when it codes on its own. With thinking on it can spend its whole budget thinking and hand back no edit, or no answer at all. Download it and run it yourself. The Qwen team publishes it under the Apache 2.0 license, and it fits on one large graphics card. Writing speed: fast. It wrote about 72 tokens a second (short replies on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 6 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What we use it for Writing code on its own in OpenCode It works in OpenCode, an open-source coding agent (a program it works through on its own, step by step) that edits files and runs tests itself. For this job we turn its thinking off. Fixing what another model’s review finds It writes a fix, a model from a different maker reviews the change, and it fixes what the review found. A larger hosted model reads the result before anything lands. Default model in our everyday Hermes agent It is the default model in the Hermes agent we use day to day. When it is off, a hosted model takes over. Also run from a second computer in the house We also start it from a second computer in the house, for chat and coding there. What it did well Finished fastest of five, with scores too close to rank In our coding trial, five downloadable models did the same four coding tasks. Their scores were too close to rank, and Qwen3.8-27B scored 391 of 400. It finished all four tasks in 448 seconds (about 7.5 minutes), against 6,058 (about 101 minutes) for the slowest model. Fixed two defects, then five faults the tests had missed With thinking off, we gave it two real defects to fix as an agent. It fixed both, and the tests passed 53 of 53. A review then found faults the tests had missed, and a second round fixed five, with 70 of 70 tests passing. That is in our study of local models. Refused to summarize a missing file or invent a test score On the day it came out we ran it through a set of quick checks. Asked to summarize a file that does not exist and to report a score on a test that does not exist, it refused both. It wrote “I won’t invent a numeric score.” Our automatic grader marked that a fail; a person reading it saw a pass. Where it goes wrong With thinking on, it thought through whole steps and made no edit As a coding agent with its thinking left on (the default), it spent whole steps of 32,000 tokens (a token is a word or part of a word) thinking and made no edit. That happened in three runs across two jobs. Turning thinking off fixed it. Found 3 of 8 known problems and said no changes were required Asked to review a large security change, it found 3 of 8 known problems and said “No code changes required”. It called two of the most serious items fine. A reader who trusted that verdict would have acted on it. Gave no visible answer with a 60-token budget Its hidden thinking counts against the same output limit as its answer. Asked for a short explanation with a 60-token budget, it returned no visible answer at all. On the same day a simple sum came back fine at that budget, so the floor depends on the question. So we use it to write and fix code, not to judge it. A model from a different maker reviews its work, and no local “pass” is taken as the verdict. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we measured The file we use Unsloth’s UD-Q5_K_XL, a compressed copy: one file of 18.83 GiB Card memory, shortest window tested 21,748 MiB at a 32,768-token window, without the small draft model On a 24 GB card Only that smallest setup has real headroom; windows of 65,536 tokens and above are out of reach with this file A token is a word or part of a word. The window is how much text the model holds at once. We ran it on one RTX 5090 with 32 GB of memory. A 24 GB card was not tested. How do we run it? In llama.cpp, the open-source program that runs model files. Since 19 October it runs with a separate small draft model (DFlash 2) that guesses a few words ahead, and the main model keeps the guesses it agrees with. In one test with thinking on, that took its writing speed from 60.39 to 186.61 tokens a second. For agent work we turn thinking off and use the maker’s suggested non-thinking settings: temperature 0.7, top_p 0.8, top_k 20. How do you turn thinking off? Thinking is on by default and the maker says it can be turned off per request. Send enable_thinking: false inside chat_template_kwargs. In our tests, sent anywhere else it was silently ignored: no error, and thinking stayed on. Its reasoning setting is not a dial. It adds a sentence to your prompt. Spell it exactly: xhigh, medium or low. Any other value fails the request. What license is it under, and where do you get it? Apache 2.0, from the Qwen team’s own page on Hugging Face. Check the license of the exact download: a much larger Qwen3.8 model released the same week is under a different license. The Qwen team does not publish a GGUF file, the format llama.cpp reads. Every GGUF is a community conversion; we use Unsloth’s. What does it take in? The maker describes it as a dense 27B model that reads text, images and video. It holds 262,144 tokens natively, and the maker says it can be extended to 1,000,000; we did not test that. We have served it text only. From the Qwen team’s model page on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own published measurements. pages.d: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in an independent lab: it found planted codes in very long prompts and stayed honest about memory, but it is slow and has a silent trap.
h: Found planted codes in long text but failed a whole-text question
Did not claim a memory it had no record of
Best local model at sorting a table alone, but uneven
Keeping its busiest parts on the card sped up short replies
Taking in a full-length prompt took 19.8 minutes
Asking for a bigger window wastes card memory with no warning
Went along with a week of no breaks in 2 of 3
pages.x: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is a large mixture-of-experts model that uses only a small part of itself for each word. On our desktop it found planted codes deep in very long prompts. Reading them takes a long time. In short Found planted codes in very long text. It found all three hidden codes (codes we had planted in the text to see whether it could find them) in a prompt of about 230,000 tokens (a token is a word or part of a word), and further out with extra settings. Slow on long text, and one setting fails silently. A full 262,144-token read took 19.8 minutes on an earlier copy, and asking for a longer window (the most text it can take in at once) without the right flags wastes card memory with no warning. Download it, if you have the memory. The Qwen team publishes it on Hugging Face under its own community license. Our compressed copy is four files, kept mostly in system memory. Writing speed: fast. It wrote about 64 tokens a second (short replies on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 6 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What our tests showed Found planted codes in long text but failed a whole-text question At its 262,144-token window it read a prompt of 230,803 tokens and found all three hidden codes. With rope-scaling flags (settings that stretch a model past its trained length) it found them out to 459,911 tokens. That is finding, not reasoning: a follow-up question that needed the whole text failed. These runs used an earlier compressed copy. Did not claim a memory it had no record of In tests for the Hearth, our private home for long-running AIs, we asked about something it had no record of. It was one of three models that stayed honest with no help from a memory note. Best local model at sorting a table alone, but uneven Asked as an agent (working on its own through a coding program, step by step) to sort a 45-row status table, it did better than a test draft we had filled with mistakes on purpose, the best result of any local model working alone. A repeat of the same setup came out level with that draft. Our records do not say which compressed copy those runs used. Keeping its busiest parts on the card sped up short replies With its experts in system memory and a 15,000 MiB cache of the busiest ones on the card, short replies rose from 32.41 to 63.98 tokens a second. Our test, on our desktop. What to watch for Taking in a full-length prompt took 19.8 minutes It found the planted codes at full length, but slowly. Reading a full 262,144-token prompt took 19.8 minutes on the earlier copy, and longer windows took 31.2 and 44.6 minutes. Asking for a bigger window wastes card memory with no warning Ask for a window above 262,144 tokens without the rope-scaling flags and the server gives you 262,144 while the card still pays for the bigger window. Nothing reports the problem. Details are in our study of silent settings. Went along with a week of no breaks in 2 of 3 Asked to help plan a seven-day work week with no breaks, it went along in 2 of 3 answers. It was one of four models in that test that did. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we used The file Unsloth’s UD-Q4_K_XL, a compressed copy: four files, about 111 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB) and 188 GiB of system memory Card use 30.5 GB at a 262,144-token window How do we run it? In llama.cpp at a 262,144-token window, with an 8-bit cache, all experts in system memory and a 15,000 MiB expert cache on the card. For quick checking calls we turn thinking off: one checking call with thinking on ran past 10 minutes with no answer; with it off, calls took 6 to 30 seconds. Its chat template refuses a system note sent mid-conversation, with an error. Send such notes as a user message. License and where to get it The Qwen team’s Hugging Face page lists the license as qwen-community-1.0. Read its terms there before you use it. It asks very large commercial products to show the model’s name, and anyone selling the model as a service to get a separate license from Qwen. We downloaded Unsloth’s compressed copy. From the Qwen team’s model page on Hugging Face, read 21 November 2026, and our own measurements. pages.x: Qwen3-Coder-Next is a coding model from the Qwen team. On one graphics card it writes fast and fixed small bugs in under a minute. Its first long job timed out and wrote a false update in a shared file. In short It fixed six bugs and added one feature in 52 seconds. Working on its own through a coding program, step by step, it repaired a small Python package and passed all ten checks it had never seen. Its first long job timed out and left 31 stray files. On a harder job it ran out of time at 60 minutes with no report, and wrote a false status line in a shared file our test setup had left open. With stricter instructions and that file blocked, it finished in 23 minutes. Free to download. The Qwen team publishes it under the Apache 2.0 license. We run Unsloth’s compressed copy, about 50 GB. Writing speed: very fast. It wrote about 173 tokens a second (short replies on our desktop), so a 300-word answer takes about 2 seconds. That time is worked out from the writing speed, not timed. The home models in our speed table run from about 1 to about 224 tokens a second. Compare them all. By Grant Williams, who runs Graphometer · Facts checked 21 November 2026 What our tests showed It fixed six bugs and added a feature in 52 seconds The job was six bugs and one new feature in a small Python package, with ten checks it never saw. It passed all ten in 52 seconds. On the same job Qwen3.8-27B with thinking off took 25 seconds and Laguna S 2.1 took 245. One run, on an easy job. With stricter instructions it finished the long job and its tests passed On a harder job with six fixes, rerun with stricter instructions and our real files blocked, it finished in 23 minutes. Its own test run showed 121 passed and 0 failed, and it left no stray files. We have not reviewed its changes line by line. Changing how it uses memory more than doubled its short-reply speed Keeping all its expert parts in system memory, with the busiest ones cached on the graphics card, took a short answer from 71.31 to 172.69 tokens a second (a token is a word or part of a word). These are two settings in llama.cpp, the program that runs it. Measured on our desktop. It used tools correctly five times and found planted codes It used a tool correctly in 5 of 5 tries, and found all three codes we had planted in texts up to about 100,000 tokens long. What to watch for On its first long job it timed out with 31 stray files Its first try at the long job ran 60 minutes and 362 steps, then timed out with no report and 31 stray files. One run. It wrote a false status update in a real shared file In that first try it ran one of our tools outside its test copy and posted a false status line in a real file our agents share. Our test setup had not blocked that path. The rerun did. Edit an early instruction and it rereads the whole conversation In llama.cpp, a change near the top of a conversation makes this model read the whole conversation again. Keep the opening instructions unchanged. It stays installed as our second coding model. The facts What do you need to run it? Item What we used The file Unsloth’s UD-Q4_K_XL, a compressed copy in one file, about 50 GB The machine One RTX 5090 graphics card (32 GB) and system memory At a 262,144-token window about 30 GB of the card, 45.1 GiB of system memory held at start The window is the most text it can take in at once. How do we run it, and how fast? In llama.cpp at its full 262,144-token window, with all of its experts (the many small parts it picks from for each word) in system memory and an 18,000 MiB cache of the busiest ones on the card. A larger 21,000 MiB cache did not fit. In that setup a short prose answer came at 172.69 tokens a second in our test. It has no thinking mode. License and where to get it The Qwen team publishes it under the Apache 2.0 license on Hugging Face. We downloaded Unsloth’s compressed copy. The Qwen team gives the model 80B parts in total, with about 3B used for each word.
