pages.t: Muse Glimmer 30B: draft length 16, not 3, in llama.cpp
pages.d: On one RTX 5090, raising the draft length from 3 to 16 tokens gave 2.17 times the throughput across six structured prompts.
h: A longer draft more than doubled structured speed
Acceptance rate ranked the settings backwards
The full 131,072-token context fits with the drafter
The license is plain Apache 2.0, with a usage policy beside it
Thinking has no off switch, and its strength setting is a sentence
Structured output, tool calls and other checks
Same label, different files; same name, different templates
Two grades from our test suite are wrong
pages.x: On one RTX 5090, raising Muse Glimmer 30B's draft length (how many tokens a small helper model guesses ahead) from llama.cpp's default of 3 to 16 took six structured prompts (code, JSON and a table) from a median 116.505 to 253.19 tokens a second, 2.17 times as fast, with each prompt run once per setting. In short Ask the helper model for its full block of guesses (--spec-draft-n-max 16), tested one request at a time. The two flags on Meta's model card, -md and -ngld 99, turn it on but leave llama.cpp's default of 3. llama.cpp trims 16 to 15, and 15 is what the fast run used. What to do Check one line in your server log. If it prints n_max=3 just above block_size=16, you are on the slow setting. The check Expect less on prose. Against the same model with no helper, the best prose result was 1.51 times as fast; structured output reached 3.32 times. By Grant Williams · Published 16 August 2026 Download this study's data (zip, 0.4 MB) 01 What to do Turn on the helper model, then set its draft length. This model gets its speed from speculative decoding: a small draft model guesses the next few tokens (word pieces) and the main model checks them all in one step. Meta's draft model, DFlash, is a separate file trained to guess a block of 16 tokens in one pass. The speed runs below used this command, with the draft flags added or changed: llama-server \ --model Muse-Glimmer-30B-KQuant-17GB-Q4_K_M.gguf \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port <scratch> --alias muse-glimmer-30b \ --jinja --ctx-size 8192 --parallel 1 --n-gpu-layers 99 \ --threads 24 --threads-batch 24 --flash-attn on --timeout 3600 Meta's model card turns the draft model on with two flags: -md dflash-Muse-Glimmer-30B-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngld 99 Then add --spec-draft-n-max 16. That one flag took the structured prompts from 116.505 to 253.19 tokens a second. --spec-draft-n-max 8 reached 208.29 and draws no warning. Check the startup line With only Meta's two flags, the server prints: common_speculative_impl_draft_dflash: - n_max=3, n_min=0, p_min=0.00 common_speculative_impl_draft_dflash: - block_size=16, mask_token_id=201818, n_extract=5 n_max=3 is llama.cpp's general default, set for ordinary draft models. block_size=16 is what this drafter was trained for; the server prints it and does not use it. With the flag, the log reads: common_speculative_impl_draft_dflash: - n_max=16, n_min=0, p_min=0.00 common_speculative_impl_draft_dflash: requested draft size (n_max=16, n_min=0) exceeds the trained block size 16 -- clamping to 15 Passing 15 lands in the same place without the warning. Defaults can change; this line tells you which case you are in. Other settings Tune by speed, not by acceptance rate. Acceptance rate (the share of guessed tokens the main model keeps) ranked the three structured settings in exactly the wrong order here. Measure end-to-end speed on your own work. Evidence Make sure your llama.cpp supports the model. Meta's card says to run llama-cli --version and require 10353 or higher. That works on a release build only; a build from source prints a line like version: 0.1.0-dev (build 1, commit 3cb7ffb), with no number to test. Meta's second check works on any build: grep -c LLM_ARCH_MUSE_GLIMMER src/llama-arch.cpp Expect startup warnings. With the drafter, every load printed dflash requires ctx_other to be set and [spec] failed to measure draft model memory; Meta documents the second as harmless, and the model served normally. Every load also printed special_eot_id is not in special_eog_ids; no run showed a stopping problem, so that line is an open observation, not a known fault. Strip code fences before parsing JSON. With a strict JSON schema the model wrapped a correct object in a markdown fence, so json.loads(message.content) is not safe here. Evidence Thinking cannot be turned off; set how much with reasoning_strength (low, medium, high, the default). For a hard cap, llama.cpp's --reasoning-budget is the flag; we did not test it. Measure the token budget your own prompts need. Evidence Prefer Meta's long-named files. Short-named twins, also re-hosted by Unsloth, carry an older chat template that adds its own default on top of your reasoning instruction. Its error string says "Onyx". Evidence 02 What we found A longer draft more than doubled structured speed Meta's model card publishes this table for our exact hardware: an average over a prompt set it does not publish, batch size 1, greedy decoding (always the most likely next token), through llama.cpp. GPU Baseline, no speculation With DFlash Speedup Nvidia RTX 5090 74.9 233.4 3.1x Meta's figures, in tokens a second, quoted from its GGUF model card as read on 2026-08-16. Our runs, with the prompts split into prose and structured (both sets are printed under How this was measured). Run A has no draft model; run B adds Meta's two flags; runs C and D add a draft length. Run Draft flags Prose t/s vs run A Structured t/s vs run A A none 76.22 base 76.345 base B the two flags the card documents 79.07 1.04x 116.505 1.53x D B plus --spec-draft-n-max 8 114.46 1.50x 208.29 2.73x C B plus --spec-draft-n-max 16 114.86 1.51x 253.19 3.32x t/s is tokens a second of writing. Each cell is the median of six different prompts, one call each (n = 6), the same prompts in every run. "vs run A" divides by run A of the same kind of prompt, never by Meta's number. Runs are lettered in the order they ran, so D sits above C. No interval is computed. Our no-draft speeds, 76.22 and 76.345, are 1.8 and 1.9 percent above Meta's 74.9. Our fastest structured median, 253.19, is 8.5 percent above Meta's 233.4, and 3.32 times our base against their 3.1 times theirs. The two speedups measure different things: theirs averages an unknown mix, ours is six structured prompts. Why the default costs so much. Meta trained DFlash to produce a block of 16 tokens and prints Block size | 16 in the drafter's specification table. llama.cpp's --spec-draft-n-max defaults to 3, a sensible value for the ordinary draft models it was written for, and this build does not read the block size from the file. Meta's card documents -md and -ngld 99; the string --spec-draft-n-max appears in neither of Meta's readmes. A block drafter asked for three tokens at a time throws away most of what it computed. Each document is correct on its own; followed together, they leave structured output at 116.505 tokens a second instead of 253.19. Run B is Meta's two flags, not Meta's full command, which is this, and which we did not run: ./build/bin/llama-server \ -m Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF/Muse-Glimmer-30B-KQuant-17GB-Q4_K_M.gguf \ --mmproj Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF/mmproj-Muse-Glimmer-30B-Q4_K_M.gguf \ -a muse-glimmer-30B \ -ngl 99 -c 131072 -np 4 \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 \ --jinja \ --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 64 and adds -md Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF/dflash-Muse-Glimmer-30B-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngld 99 for speculation. Ours was text only, one slot instead of four, 8,192 tokens of context instead of 131,072, and greedy, because greedy at batch size 1 is how Meta's card says it measured speed. That command does not set --spec-draft-n-max either, so anything built from it starts at llama.cpp's default. Prose gains less. The flag that gave 3.32 times on structured output gave 1.51 times on prose, so one averaged speedup, ours or anyone's, cannot tell you which you will get. The speculation-gate study (a 397B mixture-of-experts model) found an ungated draft made prose slower than no draft while making structured output faster, and the Qwen3.8-27B field card found the same direction on a dense 27B. Their sizes do not carry over here. Acceptance rate ranked the settings backwards Same runs; counters summed across the six prompts of each row (n = 6, one call per prompt). Run Prompts Draft tokens generated Accepted Acceptance Tokens per target step Writing t/s B structured 4,601 3,408 0.741 3.22 116.505 D structured 9,023 3,964 0.439 4.49 208.29 C structured 13,204 4,212 0.319 5.75 253.19 B prose 6,926 2,689 0.388 2.16 79.07 D prose 16,36

pages.t: Where to put an instruction so a chat model follows it
pages.d: Tests compared the system prompt with a short note before the latest message, using instructions about follow-up questions and memory claims.
h: Telling works. A first-person description did not. Once is not enough.
The same result at larger scale
Some models then denied a real line
It does not fix who said what
One model read the note as the user's own words
Placed after the message, it turns formulaic
On some engines it costs time before every reply
Check how your template delivers it
What to do if you run an assistant with a long history
pages.x: On Qwen3-30B with one long conversation history, an instruction to ask the user a question back drew a question in 3 of 60 answers from the system prompt or memory, and in 6 of 6 as a short note labelled as coming from the system, right before the user's message. In short Send the instruction as a short note, as its own message, right before the user's newest message, with every message. Put before the first message only, the 30B still asked on the second message and not on the third (in two three-message conversations: 2 of 2, then 0 of 2). Only 1 of the 3 asks from the system prompt or memory was a real follow-up, and 1 of the 6 with the note was a stock health check-in (a welfare question that could be asked in any conversation). What to do In three models the note stopped the made-up memory, not the belief behind it. Asked about a song the user never played, Qwen3-30B, Qwen3-235B and GPT-4o said yes and described the moment in 13 of 15 answers without the note and in 0 of 27 with it, but 16 of those 27 still assumed the moment happened. The made-up memory Check how your model's chat template delivers the note, and watch its costs. The chat template is the part shipped with each model that turns messages into the text the model reads. Of 19 model files tested, 5 templates silently dropped a note labelled as coming from the system and 4 refused it with an error. The side effects differ by model: three models that gave back a line the user really wrote denied it once the note was added, and on some engines the note costs time before every reply. The template check · What the note costs By Grant Williams · Published 26 October 2026 Download this study's data (zip, 15 KB) This page is for you if you run a chat model with a long system prompt (the standing text the model reads before every conversation) or a long conversation history, and you want it to keep following a standing instruction. What it found: put the instruction in a short note right before the user's newest message, then check how your model's chat template actually delivers that note. A chat template is the small program shipped with each model that turns a list of messages into the text the model reads. The note is short, and it worked on several model families. It also has side effects, and they differ by model. We gave the same two instructions to open models run on our own machine and to GPT-4o. The first was to ask the user a real question back. The second was not to claim a memory the model does not have. The ask-back instruction changed little in the system prompt and in the model's persistent memory (text an agent framework saves and loads into the prompt every turn). The honesty instruction changed little in the system prompt; we did not try it in persistent memory. Placed as a short note right before the user's message, both did better. We also asked about something that never happened. Without the note, models said yes and described the moment in 13 of 15 answers. With the note, none did, in 0 of 27 answers. That stopped the made-up description, not the belief: 16 of those 27 answers still assumed the moment happened (section 04). 01 What we tested Every model saw the same long conversation history before one new message. The history is a real conversation between one user and a long-running companion role. The history is 166 messages, about 106,000 tokens on the tokenizers that reported it that way (a tokenizer is the part that splits text into tokens). Full prompts in this exam, system text plus history plus the new message, ran from about 106,000 to about 113,000 tokens. A token is a piece of a word. A model's context window is how many tokens it can hold at once. Above the history sat the system prompt, the standing text a chat model reads before any conversation. Here it was a persona text (a description of the role the model plays) plus four short persistent memory sections. An agent framework, which is software that adds tools and memory around a model, keeps those sections and loads them into the system prompt on every turn. Together they came to 15,131 characters. We tested two instructions: Ask back. When something the user raises matters to them, ask a real follow-up question about them or what they think. Offers of help do not count. Do not invent memories. If the user asks about something that is not in the record, say so plainly and do not describe it. Then we moved the instruction around (the placement test). We put it inside the system prompt, inside the persistent memory, at the end of the system prompt, as a short note placed as its own message right before the user's message, and attached after the user's message. Each answer was read by hand and sorted under fixed headings. The table below uses a few terms. Temperature, top-p, top-k and min-p are sampling settings that control how random a model's word choices are. An expert is one of the groups of weights that a mixture-of-experts model switches between. Loopback means the server could only be reached from the same machine. A snapshot is a fixed, dated version of a hosted model that its maker keeps available by name. Machine One desktop with one NVIDIA RTX 5090 (32 GB). The Qwen3-30B placement run kept 30 expert blocks in system RAM. GPT-OSS 120B kept the experts of 23 of 36 layers in system RAM. This page does not claim every mixture-of-experts file did this. One model at a time, served by llama.cpp. Placement test 2026-10-03. Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 (Q8_0) and Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 (UD-Q3_K_XL, 6 of 8 experts), window 131,072 tokens, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8, top-k 20, min-p 0. The 30B server listened on loopback only. Three user messages, two answers each, so six answers per set-up. All first messages of a fresh conversation unless stated. False-memory probe 2026-10-03 to 10-04. The two Qwen models above, GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-11-20, temperature 0.95, top-p 0.9) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (adaptive thinking, effort high), both by API. One question about a song the user never played, one about a real line the user once wrote. Three answers per cell. The larger exam 2026-10-05 to 10-09. 24 local model set-ups on three memory traps and two honesty questions, with and without a memory note, three answers per cell; eight everyday messages with the note. GPT-4o's three API snapshots (2024-05-13, 2024-08-06, 2024-11-20) answered the same items on 2026-10-17. A second history 2026-10-07 to 10-08. A different long-running companion role's history, 18 local model set-ups, one song-never-played question, three answers per cell, read blind from lettered copies. Quantization Each local model ran at the quantization named beside it in the data package. Quantization stores a model's weights at lower precision so it fits in memory; it can change behaviour, so every count here belongs to the file named. 02 Where the instruction sits On the Qwen3-30B, the ask-back instruction anywhere in the system prompt did almost nothing. We tried ten set-ups. They were two wordings in a marked section, lines added to the persistent memory, everything at once at the top, the same with the two stock check-in lines left in the memory, the instruction at the very end of the system prompt (two wordings), more random sampling, and two set-ups with only about the last 20,000 tokens of history. That is ten. Across all ten, the hand count found 3 of 60 answers that asked the user anything, and only one was a real follow-up. That one came with the full history and the lines added to the persistent memory. The other two came with only about the last 20,000 tokens of history and a line saying that earlier history was not shown. One was a request to set up a working session. The other carries the hand count's health-check label: it asked about breathing, light and whether the user had seen their own face, not about what the user had just said. The hand count kept both. With no instruction at all, 0 of 6 asked anything. The same paragrap

pages.t: OpenRouter’s MiniMax email: the full letter and what our logs show
pages.d: OpenRouter says 7,619 of our requests to MiniMax models may have been read. The full letter, and what its own log of our account shows.
h: If you got the same letter
What is known, and who said it
Our 7,619 requests: OpenRouter’s log and our records
What OpenRouter’s log of our account shows
What the two studies’ records hold
What the prompts in those two studies held
What a “Zero Data Retention” label can tell you
pages.x: OpenRouter says a third party may have read the prompts and outputs of 7,619 of our requests to MiniMax models, and its log of our account shows all but one came from the API key (the access key a program sends with each request) that two studies published on this site used. In short What the letter says. The letter says a security researcher’s test URLs in prompts to MiniMax models were opened by a third party 40 to 130 hours later, and OpenRouter says it has removed the “Zero Data Retention” label (the router’s statement about a provider’s setting) from these MiniMax-model endpoints while it investigates. The full letter What our account shows. OpenRouter’s log of our account shows all but one of the 7,619 requests came from the key our studies used, between 24 August and 4 September 2026; the last, on 8 October, was a single short request from a different key, used by a private project. Private voice tests that sent personal writing are, as far as the log shows, not in the letter’s count. Our requests If you got the same letter, check your own account. Filter OpenRouter’s Activity and Logs pages by “Provider is MiniMax”, see which API key sent each request, and rotate (cancel, and replace where you still need it) any key, password, token or signed URL that appeared in those prompts or answers. The steps By Grant Williams · Published 21 November 2026 Download this study's data (zip, 9 KB) This page is for anyone who got OpenRouter’s email about MiniMax models, or who sends prompts through a model router (a service that passes your prompts on to AI models). Graphometer is a paying OpenRouter customer. 01 If you got the same letter Sign in to OpenRouter and open the Activity and Logs pages. On each, use the filter “Provider is MiniMax”. This is how we checked our own account. The Activity page limits a filtered view to 31 days, so step through the letter’s dates a month at a time. It shows how many requests went to the provider, and from which API keys. The Logs page shows each request’s date, model, provider, token counts and which API key sent it. On our account the times were shown in US Eastern time; the letter gives UTC. Work out what those prompts contained. If you did not keep the prompts, the API key behind each request tells you which tool or script to look at. Rotate any key, password, token or signed URL (a web link that carries its own access permission) that appeared in those prompts or in the answers, starting with the one that can do the most. Rotating means cancelling the exposed one so it no longer works, and issuing a new one where you still need it. Remember the outputs too. The letter says prompts and outputs may have been read. 02 What the letter says The email reached the site’s owner on 21 November 2026. Its heading is “Requests you sent to MiniMax models may have been read”. Here is the whole text, exactly as received. It shows no recipient name or address. The one button is shown in square brackets. The email as received is shown under the text. The letter, 21 November 2026 Requests you sent to MiniMax models may have been read Hi there, A security researcher placed unique test URLs in prompts sent to MiniMax models from July to October 2026. A third party accessed those URLs 40 to 130 hours after the requests were sent, whether MiniMax served a request directly or another provider forwarded it to MiniMax. With one exception, the same tests on other models at those providers were not accessed, and none of the AWS test keys were used. Your account sent 7,619 requests to MiniMax models through MiniMax, from August 24 at 01:07 to October 8 at 22:36 UTC. AtlasCloud, Novita and StreamLake have told us they forwarded OpenRouter requests for MiniMax models to MiniMax. Based on what the researcher and these providers have reported, the issue sits with MiniMax and the providers that forwarded to it, not with OpenRouter. We are passing on what they have told us. MiniMax told StreamLake that content moderation was enabled on its endpoints before October 22 and that it has since enabled Zero Data Retention. We have asked MiniMax for its own account and have not received one. This means a third party may have read the prompts and outputs of these requests. While we investigate, we have removed the Zero Data Retention label from these MiniMax-model endpoints. [Review your activity] Rotate any keys, passwords, tokens or signed URLs that appeared in those prompts or outputs, starting with the most privileged. We will email you again if MiniMax’s or the providers’ findings change this notice. For questions, contact support@openrouter.ai. The OpenRouter Team The email as received on 21 November 2026. The transcription above is the text. 03 What is known, and who said it As of 21 November 2026, the facts below come from the letter. We have not checked any of them ourselves. Each line says who said it. The test. The letter says a security researcher put unique test URLs in prompts sent to MiniMax models from July to October 2026, and that a third party opened those URLs 40 to 130 hours (about two to five and a half days) after the requests were sent. Our explanation of why that matters: each test URL was a web address made for that one prompt, so a visit to it means someone or something had the prompt. The letter does not name the researcher. The path of one request. As the letter describes it, a request goes from the customer to OpenRouter, from OpenRouter to a provider, and from that provider on to MiniMax when the provider is not MiniMax itself. The letter says the URLs were opened either way. The other models. The letter says that, with one exception, the same tests on other models at those providers were not opened, and that none of the AWS test keys (keys for Amazon Web Services, a cloud service) were used. The providers that passed requests on. The letter says AtlasCloud, Novita and StreamLake told OpenRouter they forwarded OpenRouter requests for MiniMax models to MiniMax. What MiniMax is reported to have said. The letter says MiniMax told StreamLake that content moderation (checks on content) was enabled on its endpoints (the addresses that receive requests) before 22 October, and that MiniMax has since enabled Zero Data Retention. The letter does not say what that setting covers. This is OpenRouter passing on what StreamLake passed on. The letter says OpenRouter asked MiniMax for its own account of events and has not received one. The label. The letter says OpenRouter has removed the “Zero Data Retention” label from these MiniMax-model endpoints while it investigates. Other accounts report versions of the letter with different numbers and dates. The story is discussed in a Hacker News thread and written up by RuntimeWire, Startup Fortune and The CyberSec Guru. Anything in them that goes beyond the letter is their own reporting, and we do not repeat it here. 04 Our 7,619 requests: OpenRouter’s log and our records We checked two ways. On 21 November 2026 the site’s owner signed in to our OpenRouter account, and we read its Activity and Logs pages with the filter “Provider is MiniMax”. We also examined the records of two studies published on this site: an agent-permission pilot and a GPT-4o comparison. What OpenRouter’s log of our account shows 20 Aug to 19 Sep 2026 About 7,620 requests with provider MiniMax. The page shows the figure rounded, as “7.62K”, not the exact count. All came from the API key our studies used, to MiniMax M3 and MiniMax M2-her. 19 Sep to 19 Oct 2026 Exactly 1 request with provider MiniMax, to MiniMax M2.7, from a different key, used by a private project. That one request 8 October, 22:36 UTC: 42 tokens (a token is a word or part of a word) in and a 3-token answer. The log holds no text, so we cannot say what it asked. In between No rows with provider MiniMax from 02:00 UTC on 4 September to 22:00 UTC on 8 October. About 7,620, rounded, plus that one request agrees with the letter’s 7,619. The letter’s window sta

pages.t: Which Qwen should I run?
pages.d: A guide to the Qwen family: which generations are open, what runs on your GPU and RAM, how to start a Qwen in Ollama, and when a hosted API is better.
h: The chooser: what your machine can actually run
Your first Qwen, without being an infrastructure person
The big ones, on one desktop
pages.x: On one desktop with a 32 GB RTX 5090, the Qwen3.6 35B and 27B ran fully on the graphics card at 227 and 72 tokens a second; one configuration each, July 2026. In short Pick by your graphics card's memory. The chooser's picks: No real GPU: the sub-1B and 2B-class models, as utilities and pipeline testers only; anything bigger belongs to the API (the 0.6B ran at 857 tokens a second on our GPU, July 2026; CPU-only speed untested here). 8 to 12 GB: the 4B and 9B-class at 4-bit (maker's sizing; not run here). 16 GB: a 14B-class at 4-bit, or the 27B at 4-bit with part of it on the CPU (file-size arithmetic; not run here). 24 GB: the Qwen3.6 27B at 4-bit (arithmetic; we ran it only on a 32 GB card). 32 GB: the Qwen3.6 35B, the 27B, or a 30B-class vision model, fully on the card (measured). 32 GB plus RAM: the Qwen3.5 122B at 26 to 38 tokens a second with roughly 96 GB or more of RAM, the 397B at 14 to 20 with roughly 176 GB or more (one configuration each, August 2026; we measured only on 188 GiB). None of these: hosted Qwen. The chooser For a first Qwen, use Ollama and start with the output limit at 4,096 (a starting point that worked for our jobs; some questions need more). Two commands start the Qwen3.6 27B on a card with about 20 GB of memory or more. With a low output limit, the model's thinking can use it all and return nothing. Known-good settings files are below. Your first Qwen · Settings files As of August 2026, hosted Qwen was cheaper; local keeps your prompts on your machine. Our rule of thumb: privacy-sensitive or high-volume, predictable work runs local; frontier-quality one-offs and million-token contexts (room for a million tokens of text at once) run hosted. Local or hosted By Grant Williams · Published 9 August 2026 01 The family on one screen Qwen is an unusually wide open model family: real Apache-licensed weights from under one billion parameters to a 397B mixture-of-experts (a design where only part of the model works on each token; see the box in section 02), plus API-only frontier tiers above that. That width is the point of this page. We run the family for real on one desktop, from the small daily drivers (the models we use every day) to the 122B and 397B, so the guidance here is what we measured, labeled as measured, next to what the vendor claims, labeled as claims. Four generations matter today. The one-line version: 3.5 and 3.6 are the open ones you can run; 3.7 is API-only; 3.8 is now open too, in two very different sizes and under two different licenses. Qwen3.5 (open) The current big open generation: mixture-of-experts models topping out at the 397B and the 122B we serve here, Apache 2.0, with built-in speculative-decoding heads (built-in guessing heads). Our measured deep-dive is the Qwen3.5 pair field card. Qwen3.6 (open) Open weights: a 27B and a 35B mixture-of-experts, Apache 2.0, files verified on the official organization. Our daily drivers below come from this generation and its predecessors. Qwen3.7 (API only) Max, Plus and Flash tiers on the official API and aggregators; the vendor states they are proprietary. No 3.7 weights have ever shipped. Qwen3.8 (open, in two sizes) The Max is live as an API, and both promised open releases have now shipped: a 2.4-trillion-parameter Max-class model on 2026-08-12 under a custom license with revenue thresholds, and a 27B on 2026-08-14 under Apache 2.0. Two models, one version number, two different licenses, so check the file in the repository you actually download. Verified status, revisions and the fake-repository warning live on our Qwen3.8 release watch; the 27B's measured record, taken on the day it shipped, is the Qwen3.8-27B field card. This page: published 9 August 2026, last updated 14 August 2026. Generation status checked 2026-08-09; the Qwen3.8 row refreshed 2026-08-14. The release-watch page carries the dated table and updates as things actually ship. 02 The chooser: what your machine can actually run Rows marked measured come from recorded runs on our machine (a single RTX 5090 with 32 GB of VRAM, the graphics card's own memory, and 188 GiB of system RAM; dates given). Rows marked arithmetic are file-size reasoning we consider sound but have not run. Rows marked vendor are the maker's sizing. Speeds are warm generation in tokens per second (t/s), one configuration each, not benchmarks. Your hardware What we would run Speed seen Basis Laptop or desktop, no real GPU The sub-1B and 2B-class tags (Ollama's model names) as utilities and pipeline testers; anything bigger belongs to the API see basis carried over from other hardware: the 0.6B measured 857 t/s on our 32 GB GPU (July 2026); CPU-only speed untested here, but this size class runs acceptably on CPUs generally (vendor and community consensus, labeled as such) 8 to 12 GB VRAM The 4B and 9B-class tags at 4-bit (weights compressed to about 4 bits each) untested here vendor sizing; we have not run these sizes and say so 16 GB VRAM A 14B-class at 4-bit comfortably; the 27B at 4-bit with partial CPU offload untested here arithmetic from file sizes 24 GB VRAM The Qwen3.6 27B at 4-bit (a 17 GB download) see basis arithmetic; measured only on our 32 GB card (72 tokens per second, July 2026), where it never had to squeeze 32 GB VRAM The sweet spot we live on: the 35B mixture-of-experts as the fast generalist, the 27B, and a 30B-class vision model, all fully on GPU 227 / 72 / 291 t/s measured, July 2026, Ollama serving (qwen3.6:35b / qwen3.6:27b / the 30B-class vision tag, in that order) 32 GB VRAM + roughly 96 GB or more RAM The Qwen3.5 122B: every layer on GPU, expert blocks moved to the CPU side in system RAM, speculation on with its confidence gate set 26 to 38 t/s measured, 2026-08-05/06, llama.cpp serving on a 188 GiB machine; full story on the field card 32 GB VRAM + roughly 176 GB or more RAM The Qwen3.5 397B, same technique, more patience 14 to 20 t/s measured, 2026-08-05/06, same 188 GiB machine; low end is thinking replies None of the above fits Hosted Qwen: the same open weights served by API providers, or the official frontier tiers n/a section 06 The RAM rule behind those floors: at the quantizations we run, the 122B's weights are a 73 GB file and the 397B's are 150 GB, and the technique copies weights into RAM, so the weights plus operating-system headroom must fit. We measured both models only on a 188 GiB machine. With less RAM than the weights, the model streams from disk instead, which we did not measure here and which is dramatically slower. Quantization tier (how far the weights are compressed) changes everything; ours are named on the field card. Behind that table are three questions, and they are worth asking in order, because a yes to one does not imply a yes to the next. Does it load? Does it generate at a speed you can work at? Does it still do that with enough context to be useful for your actual task? Most sizing advice answers only the first and lets the reader assume the rest. The 397B on this machine loads at the placements we use (which blocks sit on the GPU and which on the CPU), generates comfortably, and has never been fed a prompt longer than 4,367 tokens: three different answers about one model. Total parameters and active parameters are different numbers Every name in this family carries two: the 122B is a 122.1 billion-parameter model of which 9.8 billion compute for any given token, and the 397B is 396.3 billion of which 17.4 billion do. Those are header sums, read out of the files on our disk on 2026-08-08 by adding up tensor shapes (899 tensor headers in one file and 1,118 in the other) rather than figures quoted from a model card, and they are the served text stacks: each file also carries a built-in guessing head, 2.5 and 6.6 billion parameters, which the field card counts separately. The architecture is why: the smaller model holds 256 routed experts and fires 8 of them per token plus one always-on shared expert; the larger holds 512 and fires 10, plus its shared expert. Under

pages.t: Qwen3.5 122B and 397B speeds on one RTX 5090 desktop
pages.d: On one desktop, the 122B ran at about 26 to 38 tokens per second and the 397B at about 14 to 20, depending on the prompt.
h: The guessing feature: faster with a cutoff, slower on creative text without one
The two models on one hard puzzle
The two models, read from the files
中文摘要：Qwen3.5 现场记录卡（122B 与 397B）
pages.x: On one desktop with an RTX 5090 graphics card and 188 GiB of system RAM, one compressed file of each model wrote about 26 to 38 tokens (word pieces) a second for the 122B and about 14 to 20 for the 397B, depending on the prompt, with the model's built-in guessing feature set up as described below, one request at a time. In short On these two models, use the built-in guessing feature, but set its confidence cutoff yourself. Without the cutoff, the 122B wrote two creative prompts slower than with the feature off. The full command is in What to do. Make sure the model fits in system RAM, and copy it in rather than memory-mapping it. Memory mapping cut the 397B's prompt reading by 82 percent. Check that the model fits in system RAM Give the thinking room. With too small an output-token cap, the request succeeds and the answer comes back empty. Thinking and empty answers By Grant Williams · Published 8 August 2026 中文摘要 (Chinese summary, synced 2026-08-11) 01 What to do Check that the model fits in system RAM. Disk: about 75 GB for the 122B, about 151 GB for the 397B. RAM: enough for the weights (73 and 150 GB) plus the system; we had 188 GiB. With less, weights stream from disk and every number here changes, in ways we did not measure. Our setups use 23 to 28 GiB of a 32 GB graphics card; a smaller card means keeping more expert blocks on the CPU, which we did not measure. Turn on the guessing feature with a confidence cutoff (--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-p-min 0.75). Each file carries a multi-token-prediction (MTP) head that guesses the next few tokens; the full model checks them in one batch and keeps only tokens it would have written anyway (speculative decoding). The cutoff drops unconfident guesses. In our llama.cpp build the cutoff defaults to 0.00, meaning none, and the quantizer's published command lines leave it out. Test it on open-ended prose, not only structured prompts. Copy the model into RAM instead of memory-mapping it (--no-mmap). Memory mapping reads the file from disk as needed and hurts prompt reading most. The flag currently prints a deprecation warning pointing at its replacement; it still works. Set a generous output-token cap when thinking is on. 2,000 to 4,096 output tokens is a starting range that worked for our jobs on these two models, not a safe number, because the floor depends on the task; hard problems need far more. No universal safe number exists. Measure the floor for your own task (Empty Answer carries the method). Short factual replies with thinking off are fine small. For long prompts, read the prompt in bigger chunks (-b 4096 -ub 4096 instead of the defaults -b 2048 -ub 512). At a 131,072-token context with no memory mapping, prompt reading rose on a 48,029-token prompt from 224.5 to 932.2 tokens a second on the 397B, and on a 48,027-token prompt from 520.2 to 2,101.7 on the 122B. The batch-size study carries the full sweep, including the 8,192 setting that did not load. The full command below uses 65,536. Use a current llama.cpp. The caching fixes this design needs postdate July mainline builds, by our account; on an old build multi-turn caching misbehaves. With the fixes, the second turn re-read only 4 to 37 tokens instead of the whole history. Leave graphics-memory headroom. --n-cpu-moe N keeps the routed experts of the first N blocks on the CPU. One block too many loads all its weights, then fails minutes later. The guessing head costs +2.6 GiB on the 122B and +3.8 on the 397B. Wait for the health check, not the start message. Load time is mostly cache state; do not read a 100-second load as a failure. Keep the checksum output, not just the checksums. Check file count and checksums against the repository listing and save the output. One of our two checks survives as a saved file; the other does not. The full command llama-server --jinja --ctx-size 65536 --parallel 1 --n-gpu-layers 999 \ --no-mmap --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 6 --spec-draft-p-min 0.75 \ --threads 24 --threads-batch 24 --flash-attn on --min-p 0.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 \ --n-cpu-moe 38 --temp 0.6 That is the 122B's command as we serve it. The 397B's is identical except --n-cpu-moe 57 and --temp 1.0. Both files suggest 0.6; the 397B's 1.0 is our choice, a departure from the file and from the maker's published thinking-mode settings, which also say 0.6. 02 What we found Writing speed is how fast the answer comes out; prompt reading is how fast the prompt goes in. Both in tokens a second (t/s). What 122B 397B Real thinking replies, sustained 27 to 29 t/s (four long recorded generations) 14 to 17 t/s (twelve recorded tasks) Structured test prompt, with the cutoff 38.25 t/s 19.5 t/s No speculation at all 24.5 t/s 10.4 t/s Prompt reading (no memory mapping, August) 865 t/s short, 717 t/s across a 29.7K prompt 374 to 417 t/s Load, to answering 20 to 24 s warm foreground; 99 to 107 s on a managed restart (restart by the service manager) with a cooler cache 160 to 215 s across all recorded starts Speeds are end to end. Prompt reading declines with depth. One configuration per model, not a benchmark of the models. The guessing feature: faster with a cutoff, slower on creative text without one At identical placements (the same blocks on the card), the guessing head took the 397B from 10.35 to 19.55 t/s on the structured test prompt, an 89 percent gain, and the 122B from 24.5 to 26.1 on prose and from 24.6 to 38.25 on structured output. The bigger model pays more per step, so saving steps pays more. Without the cutoff, our placement tests (moving more or fewer blocks onto the card) accepted 82 to 90 percent of guesses and gave the fastest numbers. But on the 122B's set of fifteen test prompts, the two open-ended persona prompts accepted only 25 and 30 percent of drafted tokens, and writing fell to 16.1 and 18.2 t/s, below the 24.5 with speculation switched off. When three quarters of guesses are thrown away, checking them is pure overhead. The same server was fine on reasoning, lists and code. With the cutoff at 0.75, acceptance rose to 88 to 95 percent on every shape measured. On the 122B, speculation with the cutoff beat no speculation on prose as well as structured output; on the 397B that win is measured on the structured prompt only. The cutoff cost almost nothing on predictable text (the 397B: 20.4 without it, 19.5 with it, same prompt). Where the weights live decides whether guessing pays. On these two models, whose weights fit in RAM, speculation paid 7 to 89 percent. On GLM-5.2, a 744B model on the same machine whose CPU-side weights exceed RAM, the same flags were slower (1.5 to 3.7 t/s against 4.0 to 6.0 without): with weights partly on the SSD, checking a batch multiplies disk reads. On the dense Mistral Medium 3.5, the same idea with a separate draft model pays about fourfold. Memory mapping and load time Turning memory mapping back on cost the 397B 29 percent of writing speed and 82 percent of prompt reading (396 down to 69.5 t/s), and slowed its load. The 122B's prompt reading fell from 865 to the 330-to-400 range. A cooler cache made the 122B's load about five times as long. Graphics memory Only every fourth block keeps a key-value cache (the stored memory of past tokens), with 2 key-value heads, so a 65,536-token context costs 1.50 GiB of cache on the 122B and 1.88 GiB on the 397B, worked out from the file headers. The measured setups: Setup VRAM used Free 122B default (64K, with the guessing head) 25,215 MiB (24.62 GiB) 7.22 GiB 122B max-GPU (most blocks on the card) 27,807 MiB (27.16 GiB) 4.69 GiB 122B at 128K context 27,007 MiB (26.37 GiB) 5.47 GiB 397B default (64K, with the guessing head) 24,070 MiB (23.51 GiB) 8.34 GiB 397B max-GPU (most blocks on the card) 28,449 MiB (27.78 GiB) 4.06 GiB Whole-card readings, including roughly 0.7 to 1.0 GiB of desktop. The GiB conversions are exact. The file headers predict each block's cost on the card (1.27 GiB on the 122B, 2.16 on the 397B); the measured slopes were 1,296 and 2,3

pages.t: Qwen3.8-27B at 256K context on one RTX 5090: Q4 with MTP wrote faster than Q5 without it, Q5 stayed closer to the reference
pages.d: On one RTX 5090 at 256K, Q4_K_XL with MTP wrote faster than Q5_K_XL without it; Q5_K_XL matched an 8-bit reference more closely than Q4_K_XL on one text.
h: How closely each file matches the reference
The long read and the crash check
Why Q5_K_XL could not use MTP at 256K
Since October: a separate draft model
pages.x: At a 262,144-token window on one RTX 5090, Q4_K_XL with MTP on wrote structured replies (thinking off) at 144.7 tokens a second about 20K tokens deep, against 60.7 for the larger Q5_K_XL with MTP off, which matched an 8-bit reference slightly more often on one text, in single runs. In short For speed, run Q4_K_XL with MTP on. MTP (multi-token prediction) is built into these files: it guesses tokens (word pieces) for the model to check. Settings For the closest match to the 8-bit reference, run Q5_K_XL with MTP off. With MTP on, its MTP part would not start beside the 8-bit cache at this window, in both attempts. Q5_K_S with MTP sits in between, with only 664 MiB spare. Or give Q5_K_XL a separate small draft model, at a slightly smaller window (229,376 tokens). Since October, in one reasoning test (thinking on) it wrote 186.61 tokens a second, against 60.39 without. Results By Grant Williams · Published 26 September 2026 Download this study's data (zip, 91 KB) 01 What to do Closest to the reference: Q5_K_XL with MTP off. Measured command; q8_0 is an 8-bit cache, the memory holding text read so far. Set your own local address: llama-server --model Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q5_K_XL.gguf \ --jinja --ctx-size 262144 --parallel 1 \ --batch-size 2048 --ubatch-size 512 \ --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \ --n-gpu-layers 999 --threads 24 --threads-batch 24 \ --flash-attn on --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --min-p 0.0 For speed: Q4_K_XL with MTP on. Change the model filename and add these flags. They also serve Q5_K_S: closer to the reference than Q4_K_XL, and the same revision as the reference. --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 6 --spec-draft-p-min 0.75 \ --cache-type-k-draft q8_0 --cache-type-v-draft q8_0 If 128K (131,072 tokens) is enough: Q5_K_XL with MTP on, the faster baseline. Use both blocks above minus every cache-type flag, and set --ctx-size 131072. Since 19 October: Q5_K_XL with a separate draft model, DFlash 2 for Qwen3.8-27B (a Q4_K_M file of 1.1 GB) plus n-gram drafting (guessing from text already seen), on the main llama.cpp version with -ub 256, an 8-bit cache, built-in MTP off and a 229,376-token window. Keep the confidence gate (--spec-draft-p-min) explicit (why). -ub is the micro-batch, prompt tokens read at a time (more). 02 What we found Writing speed Each test read a generated ledger (a made-up list of entries), then wrote a prose letter (414 to 504 tokens) or a structured reply, a JSON list shaped like tool output (907 to 1,192 tokens; no tool ran). Rates leave out the read. Measured: prose letters, tokens a second File / setting ~20K ~48K ~100K ~230K Q5_K_XL, 256K, MTP off 60.7 55.2 49.1 34.9 Q4_K_XL, 256K, MTP on 75.2 64.8 54.9 38.4 Q5_K_S, 256K, MTP on 71.5 64.5 52.2 39.9 Q5_K_XL, 128K, MTP on* 72.0 70.5 60.8 Not run Measured: structured replies, tokens a second File / setting ~20K ~48K ~100K ~230K Q5_K_XL, 256K, MTP off 60.7 54.9 48.9 34.8 Q4_K_XL, 256K, MTP on 144.7 129.9 114.7 87.0 Q5_K_S, 256K, MTP on 137.4 126.0 110.2 82.8 Q5_K_XL, 128K, MTP on* 141.5 136.9 127.0 Not run Measured: prompt reading from scratch, tokens a second File / setting ~20K ~48K ~100K ~230K Q5_K_XL, 256K, MTP off 3,118 2,718 1,958 1,181 Q4_K_XL, 256K, MTP on 3,088 2,722 1,937 1,132 Q5_K_S, 256K, MTP on 3,001 2,667 1,905 1,124 Q5_K_XL, 128K, MTP on* 2,896 2,608 1,973 Not run Depths are approximate. *Default cache: the recorded command set no cache type; its launch comment calls it f16. How closely each file matches the reference Perplexity (how well a file predicts a fixed text), over 24 chunks of 4,096 tokens of public llama.cpp documentation, was too close to tell apart at the reported uncertainty. Measured perplexity; reported ± terms retained File Perplexity Q5_K_XL 2.7203 ± 0.02379 Q5_K_S 2.7186 ± 0.02375 Q4_K_XL 2.7206 ± 0.02379 A second test compared next-token predictions with unsloth's 8-bit Q8_0 file on 12 chunks of the same text. KL divergence measures how far the whole spread of predictions moves from the reference; lower is closer. Measured against Q8_0 on one public text File Same top token Mean KL divergence Q5_K_XL 97.830 ± 0.093% 0.004369 ± 0.000153 Q5_K_S 97.675 ± 0.096% 0.005406 ± 0.000201 Q4_K_XL 97.240 ± 0.105% 0.007839 ± 0.000345 Q4 picks the same most likely next token as the reference about 97 times in 100 on this text; Q5_K_XL is closer to 98. This is not a share of correct answers, and it does not measure MTP's effect on answers. Memory use Measured peak total card use; spare memory is arithmetic File / setting Peak MiB Spare MiB Q5_K_XL, 256K, MTP off 30,254 2,353 Q4_K_XL, 256K, MTP on 30,722 1,885 Q5_K_S, 256K, MTP on 31,943 664 Q5_K_XL, 128K, MTP on* 30,458 2,149 Q5_K_XL, 229,376, DFlash 2 draft plus n-gram, thinking on 30,647 1,960 Q5_K_XL, 262,144, DFlash 2 draft plus n-gram, thinking off 31,992 615 Peak is the largest total-card reading during each run, including desktop use. Spare = 32,607 minus peak; not a guaranteed loading margin. *Default cache (f16 per the launch comment). The 262,144 draft-model row is from letters with thinking off; the 189.26 reasoning rate below is a separate run with thinking on. The long read and the crash check At the 262,144-token window, each of the three files read a 229,152-token prompt and returned all 3 hidden codes, placed at about 5%, 50% and 95% of the ledger (not exact positions). Measured: reading from scratch, then a short code answer File / setting Read s Whole request s Codes Q5_K_XL, MTP off 194.086 196.9 3 / 3 Q4_K_XL, MTP on 202.377 205.2 3 / 3 Q5_K_S, MTP on 203.831 206.6 3 / 3 Whole request includes the answer and overhead. Crash check: Q5_K_XL without MTP and Q4_K_XL with MTP each completed 40 of 40 shorter mixed-text prompts at the 256K setting, each with a follow-up turn, with no crashes or empty answers. Q5_K_S was not crash-checked. Why Q5_K_XL could not use MTP at 256K In both attempts (--ubatch-size 256), the card refused these memory requests while setting up MTP: Failed CUDA allocations during MTP setup Draft cache Failed buffer Bytes f16 1,024.00 MiB, KV cache 1,073,741,824 q8_0 1,192.27 MiB, compute buffer 1,250,189,440 These are the sizes requested, not how far short the card was. Q4_K_XL and Q5_K_S loaded MTP with 8-bit draft caches at --ubatch-size 512. Two failures do not show that every other Q5_K_XL setup fails. Since October: a separate draft model With thinking on, Q5_K_XL with DFlash 2 plus n-gram drafting wrote 3,500 tokens of reasoning at 186.61 tokens a second about 20,000 tokens deep, against 60.39 without the draft model; at 262,144 the same reasoning ran at 189.26. On a plain letter with thinking off the gain was 30 to 44 percent. Reading was 10 to 15 percent slower. 03 Limits Single runs, no confidence intervals: small gaps, such as Q5_K_S against Q4_K_XL on prose, are not a stable ranking. Speed is not answer quality. The letters and structured replies are controlled shapes, not a coding or tool-use test. Two changes at once. Q4_K_XL with MTP against Q5_K_XL without changes both file and MTP. The 128K rows also differ in cache, so they isolate neither window size nor MTP. Narrow fidelity test: one public technical text, against an 8-bit reference rather than full-precision weights. Q5_K_XL is an older upload, so differences cannot be credited to compression alone. The October setup was not re-scored. Finding codes is not reasoning. One long read and a short crash check do not show reliable reasoning over a full window. Same name, different file. The data package's expected-size list names another UD-Q5_K_XL of 20,876,938,144 bytes (stated), not tested; these memory results do not apply to it. 04 Corrections and updates Update, 26 September 2026 This card follows the day-zero field card with a new test on 26 September 2026, served again at 262,144 tokens with a kept log and reading up to 229,152 tokens. It does not recover the lost 17 September log or claim a prompt filled every token. Update, 19 October 2026: a separate draft model This desktop

pages.t: Qwen3.8-27B measured on release day, one RTX 5090: its built-in drafter needs a cutoff
pages.d: Qwen3.8-27B, one RTX 5090, 14 August, 65,536 window: prose 72.4 tokens a second with drafter cutoff 0.75, 44.5 at 0. The 27B is Apache 2.0.
h: Thinking: a real off-switch, and a budget floor that depends on the prompt
Client traps (this chat template, this llama.cpp build)
The model, as read from its files
pages.x: With thinking off, Qwen3.8-27B wrote prose at 72.4 tokens a second with its built-in drafter (a part that guesses a few words ahead) set to stop guessing when unsure, against 65.9 with no drafter (65,536-token window; median of three repeats of one prompt). Two setups. This page is the 14 August test with the built-in drafter. Since 19 October this model runs here with a separate draft model instead: see that update. In short If you use the built-in drafter, turn it on and set its cutoff yourself (--spec-draft-p-min 0.75); llama.cpp does not use it unless asked. At a 65,536-token window, a cutoff of 0.75 made structured output 79.3% faster than no drafter, and a cutoff of 0 made prose 32.4% slower, at 44.5 tokens a second. What to do Turn thinking off in the right place (inside chat_template_kwargs). On this llama.cpp build, enable_thinking sent at the top level was silently ignored: no error, and thinking stayed on. The client traps Check the license of the exact repository you download. The 27B is Apache 2.0; Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B, released the same week, is not. The two licenses By Grant Williams · Published 14 August 2026 Download this study's data (zip, 0.3 MB) 01 What to do These are the settings from the 14 August test with the built-in drafter, using one compressed file of the model (Unsloth's UD-Q5_K_XL) in llama.cpp, the program that runs it. For the separate draft model used since 19 October, see that update. Turn the built-in drafter on, and set its cutoff yourself (--spec-type draft-mtp, --spec-draft-p-min 0.75). The drafter (also called the draft head, or MTP) is a small block inside the model file that guesses the next few tokens (word pieces) for the model to check. With no drafter flags you get about 66 tokens a second on both kinds of output. The cutoff stops a draft early once the drafter is no longer confident. Its default has changed twice: 0.9, then 0.75 for about fifteen months, then 0.0 from 2026-05-19, which our 2026-08-05 build follows. Pass it explicitly. The measurements If you use the ggml-org conversion, the drafter is not in its main file. That file was built with --no-mtp; the drafter ships as separate mtp-*.gguf files, so the main file alone cannot draft for itself. Turn thinking off in the request body, inside chat_template_kwargs. There it worked; as a top-level field it was ignored (below). A request body with the thinking switch in the right place (prose speed runs used max_tokens 400): {"model": "qwen3.8-27b", "max_tokens": 400, "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "..."}]} With thinking on, give the reply room, and measure your own floor. Thinking counts against the same max_tokens as the visible answer, so a small budget can come back empty. On one prompt the first budget tested that worked was 500; on another, 60 was enough. Do not copy 500 into your client. As a starting point, not a rule: we give thinking replies 2,000 to 4,096 tokens here, and structured or JSON work with thinking on starved even at 1,200. Details Spell reasoning_effort exactly: xhigh, medium or low. Any other value fails that request with HTTP 500. It also does not cap thinking: it adds a sentence to the prompt, and medium adds nothing. Choose the context window (how much text the model holds at once) by what else needs the card. 32,768 tokens was faster on both kinds of output and left more room than 65,536; if nothing else needs the card, start there. The 65,536 used here left about 7 GiB free for voice software on this desktop. With a 16-bit (f16) key-value cache (the memory that holds the text so far), 131,072 is the most this card holds; the full 262,144 needed an 8-bit cache and the drafter off (Updates). The exact command for the release-day default. Every row of the speed table below is this command with --ctx-size changed, the three --spec-* flags present or absent, and --spec-draft-p-min set to the value shown: llama-server --model Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q5_K_XL.gguf \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8198 --alias qwen3.8-27b \ --jinja --ctx-size 65536 --parallel 1 --n-gpu-layers 999 \ --threads 24 --threads-batch 24 --flash-attn on --timeout 3600 \ --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --min-p 0.0 \ --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 6 --spec-draft-p-min 0.75 02 What we found Speed by window and drafter Seven server loads, same file, build and card. Writing speed is tokens a second (t/s), the median of three warm repeats of one prompt per kind of output, thinking off. Prompt reading (prefill) is one uncached send of a 5,792-token prompt. Memory is MiB after load, on a 32,607 MiB card. Profile Window Drafter Memory used, MiB Free, MiB Prose t/s Structured t/s Prompt reading t/s Fast 32,768 cutoff 0.75 23,250 9,357 78.25 131.21 2,920.6 Release-day default 65,536 cutoff 0.75 25,470 7,137 72.43 118.69 2,902.0 Long 131,072 cutoff 0.75 29,950 2,657 77.46 111.60 2,881.87 No drafter 32,768 off 21,748 10,859 65.64 65.68 3,256.03 No drafter 65,536 off 23,850 8,757 65.87 66.21 3,234.64 No drafter 131,072 off 28,014 4,593 66.50 66.24 3,252.84 No cutoff, the trap 65,536 cutoff 0 25,460 7,147 44.52 99.86 2,894.24 One session per row. No interval is computed. A diagnostic set of runs, not a benchmark. Prose speed did not fall steadily as the window grew: 78.25 at 32,768, 72.43 at 65,536, 77.46 at 131,072. With one session per row and no repeat, this could be run-to-run variation. Structured output did fall steadily, 131.21 to 118.69 to 111.60, about 15% from end to end. A bigger window costs little memory. The model is dense (all of it runs for every token, unlike a mixture-of-experts model), and only 16 of its 64 layers keep a key-value cache, about 64 KiB per token. Quadrupling the window from 32,768 to 131,072 cost about 6,700 MiB. That is the cost of allocating the window, not filling it. What stops it at 131,072 is free space: 2,657 MiB. The full 262,144 tokens at an f16 cache would want roughly 16 GiB of cache on top of roughly 19 GiB of weights: a limit of this card, not the model. Prompt reading is fast. About 3,240 t/s with the drafter off and about 2,900 with it on: the drafter costs a little prompt reading and buys a lot of writing. The prompt cache works: sent again, 5,788 of the 5,792 tokens came from cache, so the rate printed for repeat sends means nothing and only the first send is in the table. On a smaller card. A 24 GB card holds about 24,576 MiB. On these readings the no-drafter 32,768 row (21,748 MiB) is the only one with real headroom, the drafter 32,768 row (23,250 MiB) leaves under 1.5 GiB before a desktop compositor and fragmentation are counted, and everything at 65,536 and above is out of reach at this compression. A 24 GB card, a smaller compressed file and a window below 32,768 were not tested. Against the other Qwen models measured here. 72.43 prose t/s, against 26 to 38 on the Qwen3.5 122B and 14 to 20 on the 397B (pair field card). Not a benchmark; a smaller model on this card could plausibly be faster. The drafter and its cutoff Both cutoffs were set explicitly on the command line, not left to the build's default. Asking with no cutoff made prose slower than not asking at all. The server's own counters explain it. At 0.75, four repeats of one prose prompt kept 61% to 74% of their drafted tokens, drafting 110 to 130 tokens each, with a mean draft length of 2.15 to 2.45. pages.t: Qwen3.8 release: both open models verified, under two different licenses
pages.d: Both open Qwen3.8 models verified on official files: the 2.4T Max-class under a custom license with revenue thresholds, the 27B under Apache 2.0.
h: The 2.4T download's license is not Apache 2.0
Qwen3.8-Max online: thinking can use the whole budget
The 27B ran the day it shipped
pages.x: Qwen3.8 comes as two downloads and one online model, and each got a different result. Checked 2026-08-09 to 2026-08-16; after that, treat this status as unverified. The 27B download Real, on the official Qwen organization, under Apache 2.0. It ran on one desktop the day it shipped. Do: check who owns a repository (the official one is Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B); settings are on the Qwen3.8-27B field card. The 2.4T download (the open Max-class weights) Real, on the official Qwen organization, under a custom license with revenue thresholds. The only community copy that fits this test desktop's free disk, 397.3 GB, would not load: the server program rejected it in 0.38 seconds because its compression type was not one any public build checked could read. Do: read the license; check a file's compression type before downloading. Qwen3.8-Max online (the hosted model) Thinks by default, and the thinking counts against your token limit: a 2,000-token limit on a puzzle returned an empty answer. The 2.4T download, served online, did the same at small limits. Do: allow thousands of tokens of headroom. In short Read the license for each download, not the family. The 27B download is Apache 2.0. The 2.4T download adds a name-display duty for very large products and a separate license for some businesses above fifty million US dollars in revenue. The two conditions Check who owns a repository before you download: a real Qwen release is on the official Qwen organization. If you use a community file, check its compression type against your software first. A 397.3 GB community copy of the 2.4T download passed every checksum here and still would not load. How to check Allow thousands of tokens of headroom on Qwen3.8-Max online. Its hidden thinking counts against your token limit. The measurements By Grant Williams · Published 9 August 2026 01 What to do Tell a real release from a fake. Fake repositories (online folders of model files) using the Qwen3.8 name were still up when re-checked on 2026-08-13. Three questions settle almost every case without a download: Who owns it? A release comes from the maker's own organization account. Anything else is that account's work, whatever the name says. Is anything in it? Open the file list first. Weights (the model's learned numbers) come split into large pieces called shards: a 27B at four bits is tens of gigabytes, a 2.4-trillion-parameter model is hundreds. A readme and a small configuration file are no model. Was this size announced? The 2026-08-03 announcement named exactly two open models, a 27B and the 2.4-trillion-parameter Max. Then take the link from the Qwen team's announcement or the official organization page, confirm the license file and sensible shard sizes, and check the checksums (fingerprints of each file) after downloading. For the 27B, compare against Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B at the revision (saved version) under How this was measured; weights that are not the maker's files at a revision you can name are not the release. This took about five minutes. Check the compression type before a big download. Community GGUF files (the format llama.cpp reads) store the weights compressed, which is called quantization. A familiar name is not a format: the 2.4T download's community file called Q1_0 is not mainline Q1_0, and only the per-tensor headers (the description of each block of weights) show its real type. Compare that type against the types your software can read. The check costs minutes; here the download cost an afternoon and 397 GB of disk. Online, budget for thinking. Qwen3.8-Max online thinks by default, and the 2.4T download always thinks. Either way the thinking is billed as output tokens (word pieces) inside your max-tokens limit. Give it thousands of tokens of headroom, or try the reasoning_effort setting (on the one prompt tested with the 2.4T download online, it did not reduce thinking). An empty answer that ends with the length stop reason (the limit ran out) is a budget failure, not a refusal. Put a JSON schema in the prompt, not only in the API's response_format field. On the 2.4T download, do not count on turning thinking off (the 27B has a working off-switch). Check each provider's terms behind an aggregator listing (an aggregator resells many companies' model services through one account). The evidence 02 What we found Which files are real Shipped and verified means we saw the weight files at a named revision, with a license. API only means the model answers online but no weights exist. Community only means real files from a named third party, nothing official. Not official means files exist under the name but none come from the maker. Model Status Evidence, with check date Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B Shipped and verified On the official Qwen organization. Its own timestamps say created 2026-08-08, last modified 10:24 UTC on 2026-08-12. Verified 2026-08-13: 213 weight shards plus an index file, 4,892.4 GB in BF16 (16-bit numbers), license file present. The name carries the 95-billion-active-parameter figure (A95B) that was press-only before the release. Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-FP8 Shipped and verified Verified 2026-08-13: 213 shards, 2,496.2 GB, fp8 dynamic quantization with 128 by 128 blocks, license file byte-identical to the BF16 one. On that date the organization's Qwen3.8 collection held exactly these two repositories. Community GGUF copies of the 2.4T download Community only One real set, from the community quantizer unsloth, verified 2026-08-13: 312 GGUF files, 397.3 GB to 4,893.2 GB. No official GGUF. The smallest was downloaded here and matched its checksums, and it could not be loaded (below). Qwen3.8-27B Shipped and verified Published about 11:00 EDT on 2026-08-14 and verified the same day: 18 safetensors plus an index, 32 files, and a LICENSE file read in full and kept. That license is Apache 2.0, byte-identical in the official FP8 repository. No official GGUF; the community conversions include one from the llama.cpp project's own organization, published the same day. Measured on the Qwen3.8-27B field card. Qwen3.8-Max online API only Live since 2026-08-03 on Alibaba Cloud Model Studio and on aggregators; measured below. Per the model card, checked 2026-08-13, vision input, the non-thinking mode and the million-token default context are extras of Qwen3.8-Max online, not in the 2.4T download. Third-party "Qwen3.8" repos Not official Re-screened 2026-08-13: every third-party 27B repository previously catalogued under the name still held zero weight tensors, and new mirrors and placeholders using the Max name appeared around the release. Qwen3.7 family API only Max, Plus and Flash tiers on the official API and aggregators (checked 2026-08-09). The vendor states they are proprietary; no 3.7 weights have shipped. Qwen3.6-27B and 35B Shipped and verified The newest open Qwen weights until 2026-08-12. File trees and Apache 2.0 license files confirmed on the official organization (checked 2026-08-09). The 2.4T download's license is not Apache 2.0 Qwen3.6, the previous open release, shipped under Apache 2.0. The 2.4T download does not. Both of their repositories hold the same Qwen3.8-Max License, 3,390 bytes, read on 2026-08-13: an MIT-style permission grant with two conditions. Name display above consumer scale. Products or services built on the model with more than 100 million monthly active users, or more than twenty million US dollars in monthly revenue, must display the model name prominently. The revenue test is monthly, not annual. A separate license above fifty million. Businesses offering the model as a service, or offering an "AI Work Assistant" product, whose aggregate revenue exceeds fifty million US dollars in any consecutive twelve months, must obtain a separate license from Qwen before commercial use. Internal use is exempt. The operative clause, verbatim Such licensees "shall obtain a separate license from Qwen before Using the Software or its derivative works for any commercial purpose." pages.t: What reasoning effort changes on Qwen3.8-27B
pages.d: In the tested Qwen3.8-27B template, xhigh adds a 42-token instruction, medium adds none and leaving the setting out gives the same prompt as xhigh.
h: The experiment, and the limitation that came out of it
Observed: the injection is a fixed-size block
Observed: what it does to thinking, and to answers
Observed: the hosted 2.4T test, and what converges
The version boundary: llama.cpp b10290 and b10453
Special values, two paths, and one escape hatch
If you send reasoning_effort to Qwen3.8
pages.x: On the Qwen3.8-27B model file we served on one RTX 5090, once the server passes the setting on to the model file's template, it is a sentence added to your prompt, not a dial: xhigh adds 42 tokens (words or parts of words), low adds 30, medium adds none, and leaving the setting out gives the same prompt as xhigh. In short Send medium if you want your prompt left alone. Of the three levels, medium is the only one that adds no instruction. Leaving the field out is not neutral: it gives the same prompt as xhigh, byte for byte. What to send To turn thinking off, send none as its own top-level field, not inside chat_template_kwargs. At the top level, the llama.cpp server turns thinking off (HTTP 200). Inside chat_template_kwargs, the object llama.cpp passes straight to the template, the same word is an error (HTTP 500), on both builds tested. The two paths Check your own server in two requests. Send the same message at xhigh and at medium and compare the reported prompt_tokens: if the counts differ, something is rewriting your prompt from that field. On llama.cpp it depends on the build: on the older build we tested, a top-level value other than none never reached the template. The check By Grant Williams · Published 16 August 2026 Download this study's data (zip, 0.1 MB) 01 Summary The reasoning_effort field, on the Qwen3.8 build we served, is implemented in the chat template that ships inside the model file (the instructions that turn your messages into the text the model reads), not in the sampler and not in the serving runtime. The template maps the value to a string it calls reasoning_instructions and injects that string as a system message ahead of your own message. That single implementation detail explains everything below. Everything in this section describes a server that applies the GGUF's (the model file's) own chat template. On llama.cpp that means --jinja with no --chat-template or --chat-template-file override, which is the configuration both of our builds ran and which section 03 states in full. A server that substitutes a built-in template renders a different prompt, and none of these numbers describe it. The three levels inject three different amounts of text, and the amounts are fixed. On the served template, xhigh injects a system block of 42 tokens, low injects 30, and medium injects zero. Those deltas were identical on all three test prompts, whose lengths differ, so the injection is a constant added to your prompt rather than anything proportional to it. Medium is not a middle setting. It is the absence of a setting. The template has an xhigh branch and a low branch and no medium branch, so medium falls through with the instruction string empty and the rendered prompt carries no system message at all. Omitting the field is identical to sending xhigh. The template's default is xhigh, so the rendered prompts (the exact text the server built for the model) for "field absent" and for xhigh were byte-identical, and the generations they produced were byte-identical too. There is no "unset" state. What moved most consistently was answer style, not thinking volume. On the local 27B, low produced the least thinking on all three prompts (62% to 73% of what xhigh spent on the same prompt), but medium was erratic: 85% and 97% of xhigh on two prompts and 3.3 times xhigh on the third. xhigh gave the tersest answer on every prompt and medium the longest, by factors of roughly 2 to 3. These are three prompts at one observation each (section 04), so read them as three readings, not as a rate. The hosted 2.4T test had shown the same style direction three days earlier. On the hosted 2.4T-A95B, thinking spend did not order by effort. One call per level: 184 reasoning tokens at xhigh, 197 at medium, 168 at low. A 17% band with the nominal maximum-effort setting in the middle of it, from three calls split across two providers. That is not a measurement of a small effect; it is a failure to see a large one. Section 07 carries the cost figures and the provider confound that comes with them. The same three integers appeared on both runs. The hosted study recorded server prompt-token counts of 112 / 70 / 100 for xhigh / medium / low on a marble-probability prompt and wrote "mechanism unknown". Our locally rendered prompts for the same three levels on the same message tokenize to 112 / 70 / 100. Two different models on two different serving stacks: the hosted counts are an unexplained observation that is consistent with the injection we can read locally, and nothing more. Section 07 says exactly what that does and does not license. On llama.cpp, whether the field reaches the template at all depends on your build. On the older build we tested, b10290, the OpenAI-compatibility layer handled the value none and left every other value unhandled, under a source comment saying those values are model-specific and not yet handled. The effect on the wire is that every level rendered the default prompt: xhigh, medium, low, absent and even the nonsense value ultra all rendered the same 112-token prompt. On the newer build, b10453, the field reaches the template, the three levels render three different prompts, and ultra returns HTTP 500 (a server error). Those are the two builds we ran. The run log attributes the change to pull request #26941, reported merged on 2026-08-14 and first shipped in b10434; section 08 says which parts of that we measured and which parts we are repeating. There are two paths into the template, and they disagree about one word. Passing effort inside chat_template_kwargs always worked, on both builds, because it is generic passthrough. Passing it at top level (as its own field in the request body) is the path the merge added. The word none is intercepted by the server's OpenAI-compatibility handler on the top-level path (it turns thinking off, HTTP 200) and passed straight through to the template on the chat_template_kwargs path, where it is not a valid effort and raises (HTTP 500). Same word, two paths, opposite outcomes, on both builds. Everything on this page is one model family, two deployments, two builds, on the dates stated. The local run is a single observation per cell (one prompt at one effort level); section 04 explains why, and why we think it is still worth reading. 02 What the setting actually is The clearest way to state this is to show the prompt the server built. This is the local 27B's own render of the same user message under three effort values, retrieved from the server's /apply-template endpoint, on a server started with --jinja and no template override, so the template being rendered here is the one inside the GGUF. /apply-template is not the endpoint you generate through, so we checked it against the one you do. On the four marble conditions we ran both ways, the prompt-token count the server reported for a real /v1/chat/completions generation is the same as the token count of the retained render: 112 for xhigh, 70 for medium, 100 for low, 112 for the field omitted. The two endpoints also share their prompt-construction call in the source of the build we ran, but the matching counts are the part we can hand you as a record. reasoning_effort: "xhigh" renders <|im_start|>system Reasoning effort is set to xhigh. Please think carefully through the task, validate key assumptions, consider plausible alternatives, and prioritize correctness, consistency, and clarity in the final answer.<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user A bag holds 3 red, 4 blue and 5 green marbles. ...<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant <think> reasoning_effort: "low" renders <|im_start|>system Reasoning effort is set to low. Keep your thinking brief and focused, moving directly to the conclusion without unnecessary elaboration.<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user A bag holds 3 red, 4 blue and 5 green marbles. ...<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant <think> reasoning_effort: "medium" renders <|im_start|>user A bag holds 3 red, 4 blue and 5 green marbles. ...<|im_end|> <|im_start|>as

pages.t: Two small robots connected to AI at home
pages.d: One desk robot opened a Wi-Fi hotspot with no password. One wheeled robot fell over after 83 minutes. What we found connecting two robots to AI at home.

What the XGO Rider 2 did in our tests
