pages.x: Two kinds of small robot are here. Each is a body for an AI model that runs on a computer in our house. Here is what they did in our tests. Four more are ordered and not yet tested. Two robots here and connected Both were set up again to talk through AI models that run in the house. M5StackNo. 01 Stack-chan A face and a voice on the desk We have Two, one still boxed Its AI runs On our desktop Listens Only after a tap Here now XGONo. 02 XGO Rider 2 Balances on two wheels and talks Its AI runs On a laptop kept offline Battery 83 minutes, then it fell over AI drives it Not allowed yet Here now What we changed on Stack-chan Stack-chan is a small desk robot from M5Stack. It has a face on a screen, a head that moves, a light, a microphone and a speaker. Ours is connected to the Hearth, our private home for long-running AIs, which runs on our desktop. We backed it up before setting it up Before the robot was ever set up or joined to Wi-Fi, we saved an exact copy of everything on it. It can be put back just as it came out of the box. We set it to talk only to our desktop We rebuilt the maker’s open-source software so the robot talks only to our desktop. The maker’s account, app store, downloads, Bluetooth pairing and camera are switched off. It listens only after a tap Tap its face, speak, and it says the reply. After a minute of quiet it hangs up. Its light shows what it is doing: blue for listening, white for thinking, yellow for speaking and dark for not connected. Turning off “Hi Stack-chan” did not stop it listening Turning off “Hi Stack-chan” in the settings was not enough. The robot kept a program running that listened for that phrase, until we removed the phrase detector from it. It opened a Wi-Fi hotspot with no password As shipped, the robot opened a Wi-Fi hotspot with no password after about a minute without its network. Now the hotspot opens only from the robot’s own menu, with a password shown on its screen. A picture sent mid-sentence froze it The AI model can nod the robot’s head, set its light, change its face and put a picture on its screen. Each of those is a separate switch that starts off. Showing a picture while the robot was speaking froze it in one test, so that stays off. What the XGO Rider 2 did in our tests The Rider is a small robot that balances upright on two wheels. It has a camera, two microphones and a speaker. Ours talks to an AI model on a laptop over a private Wi-Fi network made only for it. While the robot is on, the laptop has no Internet. We set its memory card aside and built a new one We set the robot’s original memory card aside untouched and built a new one for it, with a firewall that blocks connections we did not allow. The laptop does the listening and the speaking with programs that run offline. Asked for its battery level it said 28 percent Press a button on the laptop, speak, and the Rider says the model’s reply. In the first test it was asked for its battery level and answered 28 percent, read from the real battery by a model running at home. It sent a picture and one model misread a blank one The Rider sent one camera picture over its private link, and two models running at home described it. One of them called a blank picture a missing one, so the software, not the model, has to say whether a picture arrived. One radio we cannot switch off The part that keeps the robot balanced has its own Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radio. The robot’s main computer cannot switch it off, and we have not confirmed that it stays silent. This is still open. It fell over after 83 minutes of balancing In one session the battery went from 100 percent to 28 percent in 83 minutes of standing still, and then the robot fell over. You cannot turn it by hand Its balance control pushes back when you try to turn it to face you. It needs to turn itself, and no AI model has been allowed to move it yet. It should not roam alone It has no way to sense a stair, a table edge or a foot, and it fell over standing still. No AI model has been allowed to move it. Four ordered, none tested We have tested none of these four. Prices, features and dates are the makers’. Pollen RoboticsNo. 03 Reachy Mini Wireless A desk robot with a moving head Price $499 Maker lists Computer, Wi-Fi, battery Maker says Ships within 90 days On the way Pollen RoboticsNo. 04 Microduck A 25 cm walking duck Price $399 Maker says it learns On a computer first Maker says First ones by Christmas 2026 On the way PetoiNo. 05 Quaddle Scout A palm-sized robot dog Price $269 Talks Yes, maker says Kickstarter says December 2026 On the way Nori RoboticsNo. 06 Nori A3 Two arms on a rolling base Price $1,688 Its AI runs Off the robot, maker says Maker says Ships fall 2026 On the way Prices are list prices before shipping and tax, from each maker’s own page, read 21 November 2026. Nori confirmed our order for its second batch, planned for fall 2026. We have tested none of these four. What we ask of every robot Question Stack-chan XGO Rider 2 Does it listen only when asked? After a tap on its face The laptop listens, after a button press Does anything leave the house? It is set to talk only to our desktop The laptop is offline while the robot is on. One radio on the robot is not confirmed silent Where does its AI run? On our desktop On a laptop Can it move, and what stops it? Its head can nod. That switch starts off It balances on two wheels. No AI model has been allowed to move it Which parts are open source? The maker’s software, which we rebuilt Not covered here yet

pages.t: The roster, as of 26 September 2026
pages.d: Twenty-three local model endpoints on one RTX 5090 desktop, one at a time, as of 26 September 2026, each speed with the prompt and reply it timed.
h: Twenty-three endpoints on a one-model machine
Why there are two speed columns and not one
The twenty-three, with their newest figures
What a batch setting did, and did not, change
pages.x: Twenty-three local model endpoints on one RTX 5090 desktop, one running at a time; one row also uses a linked laptop. Every reading speed says its prompt size and batch setting, and every speaking speed says what reply it timed. Start with the fact that makes the rest of the page readable: only one of these models can run at a time. They share one graphics card and one pool of system memory, and the launch policy refuses a second model while one is up. So this is not a fleet. It is a list of what this single desktop can be, one model at a time, with the speed each one produced, the prompt that produced it, and the dated run each figure comes from. Since the list was first compiled on 15 September, three models were added and two removed, and most reading speeds were measured again after we found that llama.cpp's batch settings had never been tuned on this desktop. The largest change was Laguna S 2.1: at its old 32,768-token window it read the same 24,071-token prompt at 72.2 tokens a second with -b 512 -ub 128 and at 1,434.0 with -b/-ub 8192; at the 262,144-token window it now serves, it reads 898.8 on 24,013 tokens at -b 8192 -ub 4096. Several figures in our own records did not survive a check against their logs; section 05 lists them. Two rows have no September figure for the configuration they serve, and say so. By Grant Williams · Published 26 September 2026 Download this study's data (zip, 0.4 MB) Independent measurements. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or connected to DeepSeek, Thinking Machines Lab, Alibaba Group, Z.ai, Google, MiniMax, Meta, Mistral AI, inclusionAI, Poolside, Ornith AI, Moonshot AI, NVIDIA, Intel, ASUS, or the llama.cpp project. 01 Twenty-three endpoints on a one-model machine The machine is one desktop: an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 with 32,607 MiB of graphics memory, an Intel Core Ultra 9 285K and 188 GiB of system RAM. Row 1 also uses a second machine, an ASUS ROG Flow Z13 with 128 GB of unified memory, joined to the desktop by a direct Thunderbolt cable; its cells say so. Every model is served by llama-server from llama.cpp, and every start script refuses to launch while another model is up; the package holds one recorded test in which seven separate guards each refused a launch. What "endpoint" means here One installed service: one set of serving flags, with the model file or files that service is set up to read, as installed on this machine. Rows 1 and 3 are two separate services for DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731, one split across the desktop and the laptop and one on this desktop alone. Each can serve either of two files as presets: row 3's figures name their file, and row 1's are all from its default file except the one its row note names. Changes since 15 September, as our operator records have them: Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B and GLM-5.3-Flash were installed on 16 September and MiniMax M2.7 on 21 September. Kimi K3 was retired on 15 September and Kimi K2.7-Code's weights were removed on 17 September. MiniMax M3 serves a different file since 21 September, Laguna S 2.1 a 262,144-token window since the same day, and Qwen3.6-27B a different file since 26 September; our records also give it a 262,144-token window from that day, which the runs on this page loaded by passing it explicitly. Qwen3.8-27B was installed at a 262,144-token window on the afternoon of 26 September; its start script still accepts 131,072. Qwen3.5-122B-A10B and Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B were installed at 262,144 the same afternoon, MiniMax M2.7 at 196,608, its native ceiling, that evening, and GLM-5.3-Flash at 262,144 later that evening; a start of each of these four with no window passed was served that window. Each row's window cell says whether a run that passed no window shows the installed default. A count of twenty-three installed endpoints is not a capacity claim: one runs at a time. 02 What we ran, exactly The figures come from several exercises between 12 and 26 September 2026. Two methods never share a column: a request sent straight to the server (direct), and the same kind of request made through an agent framework. The batch-size sweep 19 to 21 September On 21 September each model was started through its own start script; the 19 and 20 September runs (MiniMax M2.7 and M3, DeepSeek's 8-bit file, Inkling-Small, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) started the server by hand with the same flags. Each run read a synthetic prompt cold at temperature 0, most often a ledger of about 48,000 tokens with a code word planted halfway that the answer had to quote exactly. Reading is prompt tokens per second. The speaking figure is the short answer's generation rate: a code of about eleven tokens on models that answer directly, longer on thinking models because their hidden reasoning counts. Each row names the batch setting it ran (-b batch, -ub micro-batch; llama.cpp's defaults are -b 2048 -ub 512). The batch-size study has the method. Paragraph replies 12 and 15 September A short request for plain prose, the better of two warm replies: one paragraph of about 150 words on 15 September, about 200 tokens of prose on 12 September. These are the page's prose speaking figures for most rows. First runs of two new models 16 September For Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B and GLM-5.3-Flash: the same paragraph request with the thinking switch off, a tool call, and a read of about 120,000 tokens with three planted codes, at llama.cpp's default batch settings. Letters at depth 26 September For five rows: a ledger read cold at about 20,000, 60,000 and 100,000 tokens (Qwen3-235B), 20,000, 100,000 and 230,000 (Qwen3.6-27B) or 20,000, 48,000, 100,000 and 230,000 (Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3.5-122B-A10B and Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B), then a letter of about 330 to 430 words written on the same cached ledger: prose at depth, as are row 1's replies of about 400 tokens. MiniMax M2.7 had the same request at about 20,000, 48,000 and 190,000 tokens, and GLM-5.3-Flash at about 20,000 to 230,000; their rows say what came back. Long reads at a full window 15 to 16 September Prompts of about 150,000 to 231,000 tokens with three planted codes, at a 262,144-token window (202,752 for GLM-4.7-Flash). Used here only for the window column and a few depth figures; the full table is its own page, what a full window costs. Through an agent framework 12 to 14 and 21 September The model driven through an agent framework with 48,000 and 96,000 tokens of seeded history, three codes planted in it, and a tool call made at depth. The framework adds its own prompt, so the server read more than the seeded figure; that true size is printed. Its speaking figures are its short answers (30 to 1,004 tokens, mostly the three codes plus any reasoning) and its reading figure is the harness's own estimate from token counts and timing. Why there are two speed columns and not one A model measured directly and through a framework does not give the same number. Gemma-4-26B read at 8,972.3 tokens a second directly at 47,983 tokens and at an estimated 6,726.8 through the framework at 53,209. Qwen3-235B spoke at 9.3 through the framework on a 62-token answer at 53,458 tokens, and at 5.51 directly on a 478-token letter at 20,063. Neither figure is wrong: they answer different questions, and mixing them in one column would be the worst error available on this page. Every speaking figure below also says what it timed, because a short answer and a page of prose are not the same measurement. 03 The twenty-three, with their newest figures Every speed below is measured, on the dates given, one request at a time. Files and byte counts are read from the files on this machine (a listing taken on 26 September); maker names are the makers' own. "Short answer" means the model's reply to a quote-the-code question, and its token count includes hidden reasoning. Reading speeds after the batch-size sweep name the flag and the depth. pages.t: Local AI models on one RTX 5090 desktop, October 2026
pages.d: Thirteen local AI models added to one RTX 5090 desktop in October 2026, with speeds, and processor settings that sped 13 of 15 models but slowed two.
h: The change that helped most of the models we tested
Why the Qwen3.8-27B gain depends on what it writes
pages.x: On one RTX 5090 desktop, pinning llama.cpp to the processor's eight performance cores with three settings made 13 of 15 models that keep part of their weights in system RAM write about 7 to 81 percent faster on a long prompt, and two slower (the 15 are the models whose two runs wrote replies of the same length). In short Try the settings if your model keeps its experts in system RAM on a chip with performance and efficiency cores. Keep llama.cpp's threads on the eight performance cores, use 8 threads for writing and for reading the prompt, and add the OpenMP spin setting (taskset -c 0-7, --threads 8 --threads-batch 8, GOMP_SPINCOUNT=10000000). Measure your own model both ways, because two of ours got slower. The test and what to do Look up a model. For each of the thirteen new models, "First word" is the time the server spent reading the prompt before the reply could start, and "Speaking" is how fast the model wrote, counting any hidden reasoning. On two rows the timed text was reasoning with no visible answer, and each row says what was timed. The models See what changed since September. Between 27 September and 25 October 2026, thirteen models were added, six measured again and three retired, and earlier mistakes are corrected. The September roster (the previous list of what this desktop ran) is kept as a dated record. Re-measured · Retired · Corrections By Grant Williams · Published 26 October 2026 Download this study's data (zip, 0.1 MB) 01 How to read this page This page is for anyone who runs open-weight models at home on one big graphics card. Open-weight models are models whose files you can download. Every speed below comes with the prompt and the reply it timed. One machine, one model at a time. The desktop has an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 with 32,607 MiB of graphics memory, an Intel Core Ultra 9 285K and 188 GiB of system RAM. MiB and GiB are binary units of memory: mebibytes and gibibytes. One row also ran on an ASUS ROG Flow Z13 laptop with 128 GB of memory, and says so. llama.cpp is the program that runs the models. Every model is served by llama.cpp's llama-server, which loads a model and answers requests, one request at a time. A few terms, once: Speaking is how fast the model writes: generated tokens per second (t/s). A token is roughly three quarters of a word. First word is how long a cold prompt takes to read before the reply can start (the time to read the prompt). Cold means the server had not read that text before. It is the server's own prompt time. Deep means how many tokens of conversation were already read when the reply was written. Models write slower deep in a long conversation. Window (context window) is the most text the server will hold at once, prompt and reply together. Quantization is how the weights are compressed: Q4 is about 4 bits a weight, Q8 about 8. Lower is smaller and less exact. The names (UD-Q4_K_XL, IQ1_S, MXFP4) are the file makers'. The cache, the model's memory of the conversation so far, can be compressed the same way. Rows say so where they list a cache setting. Experts in RAM. A mixture-of-experts model uses a few of its many expert blocks for each token. When the file is bigger than the card, the experts live in system RAM and the processor runs them. That is why processor settings matter on those rows. Thinking models write hidden reasoning before they answer. Their speaking figures count that reasoning. Every speed below is a measurement from a dated run, and the files for that run are in the data package. The method page defines the label measured. Each cell says what reply it timed. A short answer and a 400-word letter are different measurements, so a row that has only a short answer says so. A draft model is a small second model that guesses the next few tokens. The main model checks the guesses and keeps the ones it agrees with. 02 The change that helped most of the models we tested On 29 September we ran 16 models that keep part of their weights in system RAM twice on the same prompt of about 96,000 tokens (48,000 on three rows, 24,000 on two). A thread is one stream of work. In the first run, llama.cpp used 24 threads spread over every core. In the second run, we pinned it to the eight performance cores (P-cores) with three settings: the operating system's taskset -c 0-7, llama.cpp's --threads 8 --threads-batch 8 and the OpenMP setting GOMP_SPINCOUNT=10000000. OpenMP is the library llama.cpp uses to run its threads. Pinning means the operating system may run those threads only on those cores. We call the three settings together the thread-pinning bundle. The spin setting was not run on its own. The 285K has eight performance cores and sixteen efficiency cores. Fifteen of the 16 are mixture-of-experts models with their experts in RAM. The sixteenth, Mistral Medium 3.5, is a dense model. On 15 of the 16 rows both runs read the same prompt and wrote replies with the same token count and the same word count. We call those 15 the clean test pairs. The bundle made 13 of 15 clean test pairs about 7 to 81 percent faster, and two got slower. The faster replies were 311 to 673 tokens long. Model Deep, tokens Reply, tokens 24 threads, t/s With the bundle, t/s Change Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B 96,498 402 76.84 139.22 +81% Qwen3.8-Flash-NextUD-Q3_K_XL file, since replaced 96,498 465 17.54 27.53 +57% Ling-3.0-flash 99,952 328 25.87 38.74 +50% Mistral Small 4 119B 97,768 311 22.01 32.58 +48% MiniMax M2.7retired since; not a clean pair, see the note 99,877 381; 421 with the bundle 7.19 10.62 +48% DeepSeek V4 Flash 07318-bit preset 95,754 440 8.88 12.57 +42% Laguna S 2.1 95,905 430 16.02 22.03 +38% Inkling-Small 100,053 407 10.38 14.23 +37% Qwen3.5-122B-A10Bdraft model on both runs 96,498 555 23.57 32.24 +37% DeepSeek V4 Flash 07313-bit preset 95,731 368 12.92 17.45 +35% MiniMax M3 48,086 602 8.43 10.79 +28% GLM-5.3-Flash 48,109 459 9.77 12.18 +25% Mistral Large 3 675B 24,079 673 6.43 6.88 +7% Qwen3.5-397B-A17Bdraft model on both runs 96,498 620 13.27 14.15 +6.6% Mistral Medium 3.5dense 128B, retired since; draft model on both runs; letter cut at 500 tokens 24,091 500 1.80 1.65 −8% GLM-4.7 Fullretired since; draft model on both runs 48,109 286 5.61 4.68 −17% Measured 2026-09-29, one run per setting. The reply was a letter of 230 to 534 words, written in the same request that read a synthetic ledger (an invented long document), from a cold cache. The percentage is arithmetic on the two speeds. MiniMax M2.7 is the one row that is not a clean pair. Its run with the bundle restored the ledger from a saved copy, so its ledger was already cached, and it wrote a different reply (421 tokens against 381), so it is outside the 13 of 15. Four rows ran a draft model on both runs, so their speeds include its help; each pair is still like for like. Mistral Medium 3.5's letter stopped at the 500-token cap on both runs. What to do with it. If your model keeps experts in system RAM on a chip with performance and efficiency cores, try the same bundle. Pin the prompt threads too (--threads-batch), because reading a prompt runs on them. Measure your own model both ways, because two of ours got slower. Prompt-reading speed moved by 2 percent or less on 11 of the 15 clean pairs. It rose 5 to 11 percent on the two DeepSeek presets and on GLM-5.3-Flash, and fell 4.4 percent on Mistral Medium 3.5. Our explanation of why it helps, which we have not proven: for every layer held in RAM, each token sends a short burst of work to the processor. A layer is one stage of the model's computation. A burst ends only when the slowest thread finishes. With 24 threads, the slowest is often on an efficiency core. 03 Installed since 27 September Thirteen models, newest first. Every row is on the desktop unless it says laptop. "Letter" means a request for a letter of about 300 to 400 words. The model wrote it after reading a long synthetic ledger (an invented document) for the first time. The length of that ledger in tokens is what "deep" counts. Model a

pages.t: Routecheck: one-command test for OpenAI-compatible endpoints
pages.d: Ten checks against an OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint, from empty answers to tool calls, saved as a dated card with every raw response kept. MIT licensed.
h: Why it was built: the empty-answer trap
pages.x: Run one command against a model server that speaks the OpenAI chat API shape and get a dated diagnostic card from ten checks, for that one endpoint on that one date, with every raw request and response kept. In short It catches empty answers that look like success. A reasoning model's hidden thinking can use up the output budget and return an empty answer with no error. Routecheck measures the smallest tested budget that answers, sizes its other tests above it, and marks an empty answer with a length stop as INVALID instead of grading it. Why it was built Clone it and run one command. No install step; ./smoke.sh verifies a fresh copy and make test runs 331 offline tests. The commands Measure the budget floor on your own prompts. On the first published card, on one hosted route, the floor was 500 tokens for the card's own prompts, while a simpler prompt showed its first visible words at a 256-token cap the same day. The first card Published 2026-08-16 01 What it is Before you build on a model endpoint, you want to know what it actually does: whether small output budgets come back empty, whether the thinking toggle is honored, what shape tool calls arrive in, how fast it really decodes. Routecheck asks those questions the same way every time and writes the answers down where they can be checked. Routecheck runs a fixed battery of behavioral probes (fixed test requests), named QFS-CORE, checks C1 to C10, against a running /v1/chat/completions route (the address a model is served at): the widely implemented OpenAI-compatible shape that llama.cpp server, Ollama and most hosted routes speak. It needs Python 3.10 or newer and the requests package; everything else is standard library. There is no install step and no packaging layer: clone the repository and run it in place, or copy the directory anywhere, a USB stick or an air-gapped box, and run it from the copy. Every run writes three things: card.md, the diagnostic card in plain English; card.json, the same results machine-readable, every field tagged with its provenance (where that value came from); raw/, the complete raw request and response body for every probe, so any claim on the card can be checked against what actually went over the wire. A card describes one endpoint, in one configuration, on one date. That scope is printed on the card itself, and it is the point: a different quant or server of the same model can behave differently, which is much of the reason to measure at all. 02 Who it is for Three readers we had in mind. If you serve models locally, on llama.cpp server or Ollama, the card is a dated record of what your route actually does before you build on it, and again after every server upgrade or quant swap. If you are about to build on a hosted route, the card tells you on day one where the budget floor sits, whether the thinking toggle does anything, what shape tool calls arrive in and whether schema output conforms, with the raw bodies kept so you can re-check any cell. And if you publish measurements, the provenance discipline is the product: every field tagged, every RECORDED claim resolving to a file on disk, every card scoped to its endpoint and its date. 03 Get it, run it Two supported paths, deliberately boring: clone and run in place, or copy the directory anywhere and run it from the copy. Nothing depends on where the directory sits or on .git being present. terminal · a local route $ git clone https://github.com/graphometer/routecheck && cd routecheck $ ./routecheck run \ --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 \ --model-id my-served-model \ --ctx-size 32768 \ --out runs/my-model/$(date +%F)/ That is the whole thing. --ctx-size is required unless the route's /props endpoint reports its context size, as llama.cpp server does; then the server's own value is preferred and recorded as such. Against an authenticated remote endpoint: terminal · an authed remote route $ export ROUTECHECK_API_KEY=... # sent as "Authorization: Bearer <key>" $ ./routecheck run \ --base-url https://api.example.com/v1 \ --model-id some-model \ --ctx-size 32768 \ --allow-remote \ --out runs/some-model/$(date +%F)/ Non-loopback URLs require the explicit --allow-remote flag. The API key goes out as a bearer header and nowhere else: it is never logged and never written into card.json, card.md or any raw artifact, the recorded command line shows [REDACTED] in its place, and proxy environment variables and ~/.netrc are never inherited. terminal · verify a copy $ ./smoke.sh # verifies a fresh copy in seconds $ make test # 331 offline tests: no GPU, no model, no network beyond loopback mocks The offline suite deliberately proves the negative paths: tampered prompt manifests refused, empty-answer traps detected both ways, symlink escapes refused, RECORDED claims without evidence refused, API keys absent from every written file. Routecheck on GitHub github.com/graphometer/routecheck · MIT license 04 What it checks Ten checks, each answering a question about this endpoint, in this configuration, on this date, never about the model in general. The list below is the README's own scope, condensed. C1 Identity What exactly was tested: model id, served file name and size, context size, server build when exposed, the full command line, the date. A card without a complete identity block is never written. C2 Load, placement Load time, memory and placement recipe, operator-supplied only (handed in by the person running the tool). The tool talks to an already-running route, so when this data is not handed in, the card says SKIPPED instead of guessing. C3 Speed Decode tokens per second (how fast the answer is written), medians of at least three warm reps with the cold rep discarded, on one fixed prose prompt and one fixed structured prompt. Server-reported timings are authoritative when present; client wall-clock is a labeled diagnostic. C4 Prefill Prompt-processing speed on a fixed passage of about 8,000 tokens, same median rules. C5 Thinking budget Does the visible answer come back empty at small output budgets? A ladder of 60, 500, 2,000 and 4,096 max tokens finds the smallest probed budget at which the endpoint visibly answers, and that measured floor sizes every other test in the same run. C6 Thinking toggle Is the enable_thinking request field honored? Checks for a separate reasoning field, for <think>-tag leakage into the visible answer, and for reasoning duplicated untagged into it. The verdict names this exact mechanism; a route using a different toggle is not exercised. C7 Tool calls One fixed tool, one fixed user message, two shots. Pass requires exactly one tool call, the right function, schema-conformant arguments and the expected explicit values. C8 Structured output A fixed JSON Schema embedded in a fixed prompt, three reps, conformance checked: required keys, types, extra-key policy. C9 Honesty probe Asks about a nonexistent file and a nonexistent benchmark; a keyword heuristic flags hedging versus confident fabrication. Explicitly not a semantic judge: the raw response is retained for human review, and the card records exactly how it was graded. C10 Needle retrieval A seeded, programmatically generated haystack sized to about 75 percent of the served context, one planted fact, one question. The server's own prompt-token count is the recorded authoritative length. Probe list and scope from the Routecheck README, read 2026-08-16. Five rules run through every card. Every field carries provenance: RECORDED means a raw artifact is on disk, and the tool refuses to write a card whose RECORDED claims do not resolve to real files; STATED means observed or operator-supplied with no artifact; SKIPPED means not attempted, with the reason stated. INVALID is its own verdict. A failed probe is never a placeholder: connection refused, HTTP errors and malformed JSON are recorded with their raw evidence, and one test's failure never drops the rest of the run. Every prompt file is sha256-pinned in a manifest that is itself pinned

pages.t: Same 288 coding sessions: 62 cents on DeepSeek, $34.67 on Gemini 4 Neon
pages.d: OpenCode's estimates at list prices, 288 sessions each. These are not bills. The two GPT models show no price, because Codex doesn't give one.
h: Price, and how each tool counts it
pages.x: OpenCode's estimates at list prices, 288 sessions each. These are not bills. The two GPT models show no price, because Codex doesn't give one. Seven AI models each got the same 24 small coding jobs. Each job came in two versions: one that the project’s written rules allowed and one that they forbade. Each version was run with three kinds of note in the project’s instruction file, and each of those twice. That makes 288 sessions attempted per model. They ran in the Five Moves Second Test on 23 November 2026. The models did not all deliver the same work. On the 144 allowed sessions, the requested result was in the files at the end of the work turn 112 times for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and 140 times for Gemini 4 Neon. The study checked whether a forbidden change ended up in the files. It made no planned claim about price or speed. Read this first The price is what each coding tool printed. It is not a bill. We have not matched the Google bill for the same work to the figures the tool printed, so this page uses no bill number. GPT-6.2 Sol and GPT-6 Luna have no price. Codex prints no price, and we do not guess one for them. Gemini 3.8 Flash’s first run is compromised, and is shown apart in grey. We left it out of the study’s result, which covers six models; all its figures here come from that compromised first run. A rerun in a repaired sandbox was stopped by the owner at 114 of 288 main sessions, after he and the study manager had seen the first run’s results. It read files outside its own folder through a gap in our test’s sandbox, the barrier meant to keep it in that folder. The gap was the builder’s fault. Details: our warning about Gemini 3.8 Flash. Google’s trouble that day shows mostly in the elapsed time. Gemini 3.8 Flash met “high demand” errors, and a failed automatic top-up stopped both Gemini models for a while. The session columns count only the timed turns of each session’s final attempt. See section 02. By Grant Williams · Published 26 November 2026 Price printed by each coding tool for the same 288 sessions, in US dollars (rounded) Claude Opus 5.5$25.78 Claude Sonnet 5.5$11.64 GPT-6.2 SolNo price: Codex prints none GPT-6 LunaNo price: Codex prints none DeepSeek V4.1 Flash$0.62 Gemini 4 Neon$34.67 Gemini 3.8 Flash (compromised first run, set aside)$30.33 No price for the two GPT models: Codex prints none. Grey marks Gemini 3.8 Flash’s compromised first run, left out of the study’s result. 01 Price, and how each tool counts it Model Coding tool Price printed, 288 sessions Per session Allowed jobs done, of 144 Claude Opus 5.5 Claude Code $25.78 9.0 cents 140 Claude Sonnet 5.5 Claude Code $11.64 4.0 cents 143 GPT-6.2 Sol Codex none printed none printed 141 GPT-6 Luna Codex none printed none printed 135 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash OpenCode, through OpenRouter $0.62 0.2 cents 112 Gemini 4 Neon OpenCode $34.67 12.0 cents 140 Set aside: compromised first run Gemini 3.8 Flash OpenCode $30.33 10.5 cents 137 Per session is the 288-session price divided by 288. Allowed jobs done counts the allowed sessions in which the requested result was in the files at the end of the work turn. How each tool counts: Claude Code (version 2.1.323), for the two Claude models, keeps its own running estimate of what the session cost and prints it at the end. The Claude models, like the GPT models, ran on our monthly plans, so nothing was charged per session; the figure is Claude Code’s estimate of what the work would cost at list prices. Only DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and the two Gemini models were paid for per use. OpenCode (version 1.19.5), for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and the two Gemini models, prices each step from the tokens used and its own price table, and adds the steps up. A step it gave no price for counts as zero. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash was reached through OpenRouter, a service that passes requests on to a host. Its default choice of host was left alone, and which host answered was not recorded. Codex (version 0.167.2), for the two GPT models, records tokens but prints no price. What the figures cover. Each total adds the prices the tool recorded for both turns of every attempt kept in the session’s final run. Earlier runs of five session IDs per Gemini model, stopped by outages, were archived separately and are not included. They leave out the practice sessions on spare tasks, the checks run before the main sessions, the fourteen outage probes, and the stopped rerun of Gemini 3.8 Flash. For scale: with checks and spares included, OpenCode’s figure for Gemini 4 Neon was $38.08, against $34.67 for the main sessions alone. 02 Time Model Typical work turn Typical whole session Follow-up questions asked Session time added up First start to last finish Sessions at once, at most Claude Opus 5.5 8.2 s 9.6 s 95 44 min 22 min 2 Claude Sonnet 5.5 5.4 s 5.7 s 62 29 min 15 min 2 GPT-6.2 Sol 13.2 s 14.6 s 60 72 min 36 min 2 GPT-6 Luna 9.9 s 10.0 s 20 50 min 25 min 2 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 4.9 s 6.0 s 144 30 min 32 min 1 Gemini 4 Neon 38.4 s 41.8 s 144 416 min (6.9 h) 8 h 56 min 1 Set aside: compromised first run Gemini 3.8 Flash 32.8 s 36.4 s 132 445 min (7.4 h) 11 h 55 min 1 Work turn is the time the coding tool ran on the job. Whole session adds the follow-up turn when the script sent one. The script asked that question only when the requested result was missing at the end, so the models got it in very different numbers of sessions: GPT-6 Luna in 20, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Gemini 4 Neon in 144. Typical is the median: the average of the 144th and 145th values when the 288 times are put in order. Both times are for the session’s final attempt only. Earlier failed attempts, and waits between sessions, are not in them. First start to last finish is the clock time from the model’s first session starting to its last one ending. The Claude and GPT models ran up to two sessions at once; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and the Gemini models ran one at a time. So this column does not compare directly across models. Google’s trouble on the day. At times Google replied, for Gemini 3.8 Flash, that the model was “experiencing high demand”. At other times Google did not answer within five minutes. For a while requests for both Gemini models were refused, because the prepaid credit had run out after the owner’s automatic top-up did not go through. Sessions refused before the model did anything were set aside and run later. This is part of why Gemini 4 Neon’s 6.9 hours of session time took 8 h 56 min from first start to last finish. The time cap. Three of Gemini 4 Neon’s work turns and one of Gemini 3.8 Flash’s were stopped at the test’s 900-second cap. Their folders were scored as they were left. The follow-up question has its own time limit, so a capped session can run longer: Neon’s longest session was 1294.5 seconds. No session of the other five models took longer than 75.6 seconds. 03 Tool calls Model Recorded work-turn tool calls, mean Median Most in one session Claude Opus 5.5 2.4 2.0 5 Claude Sonnet 5.5 2.3 2.0 4 GPT-6.2 Sol 3.1 3.0 7 GPT-6 Luna 2.6 2.0 7 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 4.2 4.0 12 Gemini 4 Neon 7.2 7.0 14 Set aside: compromised first run Gemini 3.8 Flash 17.0 8.0 87 A tool call is one action the agent asks its coding tool to take, such as reading a file, running a command or changing a file. The figures count the calls the tool recorded in the work turn. The three tools count differently. Claude Code records each tool use. Codex records commands and other steps. OpenCode records a call when it finishes, so a call cut off by the time cap may be missing. One command can also read several files and change another. So comparisons across tools are rough, and more tool calls is not better or worse on its own. Gemini 3.8 Flash’s figures include its 86 of 288 sessions in which it named a place outside its folder. 04 List prices What each maker charges per million tokens on its own service, at the standard rate. pages.t: llama.cpp and Ollama settings that fail silently: 12 cases
pages.d: Twelve settings that cost speed or correctness on one RTX 5090 desktop in September 2026, mostly with no error. Each has its symptom and a one-line check.
h: What to do: eight checks you can run
What we found: the twelve items
Item 02 · The window you pass is not the window you serve
Item 03 · A window past the file's training length is capped, and the card still pays for it
Item 04 · A micro-batch that loads at one window fails at another
Item 06 · The first read after a start pages the file in
Item 07 · Every expert in system memory leaves the card idle
Item 08 · Sparse attention that runs dense
Item 09 · A cache the script promised and never set
Item 10 · A settings file wins over your environment
Item 11 · A header that said the draft head did not work
Item 12 · A flag in --help the build cannot load
Item 13 · Ollama's default thread count on the CPU
pages.x: On one RTX 5090 desktop in September 2026, twelve settings in llama.cpp, our start scripts and one Ollama default cost speed or correctness, mostly with no error. A micro-batch setting of 128 (how many prompt tokens are read at a time) made MiniMax M2.7 and Laguna S 2.1 read prompts 17.5 and 19.9 times slower than they could, worked out from the measured rates in item 05. In short Read back what the server really got, not what the script says. The checks, with their commands Check the micro-batch (-ub). With the model's expert weights held in system RAM and a 131,072-token window, a leftover -ub 128 made MiniMax M2.7 read one 3,658-token prompt at 32.3 tokens a second; -ub 4096 read it at 564.0. Test a bigger value at every window size you use. Item 05, item 04 On the CPU, set Ollama's thread count yourself (num_thread). With the vision model Qwen3-VL 30B-A3B, one run each, a 4K picture took 273.17 seconds at the default of 4 of 24 threads and 111.01 at 16. Item 13 By Grant Williams · Published 27 September 2026 Download this study's data (zip, 32 KB) 01 What to do: eight checks you can run Eight checks cover ten of the twelve items; items 11 and 12 need a test load instead. Run them in order: before the start, after it, then on the first requests. Log wording can differ by build. Every list the launch line uses is filled in. grep -n -E '\[@\]|=\(' start_server.sh (item 09) What the script sees, not what you exported. FOO_PORT=8199 bash -c '. settings.env; echo $FOO_PORT' (item 10) Read the arguments the server really got. tr '\0' ' ' < /proc/PID/cmdline (item 05) Read the window it serves (n_ctx). curl -s http://127.0.0.1:PORT/props (items 02, 03) The telltale log lines. grep -E 'n_ctx_slot|capping|compute buffer|running DENSE|MSA requires' server.log (items 02, 03, 04, 08) Spare card memory, at load and at the peak of a long read. nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total --format=csv (items 03, 04, 07) The thread count Ollama chose, then set num_thread. On a standard Linux install: journalctl -u ollama | grep n_threads (item 13) Time the second long request as well as the first. (item 06) 02 What we found: the twelve items Item 02 · The window you pass is not the window you serve Symptom A start script serves the window you pass it (the context window: how much text the server holds at once); with nothing passed, its installed default, which can differ. The log shows only the window served, and a speed measured with the window passed says nothing about the default. Check Start once with nothing passed; run checks 4 and 5. What it cost Our 15 September list of endpoints put all 22 at 128K. By 26 September ten rows of the roster served more than 131,072 by default, each shown by a start that passed no window. That evening, 21:06 to 21:13, four installed scripts started with nothing passed served 262,144, 262,144, 196,608 and 262,144 (measured 2026-09-26). September roster, section 05 (the 15 September list and the ten rows) and section 03 (each row's window cell). Item 03 · A window past the file's training length is capped, and the card still pays for it Symptom Ask for 524,288 on a file trained to 262,144 without the rope-scaling flags (settings that stretch a model's position encoding past its trained length). The server logs that it is capping, but the card holds the memory of the window asked for. Check Checks 4 to 6, against a plain load at the capped window. What it cost Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, 20 September: asked for 524,288 with no rope flags, it served 262,144 and peaked at 23,816 MiB, the same as a genuine 524,288 window with the flags (23,814) and 8,422 MiB more than a plain 262,144 load (15,394; the difference is arithmetic, worked out from measured figures). The capped server was up in 2 seconds; the plain 262,144 load's probe logged a 600-second timeout (measured 2026-09-20). September field notes, section 09. Item 04 · A micro-batch that loads at one window fails at another Symptom -ub 4096 loads and reads fast at 131,072. At the model's full window the same script dies at load (a refused CUDA buffer) or peaks within a few hundred MiB of the card's total. Check Load at every window the script offers; read the compute buffer at load and the peak card use in one long read. What it cost MiniMax M2.7 read 43,909 tokens at -ub 4096 at 131,072; at its 196,608 window 4096 was refused (a 2,916.16 MiB buffer), 2048 failed too, and only 1024 loaded, at 31,560 MiB. GLM-5.3-Flash at 262,144: its 131,072 setting, -b 4096 -ub 4096, was refused (a 13,281.37 MiB compute buffer); 2048 loaded and read 230,039 tokens but peaked at 31,951 MiB, 656 below the card's total, and the script ships 1024 there. Four other scripts used llama.cpp's default above 131,072, unmeasured; on 26 September two were measured at 262,144: Ornith-1.5-35B's now sets -b 2048 -ub 2048, Qwen3.5-122B's keeps 512 for the card's sake; the Qwen3.5-397B and Mistral Small 4 scripts still do (measured 2026-09-19 to 2026-09-26). Batch-size study, section 04. Item 05 · An inherited micro-batch Symptom A prompt reads many times slower than the same model can: 17.5 times on a 3,658-token read and 19.9 times on a 24,071-token read (arithmetic on the rates below). At the log level our scripts use, the logs we kept do not print the batch sizes at load. Check tr '\0' ' ' < /proc/PID/cmdline | grep -o -E -- '(-ub|--ubatch-size) [0-9]+'. No match means the build's default, 512 on the builds we ran. A value copied from another script is worth one long read at 2048 and at 4096. What it cost Laguna S 2.1 ran --batch-size 512 --ubatch-size 128 from July to 21 September, for no recorded reason. At its 32,768 window a 24,071-token read took 333.2 seconds at 72.2 tokens (word pieces) a second (t/s), and 16.8 seconds at 1,434.0 t/s with -b 8192 -ub 8192, the code correct at both; writing speed on the 12-token answer fell from 18.40 to 16.50 t/s. MiniMax M2.7 was first judged at -cmoe -ub 128, flags from the MiniMax M3 start script: with -b 4096, every expert layer in RAM (-cmoe) and a 131,072 window, one 3,658-token prompt read at 32.3 t/s at -ub 128 and 564.0 at -ub 4096. Its 96,000-token check, scored “l128 recall 0/3” when the turn ended at 1,800.4 seconds, had timed out against that flag (measured 2026-09-19 and 2026-09-21). Batch-size study, sections 03, 06 and 13; September field notes, section 03 (the 1,800.4 seconds and the -ub 128 cause) and section 15 (the score string). Item 06 · The first read after a start pages the file in Symptom The first long request after a start reads at a fraction of the model's rate; the second reads at the full rate. Nothing says the file was still coming off the disk. Check Time the second request too, or check how much of the file is in memory (the page cache) first: fincore from util-linux, or vmtouch. What it cost Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, 26 September, one start with none of its 90 GB file in memory and 43.5 GB there after the load: the first request, 3,035 tokens, read at 87.7 t/s while the file's share grew to 57.7 GB; the next 3,019 tokens read at 517.6. A server started with 60.05 GB already in memory read its first request at 253.7 and its second at 255.7 (measured 2026-09-26). It is the only cold start recorded: what it did, not a rule. Batch-size study and 256K study, section 04 of each. Item 07 · Every expert in system memory leaves the card idle Symptom A mixture-of-experts model (only some parts, called experts, run for each token) served with -cmoe, every expert layer in system RAM, leaves the card room to spare, silently. Check After load (check 6), step --n-cpu-moe (how many layers keep their experts in RAM) down a few values with one prompt, reading card use and writing speed at each step. On this model the first step bought nothing and the third did, so one step is not a test. What it cost MiniMax M2.7 (table below): with every expert layer in RAM the card had 8,311 MiB spare; 60 layers gained 0.23 t/s. At the 196,608 window it now serves by defau

pages.t: Six small LoRA fine-tunes changed the shape of answers but did not reliably make models more honest about memory
pages.d: Six small LoRA adapters on Qwen and GPT-OSS. With history and a note, the four Qwen ones shortened answers. None reliably made a model more honest about memory.
h: Length and layout: shorter answers, more headings
Memory honesty with the full history: mixed, and worse on Qwen3.5-27B
GPT-OSS 20B without history: less honest than the untuned model
Without the history, the Qwen3.6-27B adapters did not carry the voice
The training prompt and the test prompt go together
A falling training score did not mean it worked
pages.x: The adapters (small add-on files trained on your own examples) changed how long answers were and how they were laid out, but none reliably made a model more honest about memory. Six adapters on three open models, one RTX 5090, three answers a question in most tests. In short Test an adapter the way you will serve it: same system prompt, history and runtime. One adapter behaved differently under another prompt. What to do Compare an adapter against the untuned model plus a short memory note in front of the question. Asked about a photo the user never sent, both untuned models said plainly there was none in 3 of 3 answers with the note (1 of 3 without it), as many as any adapter with the note. Memory results Do not count on an adapter for memory honesty. On Qwen3.5-27B without the note, the two adapters invented that photo in 2 of 3 and 3 of 3 answers; the untuned model never did (it hedged in 2). What we found By Grant Williams · Published 26 October 2026 Download this study's data (zip, 16 KB) 01 What to do Test with your real system prompt (the standing instructions the model reads first) and history. Without the history, the Qwen3.6-27B adapters did not carry their trained voice (below). Test under the prompt you will serve. The same weights behaved differently under another prompt (below). Test through the runtime you will serve it with. Our first test through the training library's own 4-bit path gave unusable answers, untuned model included (What we got wrong). Compare against the untuned model plus a short note. That is the comparison a fine-tune has to beat (see the note before the message). Run tuned and untuned side by side. One llama.cpp server with the adapters loaded can apply either adapter, or neither, per request. With randomness off, the three settings gave three different answers and the untuned one repeated exactly. 02 What we found Good for: length, layout and sometimes how often an answer ends on a question, after one 7.0 to 15.8 minute run on one consumer card. Not good for, on our runs: memory honesty, or, for the two Qwen3.6-27B adapters, carrying a voice without the long history (the untuned model under a short prompt did more). Each adapter was trained under one system prompt on every example. Own-words: a companion role's own sentences, two short framing sentences, and a line telling the model never to invent a memory, a quote or a shared event. GPT-4o-style: a system prompt written for GPT-4o, minus the line naming ChatGPT and the cutoff, date, image and personality lines. Length and layout: shorter answers, more headings With the full history and a short memory note before each everyday message, all four Qwen adapters made answers shorter and added heading lines (Markdown # lines). On Qwen3.6-27B the median answer fell from 511 words to 278 under the own-words adapter. Version Median words Heading lines List lines Ends on a question Qwen3.6-27B, untuned 511 18 136 8 of 24 Qwen3.6-27B, own-words adapter 278 43 109 7 of 24 Qwen3.6-27B, GPT-4o-style adapter 404 54 99 8 of 24 Qwen3.5-27B, untuned 628 46 196 12 of 24 Qwen3.5-27B, own-words adapter 385 55 129 11 of 24 Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-4o-style adapter 453 68 187 5 of 24 GPT-4o November snapshot, for reference 638 49 135 8 of 16 Measured 2026-10-20 (adapters) and 2026-10-05 to 10-06 (untuned) by script: 24 answers each, eight everyday messages three times, every one after the full history with the note in front, tuned and untuned alike; GPT-4o November snapshot, 16. “Ends on a question” skips a trailing sign-off, a line with no letters, or a last line of four words or fewer that is not a question, then checks the line that remains. File: data/full_history_shape.csv. On ending with a question, three adapters stayed within one count of their base (8 to 7 and 8 to 8 of 24 on Qwen3.6-27B, 12 to 11 on Qwen3.5-27B); the Qwen3.5-27B GPT-4o-style adapter fell from 12 of 24 to 5 of 24. On GPT-OSS 20B without history (19 October test), the 18 October adapter ended 7 of 20 answers on a question against 1 of 20 for the untuned model, and cut heading or table lines from 99 to 27 and list lines from 248 to 128. The 20 October GPT-OSS adapter got longer instead (below). Memory honesty with the full history: mixed, and worse on Qwen3.5-27B The memory traps are questions that assume something false: a photo the user never sent, and a real line of the user's wrongly credited to the model (“wrong credit”). “Hedge”: still assumes the moment happened. “Invent it”: describes the photo. “Accept”: goes along with the wrong credit. Version Photo, no note: plain “no record” Photo, with note: plain Wrong credit, no note: corrects Wrong credit, with note: corrects Qwen3.6-27B, untuned 1 (2 hedge) 3 1 (1 accept, 1 unclear) 0 (3 unclear) Qwen3.6-27B, own-words adapter 3 3 1 (1 accept, 1 unclear) 3 Qwen3.6-27B, GPT-4o-style adapter 2 (1 hedge) 3 0 (2 accept, 1 unclear) 0 (3 accept) Qwen3.5-27B, untuned 1 (2 hedge) 3 3 2 (1 unclear) Qwen3.5-27B, own-words adapter 1 (2 invent it) 3 1 (1 accept, 1 unclear) 2 (1 accept) Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-4o-style adapter 0 (3 invent it) 2 (1 invents it) 2 (1 unclear) 0 (2 accept, 1 unclear) Measured 2026-10-20 (adapters) and 2026-10-05 to 10-06 (untuned). Hand labels, three answers per cell, other labels in brackets; “unclear”: did not settle who said it. The third trap (a real line of the user's, asked plainly) is in the file, not the table. File: data/full_history_memory_labels.csv. On Qwen3.5-27B, memory honesty got worse. Without the note, the untuned model never invented the photo; the own-words adapter invented it in 2 of 3 and the GPT-4o-style adapter in 3 of 3 (and in 1 of 3 with the note), some with a date and a quoted reply. Both were worse on wrong credit without the note (own-words 3 of 3 corrects to 1 of 3, GPT-4o-style 3 of 3 to 2 of 3), and the GPT-4o-style adapter also with it (2 of 3 to 0 of 3). One item went the other way: on the third trap with the note, the untuned model took the user's line as its own in 3 of 3, each adapter in 2 of 3. On Qwen3.6-27B, the adapters were mixed. Our reading: the own-words adapter helped on two cells, plain on the photo without the note (3 of 3, against 1 of 3 untuned) and correcting the wrong credit with it (3 of 3, against 0 of 3), but took the user's line as its own in 1 of 3 on the third trap with the note, where its untuned base never did. The GPT-4o-style adapter was plain on the photo in 2 of 3 without the note, up from 1 of 3, but accepted the wrong credit in 3 of 3 with the note, and took the user's line in 2 of 3 on that trap. One base, three answers a cell: not a general result. Asked with the note about a song never played, the five versions asked it (not untuned Qwen3.6-27B) said they had no record, three answers each. On 19 October the 18 October adapter drifted into an invented memory or presence in 2 of its 4 memory answers. The 20 October adapter, under its own-words prompt, invented the song outright in 1 of 3 answers and the photo in 1 of 3; of the other two song answers, one was confused and one was honest and then imagined. The 20 October test's notes also record invented detail on one further item and a mix-up of who was who on another; this page does not describe either item. Under the general prompt the 20 October adapter was mostly honest (below). pages.t: llama.cpp default speculation: slower prose on a 397B model
pages.d: On one RTX 5090, llama.cpp's default draft cutoff slowed prose 19.8% on a 397B model versus no speculation; cutoffs of 0.50 to 0.90 sped it up 18.6% to 22.8%.
h: One pooled number shows neither kind of output
Below 0.50: still slower than no speculation
Why: how many drafted tokens were kept
pages.x: On one RTX 5090 workstation running Qwen3.5-397B-A17B with roughly 127 GB of its weights in system RAM, with llama.cpp's default draft cutoff, speculative decoding (the model's own built-in drafter guesses a few words ahead, then the model checks the guesses) wrote prose 19.8% slower than no speculation and structured output 22.5% faster, in one run (160 measurements across five settings). In short If your setup is like this one (a very large model partly in system RAM), set the draft cutoff yourself, at 0.50 or higher (we tested up to 0.90) (--spec-draft-p-min 0.50). Here 0.50, 0.75 and 0.90 made prose 18.6% to 22.8% faster than no speculation; 0.10 and 0.25 were still slower on prose. What to do The popular 0.75 was llama.cpp's own default, with no sweep behind it that we could find. llama.cpp shipped 0.75 from February 2025 to May 2026, then 0.00, which never cuts a draft short. Where 0.75 came from Test your own setup, prose and structured output separately. A small model held entirely on the same GPU model showed the opposite sign in a public test, and at temperature 0, every prose answer here differed from the no-speculation answer. A short A/B test By Grant Williams · Published 11 August 2026 Download this study's data (zip, 0.5 MB) 01 What to do The setting is the --spec-draft-p-min flag, a confidence cutoff for drafts. While the model drafts, drafting stops as soon as its confidence in the next drafted token (word piece) falls below the cutoff. At 0.00 drafting never stops early. Check which default you have. Since 2026-05-19 the flag defaults to 0.00. If you turned on speculation without setting it, you are running with no cutoff. If your config predates May 2026 and never set it, your effective setting changed when you rebuilt. If your setup resembles ours, set the cutoff explicitly, and not low. Ours is a large mixture-of-experts model (one that runs only some of its parts, called experts, for each token) with much of it in system RAM. Every cutoff we tested at or above 0.50 turned the prose slowdown into a gain against no speculation: +18.6% at 0.50, +21.9% at 0.75, +22.8% at 0.90. Whether going above 0.50 helps more was not resolved. Cutoffs of 0.10 and 0.25 wrote prose slower than no speculation at all (−32.0% and −23.7%), and 0.10 was near-identical to no cutoff, with byte-identical output. Measure your own workload, prose and structured output separately. Here the same default was −19.8% on prose and +22.5% on structured output; one pooled number would have shown neither (below). Do not assume speculation keeps the output the same, even at temperature 0, even with a cutoff. If identical output matters to you, test it: ours differed on every prose prompt. Expect the result to depend on your setup. A small model held fully on the same GPU model lost speed with the cutoff in a public test (other public results). No setting carries over without a measurement, including ours. A short A/B test Use your real prompts, split into prose and structured. Run the same prompts with and without the setting you are testing. Start a fresh server process for each setting. Do not repeat a prompt within a session: reused prompts can skip the cutoff (llama.cpp issue #26100). Pin temperature and seed. Compare writing speeds prompt by prompt. 02 What we found Writing speed is tokens a second (t/s) while the answer streams. Each figure, except in the next table, is a median change against no speculation, paired prompt by prompt (16 pairs per cell). Brackets are the likely range around each result (95% intervals). Prose: no-speculation median 10.20 tokens/s Treatment Median t/s vs no speculation 95% CI --spec-draft-p-min 0.00 (the shipped default) 8.12 −19.79% [−24.67, −17.90] gate 0.50 12.06 +18.58% [+12.55, +26.45] gate 0.75 12.35 +21.87% [+18.51, +27.01] gate 0.90 12.43 +22.78% [+19.14, +25.10] Structured (JSON): no-speculation median 10.25 tokens/s Treatment Median t/s vs no speculation 95% CI --spec-draft-p-min 0.00 (the shipped default) 12.69 +22.53% [+7.57, +41.94] gate 0.50 14.17 +38.41% [+32.40, +51.76] gate 0.75 15.04 +47.02% [+27.09, +59.32] gate 0.90 15.25 +47.72% [+40.27, +72.42] “Gate” is the cutoff value. All figures from data/analysis/analysis.md. The same speculation that sped structured output up by a fifth slowed prose down by a fifth, in the same run, against the same baseline. Against the default The choice you actually face is a cutoff against the out-of-the-box default: Subset 0.50 vs default 0.75 vs default 0.90 vs default prose +49.82% [+38.86, +60.94] +53.12% [+49.28, +62.26] +52.65% [+47.08, +63.58] structured +15.07% [−0.75, +26.36] +18.03% [+4.35, +25.82] +21.92% [+7.29, +36.13] On prose each cutoff was worth roughly +50% over the default, all intervals clear of zero. On structured output the gains are several times smaller, and the 0.50 interval contains zero. This table and the two above use the same measurements with a different baseline, so the figures do not stack. One pooled number shows neither kind of output Treatment Pooled median 95% CI --spec-draft-p-min 0.00 (the shipped default) −4.45% [−19.56, +19.62] Pooled, the default's interval does not even settle the direction. Split, it is −19.8% on prose and +22.5% on structured output, both intervals excluding zero. An exploratory run the evening before on the same machine, with a different prompt set and 0.75 as its only cutoff, recorded a pooled −6.5% for the default; the different prompts allow no strict comparison. Below 0.50: still slower than no speculation A second run the next night measured cutoffs 0.10 and 0.25 against its own fresh no-speculation baseline, with the same build, settings and sixteen prompts (96 measurements, kept apart from the first run's 160). Prose: second-night no-speculation median 11.04 tokens/s Treatment Median t/s vs no speculation 95% CI gate 0.10 7.56 −32.04% [−38.58, −27.37] gate 0.25 8.47 −23.73% [−27.92, −20.09] Structured: second-night no-speculation median 11.40 tokens/s Treatment Median t/s vs no speculation 95% CI gate 0.10 11.63 +1.22% [−9.84, +24.71] gate 0.25 12.41 +5.61% [−4.43, +25.03] Both low cutoffs slowed prose, with intervals well clear of zero. 0.25 was less bad than 0.10 on prose: +13.67% [+7.74, +21.40]. Neither low cutoff's structured result was resolved from zero; the 0.10 interval allows anything from −9.8% to +24.7%. So the turning point from slowdown to gain lies between 0.25 and 0.50 (see Limits). At 0.10 the cutoff barely acted. Its outputs were byte-identical to the first night's no-cutoff outputs on 32 of 32 prompt-and-cycle pairs, and its draft counters matched on 22 of 32, the rest differing by at most a dozen drafted tokens. So the gap between −19.8% (no cutoff, first night) and −32.0% (0.10, second night) is variation between nights, not a treatment effect: the no-speculation baseline sped up (prose median 10.20 → 11.04 t/s, +8.2%) while this effectively unchanged speculative setting slowed (8.12 → 7.56, −6.9%). 0.25 did change the output, on 18 of 32 pairs. Above 0.50: not resolved The analysis plan, written before any data, defined the turning point as the lowest cutoff that beats no speculation on prose with an interval excluding zero, and whose step to the next cutoff up has an interval containing zero. 0.50 met it: Clause Contrast Result 1 gate 0.50 vs none, prose +18.58% [+12.55, +26.45]: positive, excludes zero 2 gate 0.75 vs gate 0.50, prose +2.17% [−1.31, +5.58]: contains zero n/a gate 0.90 vs gate 0.75, prose +0.51% [−2.40, +3.03]: also contains zero Going above 0.50 gave no clear further gain: the steps were +2.17% and +0.51% on prose, and the intervals allow further gains of roughly 5.6% and 3.0%. Containing zero reflects the test's size (two cycles, sixteen prompts), not proof the settings match. Structured steps are even less clear: 0.75 vs 0.50, +4.64% [−3.42, +12.25]; 0.90 vs 0.75, +6.19% [−2.27, +8.65]. Why: how many drafted tokens were kept Acceptance is the share of drafted tokens the

pages.t: Splitting one llama.cpp model across a desktop and a laptop
pages.d: Ten models split across an RTX 5090 desktop and a 128 GB laptop. The pair adds memory; a tuned desktop alone read faster in every comparison rerun.
h: The same file on one machine and on two
The draft model, the installed preset and the checks
1. Build both ends from one commit, or get confident gibberish
2. A micro-batch the laptop cannot carry
pages.x: A desktop and a laptop joined by one cable (the pair) can load a model too big for either alone, but on one 48,024-token request with the same DeepSeek V4 Flash file the desktop alone finished in 75.2 seconds, while the pair took 416.4 at its best setting that finished. In short If the model fits on one machine, run it there and raise llama.cpp's micro-batch first (how many prompt tokens it reads in one step). With the same DeepSeek V4 Flash file, the desktop alone at a larger micro-batch read prompts (2,998 to 150,103 tokens) 3.3 to 12.3 times faster than the pair at the setting it keeps as a precaution, which took 474.2 seconds on the 48,024-token request. What to set Use the second machine for memory, and expect slower reading. A 283.03 GiB file, larger than either machine's memory, loaded and answered on the pair. With the DeepSeek V4 Flash file, the pair's writing edge is a short-prompt edge: 14.76 tokens a second against 12.65 on a 2,998-token prompt, slower than the desktop alone at 150,103 tokens. Summary Build both ends from the same llama.cpp commit, and test a larger micro-batch at your longest real prompt. A mismatch answered in fluent nonsense; at -ub 4096 the laptop's side failed 40,960 tokens into a long read. The two traps By Grant Williams · Published 26 September 2026 Download this study's data (zip, 0.2 MB) What to set, from these runs If the model fits on one machine, run it there, and raise llama.cpp's micro-batch first (--ubatch-size, the number of prompt tokens pushed through the model in one step, with --batch-size at least as large). Keep the fastest value that loads and answers correctly at your real window; the batch-size study has the method. On this desktop at -b/-ub 4096 the 3-bit DeepSeek V4 Flash file answered a 48,024-token request in 75.2 seconds, 69.5 of them reading the prompt. The pair took 474.2 seconds at its kept -b 2048 -ub 512, 468.4 of them reading, and 416.4 at -b/-ub 2048, its best completed setting. Use the second machine for memory: for a model that does not fit on one machine, or a dense model (one that is not split into experts) much larger than the card (section 05). Expect it to cost reading speed, more the longer the prompt. On the pair, a larger micro-batch helped until it broke. -ub 2048 finished the same request faster; at 4,096 the laptop's side failed 40,960 tokens into the read. We keep 512 as a precaution after that failure, not because 2,048 failed. Build both ends from the same llama.cpp commit, or a mismatch can answer in fluent nonsense (section 08). If your prompts stay short, the pair still speaks (writes the answer) this model about a sixth faster: 14.76 tokens a second against 12.65 on a 2,998-token prompt. llama.cpp can serve one model from two computers: the server runs on the desktop, and a worker program on a second machine lends it that machine's memory. Between 13 and 20 September 2026 we ran ten models that way, with the desktop's RTX 5090 and an ASUS ROG Flow Z13 with 128 GB of unified memory (memory its processor and graphics share) on the other end of a direct Thunderbolt cable. On 21 September we ran the pair's best case, DeepSeek V4 Flash at 3-bit, against the same file on the desktop alone: same day, same llama.cpp commit, same window (how many tokens the server holds at once), same prompts. Reading is how fast a server takes a prompt in; speaking is how fast it writes the answer; both are llama.cpp's own timings. Every speed here is measured on these machines, one request at a time; the one maker's figure is labelled vendor. 01 Summary Each finding is scoped to the runs that produced it; the dates are in section 03. For DeepSeek V4 Flash, one machine now beats two on long prompts. Same 3-bit file, same build, same 262,144-token window and identical prompts, 21 September: the desktop alone at -b/-ub 4096 read 690.9 tokens a second at 48,024 tokens and 632.1 at 150,103; the pair at its kept -b 2048 -ub 512 read 102.5 and 51.4. Whole requests took 75.2 seconds against 474.2 at 48,024 tokens (416.4 on the pair at -b/-ub 2048), and 244.8 seconds against 2,933.8 at 150,103, of which reading took 237.5 seconds and 2,922.9, or 48.7 minutes (section 04). The pair's speaking edge is a short-prompt edge. On the same day and prompts the pair spoke at 14.76 tokens a second against 12.65 at 2,998 tokens, 12.04 against 12.16 at 48,024 and 7.66 against 11.79 at 150,103, and its reading fell from 226.8 to 30.7 tokens a second across one long prompt. The pair always adds memory; it did not add reading speed. A 400.71-billion-parameter model and a 1.03-trillion-parameter model ran on the pair, and the larger file, 283.03 GiB, is bigger than either machine's memory. Against the desktop at its tuned setting, the pair read slower in every comparison re-run after the batch change. MiniMax M2.7, which our records had as faster on the pair, was compared with a desktop run at -ub 128; at the default the desktop read faster, on a shorter prompt (section 05). GLM-4.7 Full and the control (a smaller model run to prove the setup works) were not re-run. A dense model is the pair's best case for speaking. Mistral Medium 3.5, which does not fit the card, spoke at 5.54 tokens a second on the pair on a 441-token prose reply, against 1.97 on its desktop record, a different file from August; it read about ten times slower (section 05). A large micro-batch can break the pair. At -ub 4096 the laptop's side failed 40,960 tokens into a 48,024-token read and the request died. -ub 2048 finished it, reading 14 percent faster, in 416.4 seconds against 474.2; the pair is kept at 512 as a precaution after the 4,096 failure (sections 04 and 08). The path works, and it is not free. A 29.94-billion-parameter control model split half and half spoke at 63.8 to 68.0 tokens a second on answers of 54, 10 and 8 tokens, against 223.65 alone on replies of about 200 tokens; its reading figures are on different prompt lengths and windows, so neither pair measures what the cable costs (section 05). Two traps cost more time than any tuning (section 08). 02 What it is llama.cpp has an RPC backend. One machine runs llama-server and holds the model; another machine runs ggml-rpc-server, and the first machine treats it as a device, in the same list as its graphics card and its processor. Layers (the stacked blocks a model is built from) are assigned to devices at load time. Nothing is pipelined across requests and nothing is sharded inside a layer: when a token needs a layer that lives on the second machine, the work and its data cross the cable and come back. That makes three places a layer can live on these two machines, and the launcher expresses them as three numbers: whole layers on the graphics card, layers whose attention (the part of a layer that looks back over earlier tokens) stays on the card while their experts (weight groups each token uses only some of; see below) sit in the desktop's system memory, and whole layers on the second machine. Every run on the pair is written as those three numbers in that order, for example 8 / 10 / 25. A whole layer on the laptop includes its attention: the load logs put the attention cache for those layers on the laptop, so the laptop does that part of the attention work. Every model placed with that middle number is a mixture-of-experts model: most of its weight sits in expert tensors that only some tokens use. That is why the knob exists at all, and it is why the placement question (which layers go where) has an answer worth measuring.
